News.title: Zelensky lashes out at EU
News.content:
Volodymyr Zelensky lashed out at the European Union over its moves to weaken sanctions on Russian oligarchs.

In his address to the UN General Assembly, the Ukrainian leader warned that beyond making life “more comfortable” for Russians, “it also gives the war more time for Putin to send poor people into the kill zone. So Russia’s revenues must remain a target.”

His criticism came after France and Luxembourg successfully pushed for sanctions exemptions for Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, Russian oligarchs, on Tuesday.

Kyiv branded the decision “shameful and unjustifiable”. The men are known to share close ties to Vladimir Putin and have net worths of $14bn and $16bn, respectively.

In his fourth address to the UN as a wartime leader, Mr Zelensky said it was paramount that the international community increased pressure on the Kremlin to stop “the madness” of the war spreading.

Under pressure from Donald Trump to halt attacks on Russian energy targets, Mr Zelensky defended his country’s aerial offensive for successfully depriving Putin of revenue for his war.

“When someone gives Russia more money through trade, they give this war more time. And that is exactly why we insist on limiting trade with the aggressor, and why we are burning Russia’s revenues ourselves,” he said.

‘End the war before winter’

Washington has recently attempted to revive the long-stalled negotiations between Ukraine and Russia. On Tuesday, Mr Zelensky implored Mr Trump to help Kyiv end the war “before winter”.

Mr Trump appeared optimistic, suggesting an agreement would happen “more quickly than people understand”.

Sergei Lavrov, the Russian foreign minister, told the UN Security Council on Wednesday that Russia was prepared to negotiate for a lasting peace but would not “pause the war”.

Mr Zelensky sought to remind world leaders that the conflict was not constrained within Ukraine’s borders at a time when the global community was distracted by a myriad of conflicts and crises.

Citing the support of Iran and North Korea for Russia, he warned that Putin’s war kept “spreading further”.

“Putin is always looking for someone who can help him kill more, kill more people for every kilometre of land, take more territory and take another country instead of simply stopping and running his own country,” Mr Zelensky said at the UN.

He noted that fighters from at least 47 countries were helping to prosecute Moscow’s war against Ukraine and urged leaders to prevent their citizens from being dragged into the conflict.

After Mr Zelensky’s address, reports emerged that Kirill Dmitriev, Putin’s envoy, was on his way to the US where he would meet Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, the Trump administration representatives.

Sources told Reuters that the meeting would take place in New ‌York on the sidelines of the UN summit.

Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, also confirmed Mr Trump had invited his Russian counterpart to attend the G20 summit of world leaders in Miami in December.

News.title: Male contraceptives could hit pharmacies in ‘three to five years’, says WHO
News.content:
Game-changing contraceptives for men could be on pharmacy shelves as soon as 2029, according to the World Health Organization.

Speaking to the Telegraph, Dr James Kiarie, head of the UN agency’s contraception and fertility care unit, said he expects male birth control to be available in just a few years, in a major expansion of contraceptive options for men.

“In three to five years, we will actually have a method available, [so] men can be more than supporters of their female partners in using contraception – men can actually be users,” he said.

On Tuesday, the WHO released its first Target Product Profiles (TPPs) for these products, setting out guidelines for the desired and minimum standards any male contraceptive product must meet.

“[The TPPs] signals that this is a priority issue for the WHO,” said Dr Kiarie.

“Currently men do not have much option in terms of their contraceptive methods. They have to either use condoms… [or] they have to use withdrawal, which has a high failure rate, or they have to use vasectomy, which is a permanent method.”

At the moment, the most advanced new product is called NES/T. It is a daily hormonal gel that is applied to the shoulders and upper arms, and suppresses sperm production without affecting testosterone levels.

Other candidates include injectable hydrogels that block sperm travel, an approach that has been described as a “reversible vasectomy”. ADAM, developed by Contraline, is in phase 1 trials while Next Life Sciences is set to trial a similar product called Plan A.

A third option is YCT-529 – the first non-hormonal, daily male birth control pill. It is currently in phase 1b and 2a clinical trials.

Dr Kiarie said it was important to have multiple options as “there’s no one size fits all” approach, but warned development could take longer than five years if clinical trials face unexpected hurdles.

News.title: England learn more in scrappy Sri Lanka win than in summer of white-ball walkovers
News.content:
You do not expect spinners to dominate at Chester-le-Street, but this hot summer has produced strange events, none more so than Jacks recording the second-best figures by an England spinner in one-day international cricket having previously only taken three wickets in 16 games at home.

Sachindu Colombage, Sri Lanka’s debutant leggie who was playing club cricket in East Anglia a year ago, laid down a marker as he impressed with three for 44 starting with the wicket of Root, his first dismissal in one-day international cricket since February.

England’s 89-run win was completed by Jacks taking three for none in four balls as Sri Lanka were bowled out for 176, their run chase a timid effort when they had a sniff of victory after restricting England to 265 and preventing them from hitting a six for the first time in an innings since 2019.

Vice-captain Jacks has evolved under Harry Brook’s leadership from an opening batsman to middle-order finisher who can chip in with the ball. “He is just a good leader with bat ball and in the field. He is buying into everything we want to do,” Brook said. “We are always talking about adapting to conditions and he has done it really well since coming back in. He could have moaned and groaned about batting in the middle order and playing as an all-rounder but has accepted that will be his place for a long time.”

Brook thought England made “just about par” on a very dry pitch and was reluctant to shower too much praise on batting consultant Kevin Pietersen, whose spin class the day before concentrated on making runs on a slow surface. “It will take time, more than one day. He’s not a miracle worker but it helps the more opportunity we get,” Brook said.

England were stretched and Pietersen will be happy. He told them to think about their approach, that in this type of game “rotation of strike is incredibly important”. He was right, they ran well, apart from Rehan Ahmed, and did not hit a six in an innings for the first time in seven years.

When England batsmen tried to force the pace they perished. Ben Duckett, Root and Brook all had opportunities to build an innings without seeing it through and it required Jacks to tip the total to more than 250. He batted within himself at first, but hit four fours in a row in the 47th over in a late burst that took England to a winning score.

News.title: Africa faces new threat as chronic disease rate leaps
News.content:
Chronic ailments like heart disease, cancers and diabetes now account for almost half of deaths in Africa and will soon overtake the continent’s infectious disease toll, new research has found.

Between 1990 and 2023 the proportion of deaths caused by non-communicable diseases (NCDs) almost doubled, from 25 per cent to 45 per cent, with heart disease and strokes now the leading killers.

The shift is not unexpected: public health experts have long warned that although African countries are making huge strides cutting infectious disease deaths through vaccinations, better sanitation and improved healthcare, lifestyle changes pose a new threat.

But the continent is not necessarily ready to tackle this “epidemiological transition”, researchers warned, in a study published in the Lancet Global Health journal on Tuesday.

“Although the epidemiological transition is well recognised, the speed and scale of NCD growth in Africa is particularly concerning,” they wrote.

“Health systems face increasing demands for chronic disease management, yet low-resource settings remain poorly equipped, underfunded, and unable to provide adequate preventive or treatment services.”

News.title: Zika mosquitoes still breeding in London
News.content:
Dr Medlock said there is still “no conclusive” evidence about how the insects arrived, but it’s possible that someone brought them back from holiday in their luggage, or that mosquito eggs were hidden on a tropical plant.

The mosquitoes are very temperature sensitive – they typically survive and multiply between 25C and 30C – and the UK has historically been too cold. But the species are gradually making their way north through Europe, after successive summers of record heat.

As temperatures drop in the coming weeks, the UKHSA hopes London’s invasive mosquitoes will die off naturally – though an unprecedented El Niño has made the predicament more challenging.

“This is a tropical mosquito, so the model has convinced me this won’t survive the winter,” Dr Medlock said. “Although we’ve got El Niño, [so] it’s very mild – it’s certainly warm enough still in East London [for the insects to survive].”

Diseases such as dengue and Zika virus do not typically circulate in Britain, but an infected traveller returning from a country where the diseases are present could carry the virus back with them.

If an invasive mosquito then bit an infected person, it could potentially catch and spread on the disease to others.

Several countries in Europe, including France, Italy and Spain, have started to see local transmission of mosquito-borne viruses, including dengue fever and West Nile virus, in recent years as the climate becomes more suitable for mosquitoes to survive and multiply.

Just last week, a third person died in Frankfurt, Germany, from malaria despite having no travel history, after mosquitoes infected with the disease were imported into the country on an aeroplane and subsequently infected eight people over the summer.

“We [already] see imported cases of malaria, dengue and chikungunya each year, with significant associated mortality and morbidity,” Dr Phillip Veal, a consultant in public health at the UKHSA, said.

“But if we [in Britain] follow the pattern of Europe, and all models suggest we will, Aedes albopictus and other Aedes species may become established. We’ve got a window of opportunity to do something, to prepare, to be ready, to fulfil our mission of protecting the public,” Dr Veal said.

Protect yourself and your family by learning more about Global Health Security

News.title: Tax rises ‘virtually inevitable’ after £8bn borrowing blow
News.content:
Tax rises are “virtually inevitable” after official figures showed the Treasury has borrowed £8bn more than expected so far this year.

Economists said the Chancellor faced an “uncomfortable” Budget after the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said spending outstripped tax receipts by £18.3bn in August, £3.5bn more than expected.

It means John Healey, the Chancellor, has borrowed £77.3bn so far this financial year, which is £8.1bn more than forecast.

Reacting to the figures, Emma Reynolds, the Chief Secretary to the Treasury, warned of “tough decisions” in Mr Healey’s Budget.

Thomas Pugh, chief economist at RSM UK, said: “The jump in borrowing in August compared to last year sets the stage for what is likely to be a much trickier Budget than Andy Burnham or Healey anticipated when they came to power.

“Another round of tax rises in October now looks inevitable.”

Philip Shaw, an economist at Investec, added: “We suspect that some tax increases are virtually inevitable.”

Ruth Gregory, deputy chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said the Chancellor would need to raise up to £14bn to restore the £24bn of fiscal headroom left by his predecessor Rachel Reeves to balance the books.

The Government’s debt interest bill soared to £8.8bn last month, according to the ONS, the biggest August figure since records began in 1997.

So far this year, the Treasury has spent £50bn on debt interest – £2bn more than forecast in March.

Nick Ridpath, an economist at the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said: “Debt interest spending is a worryingly large share of overall government spending.

“Both higher borrowing costs and higher inflation make life harder for a Chancellor who is looking to bring down borrowing and to spend more on government priorities.”

Higher prices caused by the Iran war mean the Chancellor must pay more interest on the country’s huge stock of inflation-linked debt.

Inflation is also pushing up the welfare bill. The Government spent almost £30bn in August on benefits, 7pc more than a year ago.

Despite this, the Treasury continued to see substantial tax receipts. Income tax, capital gains, and National Insurance receipts stood at £231bn in the financial year to August.

That is £16.6bn higher than the same period a year ago.

Inheritance tax receipts also grew. They have risen to £3.8bn so far this financial year, a £100m increase compared with a year ago.

Ms Reynolds, the Treasury minister, said: “At a time when debt interest costs billions of pounds that could otherwise be spent on improving lives, we must always know where the money is coming from to pay for public services.

“That is why we are committed to meeting our fiscal rules with a buffer against uncertainty.”

The figures also showed total debt rose to £2.985tn in August, taking the level just shy of £3tn.

Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, said: “Labour has lost control of the public finances.

“It takes a rare fiscal incontinence to have both the highest tax take in history and see borrowing still shoot up.”

News.title: France releases infertile Asian tiger mosquitoes to fight dengue threat
News.content:
French cities are fighting the growing threat of diseases like dengue, chikungunya and Zika in mainland Europe by releasing millions of sterile male Asian tiger mosquitoes.

Terratis, a new company in the southern city of Montpellier, is breeding infertile males on an industrial scale as a long-term solution to the rapid spread of the disease-carrying insects.

The sterile males are bred at a factory in the southern city of Montpellier and then released in urban hot zones where the mosquitoes are most prevalent. After they have mated, females reproduce only empty eggs for the remainder of their lives.

“By using this technique, the mosquitoes will have no descendants and then, in theory, we can reduce the population with each generation,” said Clelia Oliva, the founder of Terratis.

“We are confident of being able to achieve a reduction of between 70 and 90 per cent in the towns in which we are releasing the sterile mosquitoes.”

The company, which started only two years ago, has experienced a dramatic surge in demand in the last few years as France tries to deal with the invasive species.

Sports.title: Ex-England star claims Cole Palmer’s withdrawal from Thomas Tuchel’s squad ‘smells like sour grapes’
Sports.content:
Next

A FORMER England striker says Cole Palmer’s withdrawal from Thomas Tuchel’s squad “smells like sour grapes”.

The Chelsea star was surprisingly left out of the German coach’s World Cup squad this summer.



Palmer responded with a stunning start to the Premier League season and earned a recall to the Three Lions fold last week.

The attacker, 24, played the full 90 minutes of Chelsea‘s 3-0 defeat at Brentford on Friday but pulled out of Nations League action for his country due to a minor muscle problem.



The move was described as a precautionary measure – but Kevin Phillips believes there could be more in.

The ex-forward, who only won eight caps despite his goals for Sunderland earning him the European Golden Shoe in 2000, told BestBettingSites.co.uk: “It’s amazing, really, isn’t it?

“He played every minute against Brentford and then comes out a couple of days later saying he’s got a muscle injury. So who knows what’s going on there?

“For me, it maybe smells a little bit of not being picked for the squad in the summer. Maybe a little bit of, I don’t know, just obviously a bit of disappointment there.

“It is a strange one, because I’ve listened to people talk about it and I was exactly the same. Not once did I ever, ever not want to be in that England squad, even when I knew I wasn’t going to be playing. It’s the pride to play for your country.

“So for me, it smells a little bit of sour grapes that he didn’t get in the England squad during the summer.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

“It’s disappointing, because we know what a good player he is. He’s had an okay start to the season. So yeah, it’s disappointing. Of course, no one wants to see that.”

Palmer was not the only star to withdraw for Tuchel‘s latest squad. Declan Rice, Kobbie Mainoo, Marcus Rashford and Tino Livramento are also all unavailable for the upcoming four Nations League games due to fitness concerns.

But England captain Harry Kane “trusts” the five men who pulled out.

The Bayern Munich ace said: “I know the guys, I’ve spoken to the coach. Everyone has their own situation. I know how tough the summer was and I know, especially in the Premier League, how gruelling that schedule is.

“I’m in a different situation now where I have the winter break [in Germany] and I have moments to recharge. Some of the players don’t get that.



“Everyone has to look after themselves and put themselves first, and I trust all the boys.”

Sports.title: Andy Carroll cancels book signing just hours after revealing he was sexually assaulted in a ‘traumatic’ attack
Sports.content:
ATTACK HELL Andy Carroll cancels book signing just hours after revealing he was sexually assaulted in a ‘traumatic’ attack







Next

ANDY Carroll has cancelled his book signing just hours after revealing he was sexually assaulted in a “traumatic” attack in his new book.

Ex-England striker Carroll cancelled the Q&A at Dagenham Football Club before the scheduled event at 7pm this evening.



Carroll had been due to “speak candidly” during the event tonight.

But just hours before it started, the club confirmed it had been cancelled due to “unforeseen circumstances”.



The event, at Dagenham & Redbridge FC, Victoria Road Stadium, was supposed to include a book signing and live Q&A.

Carroll, 37, had posted to his Instagram two weeks ago: “I’ll be at Victoria Road Stadium sharing stories from my life on and off the pitch and answering your questions.

“It’ll be a chance to have a proper chat, look back at the journey so far and spend an evening together.”

Carroll said he had suffered a “traumatic” attack by a “celebrity mate” who was later jailed for three years.

He candidly admitted he “can’t forget” the horror in a bombshell admission in his autobiography, Owning It.

The book, which costs £22, was released today.



Carroll told how he had a “few drinks” and went to bed early, before awaking to find a “celebrity mate” assaulting him.

He threw him out his house and “smacked him unconscious” when he tried to get back in after the attack, said to have occurred in 2021.

He writes: “What happened to me affected every facet of my life.

“I’d think about it every day, making it difficult to focus on anything else, including football…

“The trauma of what happened to me hasn’t gone away.”



The ex-Newcastle and Liverpool ace told how he had debated with girlfriend Lou Teasdale, 42, whether to speak about the attack.

Carroll, who plays and acts as assistant manager for National League South side Dagenham & Redbridge, also discusses his relationship in his new book.

He and Lou, 42, began their tumultuous on-off relationship in summer 2024, following his split from wife Billi Mucklow.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Carroll admits he’s had “more fun than your average player”, as he writes about strip clubs, holidays and “having a few too many drinks”.

And the ex-Three Lions star says he was “sensible” until his career progressed and his wages skyrocketed to £200k a week.

Sports.title: Footballers with unusual hobbies, from Cristiano Ronaldo’s love of bingo to Phil Foden’s passion for fishing
Sports.content:
Next

WHEN the international break kicks in, some footballers will find themselves with plenty of time on their hands.

So, there’s no better time to sink yourself into a new hobby.



It stimulates the mind, takes you away from the pressures of daily life, and recharges the batteries to go again.

At least that’s what these footballers probably think when it comes to their chosen pastimes.



SunSport uncovers the most unusual hobbies we’ve seen the pros do, starting with something usually reserved for seniors around the country.

Cristiano Ronaldo – Bingo

In between sculpting his physique in the gym, Ronaldo’s developed a love of bingo.

Imagine him rocking up at the Mecca in Sale?

Ronaldo said in 2008: “Playing bingo can be very exciting.

“It can be very exciting because you can be there waiting for a long time for just the one number to make the game complete.

“Then you see one of your friends you are playing against get his lucky number before you.”



Paul Pogba – Camel racing

The France World Cup winner took his obsession with camel racing to another level.

In 2025, Pogba invested in Saudi Arabia-based team Al Haboob.

“I’ve watched my fair share of [camel] races on YouTube and spent time doing research in my spare time trying to understand the techniques and strategies,” Pogba told the BBC.



“And what stood out to me is how much dedication it takes from everyone involved. At the end of the day, sport is sport. It demands heart, sacrifice and teamwork.”

Eberechi Eze – Chess

The Arsenal No10 is used to facing the tightest defences to break down at the Emirates.

So, it’s no surprise he knows a thing or two about strategy, which has led him to playing chess.



The week before he downed Man City in the 2025 FA Cup final, he won £15,000 at a four-day chess tournament and is ranked in the top 15 per cent of players on Chess.com.

He has even lined up his pawns to face off against Sir Richard Branson.

Axel Tuanzebe – Hungry Hippos

When your hobby is a kids’ game and you hold a world record in it, does that mean you’ve taken it too far?

Not if you’re former Manchester United defender Axel Tuanzebe, who is a Hungry Hippos whizz.



“We have had a great day adjudicating a range of record attempts with the Manchester United football team as part of their collaboration with Guinness World Records,” said adjudicator Adam Brown.

“Axel Tuanzebe, was the bigger winner of the day and bagged himself the record for fastest time to clear a game of Hungry Hippos in a time of 17.36 seconds, beating competition from his fellow team-mates.”

Beat that, kids.

Xavi – Mushroom hunting

The Spain legend has an eye for a pass and a mushroom, unbelievably. But not THEM ones, before you get too clever.



Xavi is a mycology nut, which means he regularly hunts for mushrooms.

Former team-mate Gerard Pique and his ex-wife Shakira used to reportedly joined Xavi on a trek for some rare shrooms.

“Someone who picks mushrooms can’t be a bad bloke,” his former boss Pep Guardiola once said.



Phil Foden – Fishing

From Xavi, we go to the ‘Stockport Iniesta’ – better known as Phil Foden.

To take himself away from the stresses of Premier League football, the playmaker props himself up next to a lake and dangles out his rod.

Foden has even trekked to Spain, where he once caught a 130lb catfish.



“I was probably about six or seven and my dad had a fishing rod of his dad’s and said we should go and try it out,” he recalled.

“I fell in love with it and we ended up going every weekend. I still remember my first catch.”

Aaron Ramsdale – Dog training

Former Gunners star Ramsdale enjoys spending his downtime training dogs.

In the past, the goalie said he finds it relaxing to connect with pets and it’s how he finds peace away from the pitch.



He is the proud doggy dad to Chow Chow, Patrick. We don’t know if it was named after Vieira.

Sadly, Ramsdale ‘slove of dogs wasn’t enough to keep him at Arsenal, if Mikel Arteta’s pooch Win is to be trusted.

Matt Oakley – Piranha collecting

LEYTON ORIENT have taken a massive leap towards leaving Brisbane Road for a brand new stadium in East London.

The League One club have signed a formal Development Performance Agreement with Waltham Forest Council to explore a state-of-the-art stadium and entertainment complex.



Orient are aiming for a site in the borough with a target capacity of up to 20,000 seats — more than double their current home.

Sites at Leyton Mills Retail Park, New Spitalfields Market and Lee Valley Hockey and Tennis Centre have been rumoured, but nothing has yet been confirmed.



The club have played at Brisbane Road for 89 years, but bosses insist physical and commercial constraints mean they cannot expand their 9,271-capacity ground any further.

Majority shareholder David Gandler wants the brand new venue up and running by 2031 to celebrate the club’s 150th anniversary.



He said: “Our vision is not simply to build a football stadium. It is to create a distinctive, year-round destination for sport, entertainment and community life.

“Leyton Orient was founded in 1881, and our ambition is for the club to have a new home in place for our 150th anniversary in 2031.”

Chief Executive Mark Devlin admitted the O’s can no longer grow sustainably surrounded by local housing.

Devlin said: “Brisbane Road will always be central to Leyton Orient’s identity, but its physical and commercial constraints limit our ability to grow.”

Sports.title: Andy Carroll opens up on ‘car crash’ marriage to Billi Mucklow in new book & accuses her of ‘going back’ on France move
Sports.content:
Next

ANDY Carroll has branded his marriage to ex-wife Billi Mucklow a “car crash” and accused her of backtracking on a move to France.

As a result, former England striker Andy, 37, spent two years in the country on his own and saw his drinking spiral.



Andy and former Towie star Billi, 37, were engaged for eight years before marrying in 2022, but by July 2024 the couple’s relationship was over.

Now, ex-Newcastle star Andy is telling his side of the story in his book, Owning It.



He recalled how he was left lonely and depressed after heading to French club Amiens on loan from Championship side Reading.

“When I played abroad the original plan was for my family to come with me,” he wrote.



“I’d rather not go into detail but due to complicated family dynamics on my partner’s side, she stayed in Rod Stewart’s old house.

“She said she’d join me if I secured a job abroad, she reneged on the deal.”



Instead, Billi remained in England with the couple’s three kids Arlo, 11, Wolf, eight, and Marvel Mae, six, as well as Andy’s children from a previous relationship, Emilie Rose, 17, and Lucas, 15.

Andy, who swapped Ligue 2 side Amiens for Bordeaux two months after splitting from Billi, said he turned to booze to “mask the pain” of being apart from the kids.

In a candid confession, Andy claimed the couple’s relationship was hanging by a thread before they married and said that he only went through with it to do right by the kids.

The forward sought counselling in France which made him realise that his marriage was over and he didn’t miss Billi. It was compounded when he returned to the family mansion in Essex for the summer break and found himself hating being around his wife.

The Sun has contacted a rep for Billi for comment.



Andy, who once raked in £200,000-a-week, is now in a relationship with celebrity make-up artist Lou Teasdale, 42.

The pair met at Glastonbury through mutual connection Louis Tomlinson and hit it off immediately, with Andy taken by how fun Lou was.

He said he was staggered to find out she was stone-cold sober on their first meeting given how easy-going and talkative she was.

Sports.title: Agent reveals Gabriel Martinelli REJECTED Premier League transfer offers before leaving Arsenal for Saudi Arabia
Sports.content:
Next

GABRIEL MARTINELLI rejected offers from Premier League clubs before leaving Arsenal for Al-Hilal, according to his agent.

The Brazilian left the Emirates earlier this month after seven years with the Gunners and now plays in the Saudi Pro League.



Martinelli has wasted little time adapting to life in the Middle East after blitzing a hat-trick in just his third match.

Now his agent Marcos Casseb has shed some light on Martinelli’s departure from North London.



He revealed the winger had other offers from Europe before committing to Al-Hilal‘s “very ambitious project”.

Casseb told Itatiaia Sport: “Did he get offers? He did, yeah.



“We had offers from Italian clubs, we had offers from German clubs and we had offers from other Premier League clubs, but it was a moment when I think he needed and he also wanted to clear his head a bit, to change scenery.

“He went to the biggest club in Asia to be part of a very ambitious project. That’s a trend in Arab football right now, they’re changing the way they want to sign players.

“They’ve been trying to do that – lower the average age of the league – and their project has attracted a lot of attention.”

Martinelli ended his time at Arsenal on a high note as he lifted the Premier League title with the Gunners at the end of the 2025-26 season.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

He scored a total of 62 goals for Mikel Arteta‘s side from 278 appearances.

And Casseb believes it was the right for both parties to move on after a period of “restructuring” at Arsenal.

He added: “Arsenal underwent a massive restructuring and, last year, they won the Premier League.

“We felt it was time for him to move on, and the club had also seen it that way. It was a very good departure for him and for Arsenal.

“Besides everything else, he also became Arsenal’s biggest-ever sale and he still helped Arsenal make a lot of money from his departure.”



Martinelli started his career with Brazilian side Ituano before joining Arsenal as an 18-year-old in 2019.

He has picked up 27 caps for Brazil, scoring a total of five goals.

Sports.title: Premier League in joint call for FIFA reform amid Infantino crisis
Sports.content:
The Premier League and three of its top European counterparts will on Friday issue a joint call for urgent governance reform at FIFA amid the crisis engulfing its president, Gianni Infantino.

Sky News can reveal that English football's top flight and the top domestic leagues in Germany, Italy and Spain will publish a collective statement demanding greater consultation on key issues such as the global football calendar.

The statement was still in the process of being formally agreed between the quartet of domestic leagues on Thursday afternoon and it was unclear whether it would specifically call for Infantino to stand down.

One football insider said: "The Premier League, Bundesliga, La Liga and Serie A are going to issue a joint statement insisting that FIFA must reform to have more independent oversight and give stakeholders, including leagues, a meaningful role in decision-making."

The source said it followed a legal complaint filed nearly two years ago by the European Leagues Association - including the quartet behind Friday's planned statement - to the EU about FIFA's handling of the International Match Calendar.

The Premier League, along with others in Europe, have been at loggerheads with FIFA for some time over so-called 'calendar creep', with the potential for more frequent Club World Cups and expanded national team competitions causing alarm among the game's most important domestic leagues.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player FIFA President Gianni Infantino confirms he will stand for re-election next year

Earlier this week, Sky News reported that Infantino, who is said to be increasingly confident about surviving in his job when he comes up for re-election next year, had written to football chiefs across the globe saying he was open to talks about reforming the organisation.

Infantino has been lambasted by football industry executives and associations over his proposal to sell a 20 per cent stake in FIFA's commercial rights, including the World Cup, to private investors - including Joshua Kushner, brother of President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner.

The FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal was abandoned in July after a maelstrom of global opposition and threats to boycott tournaments organised by FIFA.

UEFA, ⁠the Asian Football Confederation, and CONCACAF - which represents countries in North and Central America and the Caribbean - called for changes ⁠to FIFA's leadership.

In a letter seen by Sky News this week, Infantino wrote to the heads of all its 211 member nations and his FIFA Council, saying he ​will ask the council whether it wants to launch an "independent external review of FIFA's current governance framework for major strategic initiatives and recommend potential improvements".

In the note, he also said ‌he would offer to hold talks with confederations, member associations and other stakeholders on strengthening FIFA's decision-making.

The proposals would examine who has a say in major initiatives, ​including the respective roles of the president, bureau, council and congress, and how to improve transparency and accountability.

Promising not to pre-judge discussions, he said proposals could be discussed when the council meets next month.

His responsibility, he said, is to serve "all 211 member associations fairly, regardless of their position on any individual matter," adding that "strong institutions do not wait for their systems to fail before considering how they can be improved".

But there was no mention of reviewing his position. Instead, the letter affirmed his intention to remain FIFA president, arguing his responsibilities are "larger than any individual proposal or disagreement".

The Premier League declined to comment on Thursday.

Sports.title: Nelson: AJ could be in 'world of trouble' against Fury
Sports.content:
Anthony Joshua will be in "a world of trouble" against Tyson Fury if he brings the same level of performance as he did in his previous fight, according to Johnny Nelson.

On Thursday, the long-awaited all-British heavyweight clash was finally confirmed for December 11 at Cardiff's Principality Stadium.

Joshua comes into the fight on the back of a major scare during his July victory over Kristian Prenga, with the 36-year-old knocked down twice in the opening round before stopping his unheralded opponent in the second.

The fight was Joshua's first since he survived a December 2025 car crash that claimed the lives of his close friends Sina Ghami and Latif 'Latz' Adodele.

Former cruiserweight world champion Nelson told Sky Sports News: "Well mentally, remember almost a year ago, AJ was involved in a horrific accident.

"That's a lot to get over and get his head around. Hopefully, he's in a great space with that.

"His last fight didn't represent him very well. If you're going on his last fight, he's in a world of trouble."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Johnny Fisher joins Andy Scott to give his prediction for Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua following the announcement of their Cardiff showdown, and believes fans are in for a dramatic night

Having taken time out of the ring after his two 2024 defeats to Oleksandr Usyk, Fury has this year recorded comfortable victories over Arslanbek Makhmudov and Mariusz Wach.

Nelson continued: "You look at Tyson Fury, his last fight was underwhelming but it wasn't worrying.

"So, the stages they're at, if you're going by their last fights, the one that's in a better condition I'd say would be Tyson Fury, because his last fight read better than AJ's last fight."

'Joshua more reliant on athleticism'

Nelson explained that he believes Joshua (30-4) has experienced a bigger drop-off than Fury (36-2-1) due to the former's greater reliance on his athleticism.

"Without a doubt, Joshua is explosive," Nelson said. "You saw the fights when he boxed people like Francis Ngannou, took them out cold.

"Tyson Fury, we've seen him box and knock people out. We've seen him go the distance. We've seen that slow burn and him winning a fight.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player George Groves gives his view on the confirmation of Fury v Joshua with the fight set to take place December 11, in Cardiff

"With AJ, it just seems that he stands out more for the knockouts than his boxing ability, even though he does have boxing ability.

"Whereas Tyson Fury, it wouldn't surprise you if he boxes his way around the ring for 12 rounds because he has that ability.

"Is AJ going to produce a crash, bang, wallop? Most people would probably be saying if it stops early inside the distance, you'd say AJ because of that explosive power.

"If it goes the distance or it's a late stoppage, you'd say Fury because he has the boxing intelligence, IQ and success of stopping people late."

'They'll bring the best out of each other'

Nelson is confident that despite both being past their prime, the long-standing rivalry between Fury and Joshua will ensure they bring the best out of each other.

"I think both fighters, not just AJ, are way past their best," Nelson added.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Tyson Fury doesn't hold back as he lashes out at Anthony Joshua as the wait goes on for the pair to confirm a much-anticipated showdown. Credit: @tysonfury

"But I also believe that because they're fighting each other, if there's ever a time that they're going to be able to turn back time for one night only, it's December 11. That one night is when they get everything.

"They understand that one mistake ruins their Christmas, ruins their New Year, ruins this beef that they've had forever and a day.

"There's a lot at stake for both fighters. They are not at their best, they're not the fighters they were, but the fighters they are today match each other perfectly, and they'll bring the best out in each other."

Sports.title: 'Pretty pants!' - Norris rules McLaren out of Baku pole fight
Sports.content:
Lando Norris says McLaren's pace in Thursday's practice sessions at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix was "pretty pants" and is not expecting to contend for pole position.

Norris was 1.5 seconds slower than pace-setter George Russell in second practice with the slow-speed 90-degree corners seemingly not suiting McLaren's car.

McLaren have brought a major upgrade package to the car in Baku, including new sidepods, engine cover, diffuser and floor edge but the new parts have not instantly given them more performance.

"We are miles off. We are up there relative and in the position we expect to be in but we are 1.5 seconds off the pace. Pretty pants," said Norris, who is 106 points behind championship leader Kimi Antonelli with nine rounds to go.

Asked if McLaren can close their practice deficit to Mercedes, he added: "I hope so. I have no idea. We will see what work we can do tonight. The car doesn't feel that bad, so it's a little knife in the heart when you see how far off you are.

"I just care about the pace and we are not very fast. I drive whatever car I get given. I just want it to be quick and it's not very quick at the moment."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Lando Norris reacts to the news that the Monaco Grand Prix will be a Sprint race in 2027

Norris aborted a lap in second practice which likely would have put him at least within one second of Russell, who topped both practice sessions on Thursday.

McLaren chief technical officer Rob Marshall says it's "early days" with the eight new items on the car and everything is working as expected.

"We had a lot of new bits on the car - a lot of learning. You put your package on and you need to learn how to dial it in and I don't think we are there yet," he said.

"I think the car is doing what we want it to do. The aero maps seem pretty happy. It's just a matter of dialling the performance in."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Craig Slater breaks down the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, including why the race takes place on a Saturday, while doing his best Craig David impression!

Russell: I'm sure the gaps will tighten in qualifying

Qualifying takes place on Friday at 1pm with the Azerbaijan Grand Prix itself on Saturday at 12pm, all live on Sky Sports F1, as Sunday is Remembrance Day in Azerbaijan.

Although you can overtake in Baku, track position is still important because it's a street circuit and Russell says "there's still plenty of work" to do for Mercedes.

"It's been a positive first day here in Baku. The car felt competitive over a single lap, and our race pace looks closely matched with McLaren and Red Bull," he said.

"I'm sure those gaps will tighten even further when we get to qualifying tomorrow."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Kimi Antonelli ends the first practice session early after a hydraulics failure on his Mercedes

Kimi Antonelli suffered a hydraulics leak in first practice, then Mercedes were forced to change his engine ahead of second practice which cost him one hour of running in total.

But, the championship leader, who is 81 points ahead of Russell, was still in second in second practice and half a second off his team-mate.

"We tried to do the maximum with what we had. We lost quite a few laps in FP1 and missing half of FP2 is never ideal, especially on a street circuit," said Antonelli.

"Overall, I feel like it was a good recovery. I feel quite good in the car. A few things to work on but looking forward to tomorrow."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Kimi Antonelli admits the early exit in P1 wasn't 'ideal' for a street circuit like Azerbaijan but was pleased with his recovery in the second practice session

How are Ferrari and Red Bull feeling?

Max Verstappen was Mercedes' closest challenger in the two practice sessions but still over eight tenths off the pace at the end of the day, despite Red Bull bringing upgrades to Baku.

Isack Hadjar was back in the car for the first time since the end of July after missing the last three race weekends due to a wrist injury he suffered in last month's summer break.

Hadjar, who has been confirmed to remain as Verstappen's team-mate in 2027, also lost valuable track time due to an engine problem in first practice but was still "pretty happy".

"It feels good. I had a good feeling. Not many laps unfortunately but this will come. I'm not really worried too much about the pace," he said.

"The feeling with this new package, we know the characteristics are the same with the car, but it feels nice - better than when I left it in Budapest."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Isack Hadjar admits he's unsure of the new contract extension details and if he'll remain at Red Bull beyond 2027, but hopes his driving will do the talking

Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton were in the top five of both sessions but the seven-time world champion feels Ferrari are missing performance on the tyres and on the straights.

"I felt generally good in the car. The track is awesome to drive. FP1 I felt very strong and I thought we were doing well but in FP2 the others took another step," said Hamilton, who has avoided a penalty for allegedly impeding Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson in second practice.

"It's trying to understand, we didn't change anything on the car, but the others took a step somehow. These tyres are really, really difficult to get to work. You do an out lap and a prep lap and they are still not in the window and still don't provide you with the grip.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson was not pleased with Lewis Hamilton after a near miss during the second practice session at the Azerbaijan GP

"When you do an extra lap, all of a sudden they switch up and you have tonnes more grip, so that's a really fine line and really difficult to get working. But we try our best and some teams do it better than others. We have to look into that.

"Then our straight line speed is not as good as Mercedes. Whether we can close that deficit tomorrow, we will try to work on tonight. Otherwise, a fun day."

Ferrari team principal Frederic Vasseur added: "The sessions were difficult to read. For sure, each parameter of performance - fuel, engine made a bigger difference compared to a normal track.

"They [the drivers] were not very pleased with the balance so we have a lot to do tonight to find a good solution for tomorrow.

Sports.title: Raphinha: ‘In my head I was leaving Barça, but a few small words can change you’
Sports.content:
For once, Raphael Dias Belloli puts the brakes on. The man who seems to be in perpetual motion, a footballer forever on fast forward, pauses, goes quiet for a moment and then, softly, utters something that says so much: “I think maybe people saw in me something I didn’t realise was there.” He did not know he was a leader, but he likes it. He did not know he was a captain, but according to his manager he is the “perfect captain”. And he did not know he was a No 9 either, but right now he is the best No 9 there is. In Barcelona or anywhere.

There was a time when Raphinha did not know whether he would be in Barcelona, when, feeling unwanted, he had accepted it was over, but this week he extended his contract to 2030. He will be 33 then: he would like to retire here and they would like him to retire here, too, a legend built on empathy and affection. “This is the best decision the club has made,” said Hansi Flick, the head coach Raphinha says changed his life. Sometimes you cannot get what you want so you have to settle for the best.

The first word Raphinha uses when training has finished and the tape starts rolling at Sant Joan Despí, when he is addressed as the world’s top No 9, is “false”. It comes with a smile; turns out there is nothing false about this 9. Seven games into the league season, the man filling in at centre-forward has scored 12 goals, plus two in the Champions League. The scorers leading the way in Europe’s other top leagues are five behind. No one in Barcelona’s history has started a season like this. And, no, Raphinha says, he has never played there before: “Even as a kid I wasn’t a 9.”

As if it is even about the goals. There may be no one as enjoyable to watch as Raphinha; no one as admirable or important either. The touch at speed is astonishing and there is a wild intensity about everything he does, only it is not wild, he says; it is worked upon, the entire system depending on him. The press defines Barcelona’s identity and it is, Raphinha says, “mechanised”. No, he is not going to reveal how but it begins with him. “As captain, he goes and everyone follows,” Flick says. “We always start with the No 9 and he has that incredible hunger and intensity, the mentality and attitude we need.”

Yet this is not what Raphinha or anyone expected. This summer Robert Lewandowski, Ferran Torres and Marcus Rashford departed, having contributed 38 league goals between them last season. They were supposed to be replaced by Julián Álvarez but Atlético Madrid refused to sell, leaving Barcelona with no striker. “There was a moment of need,” Raphinha says. “There was no No 9 for the [friendly] against Basel, so I played there.”

Raphinha backs Lamine Yamal to win Ballon d’Or – video

It was not supposed to be permanent, although Flick suspected it might be and was warming to the idea: Barcelona had not given up on Álvarez yet and the coach considered other solutions, including Anthony Gordon. This was better. Raphinha did not score but Barça got five.

“In pre-season we did a few tests: the manager liked what he saw and after Basel he told me a bit about his idea,” Raphinha says. “The adaptation came over the last two years, getting used to coming inside, closer to goal. But we tested [me as] an actual No 9 and it went well. There’s the occasional detail that has to be explained, but I’m OK. Before Elche [on the opening day], he asked if I was comfortable there or wanted to go back to my position. I said it was fine, see how it goes, we can always change back.”

Raphinha scored two against Elche, one against Athletic, two against Rayo and another at Valencia. Against Racing there was a hat-trick and another against Sevilla: right foot, left foot, header. Raphinha showed his old qualities and new, less expected ones: the movement, timing and clinical finishing of a classic No 9, efficiency to go with the intensity. Only one La Liga player has a better shot conversion rate. Against Feyenoord came two more.

View image in fullscreen Raphinha (right) is joined by Lamine Yamal – the player he says he is a ‘big brother to’ – after scoring during the Champions League match against Feyenoord. Photograph: Judit Cartiel/Uefa/Getty Images

Nor is it just about him. The point of Raphinha is that it is not even about him. Only once this season has he not scored, and against Levante he created the first two, then handed over the penalty for Lamine Yamal to add the third. Barcelona have scored five, two, five, five, five, four, seven and three, respectively in winning their first eight games.

Flick had done it again. “I always have and always will say that he changed my mentality, changed me as a person,” Raphinha says.

By 2024, Raphinha was convinced he had no future at Barcelona. His numbers were good: 10 goals and 12 assists in his first season, 10 goals and 13 assists in his second. But Lamine Yamal was emerging and, more importantly, Raphinha did not feel backed, completing 90 minutes seven times in 60 games under Xavi Hernández. It had not escaped his attention that Barcelona thought about selling him; it had not escaped anyone’s attention that they wanted to buy Nico Williams, publicly keen to reunite the pair that tore up the Euros.

Barcelona failed twice, and were all the better for it. A Photoshopped image of Williams in his No 11 shirt on social media hurt, Raphinha admitted. But Flick had arrived and if there is something even more powerful than the desire to prove people wrong, it is the desire to prove people right.

View image in fullscreen Raphinha fires in his team’s fourth goal in the 5-2 win against Rayo Vallecano. Photograph: David Ramos/Getty Images

“In my head, I knew I was leaving,” Raphinha says. “That was [mentally] done, that’s the truth. I was in Brazil and Flick called. He said come talk to him before taking a final decision. I met him and he said he trusted in me, that I was going to be important, that the team[’s play] would be good for me. In a moment like that, a few small words can change you. I felt a lot of faith in me. He gave me the confidence to play my football. I got an idea into my head: give everything, your life, regardless of the personal moment you’re in.”

Love won out, even if Raphinha is swift to add: “If you get results people are going to love you; if not, they’re not.” Feeling supported and valued changed everything. His success is a human story, his qualities human ones. He led Barcelona to the league. Flying in from the left, Raphinha scored 34 goals and provided 26 assists in 57 games. Another title followed in 2025-26 and although injuries reduced his contribution, there were 21 goals and eight assists in 33, Flick’s faith gratefully repaid.

His teammates’ faith, too. The dressing room had voted Raphinha as a club captain, third in line. He had not expected it and was genuinely touched. There was something in that moment, in the realisation of how they felt about him, how much they believed in him, that was transformative. Now Flick has named him his first choice.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen A jubilant Raphinha with the trophy after winning the Spanish Super Cup against Real Madrid. Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty Images

That moment brings pause, thought. “When I saw people had voted for me, it was like a switch had been flipped, a shift in mindset,” he says. “People could see something in me I didn’t realise was there, and that’s changed me. Before being captain, I didn’t know how much I would like it. Having that responsibility has also changed my mentality, helped me. I never thought I’d like being Barcelona captain so much. You feel you matter. It’s an honour. It’s not just wearing the armband.”

He is a natural, as pure a captain as there has been since Carles Puyol – even if he did need to be told. It is there in the relentless example he sets: Raphinha has sprinted the second-furthest distance in La Liga and Gradient Sports has measured only three players with more final-third pressures per 30 minutes out of possession. Raphinha says: “I talk less than most captains but I know people are watching. They think: ‘If this guy’s running like an animal, I have to follow.’. If you talk too much and then don’t do what you have to, people aren’t going to listen.”

Yet what teammates saw in him went deeper, to his very being. Leadership is there in the empathy, kindness and understanding too, in Raphinha returning the support that was good for him, an approach at once collective and individual. He says he can see when Lamine Yamal is drifting from games and how to reconnect him, every celebration shared with the teenager. A clip went round recently in which he quietly tells Gordon not to be afraid. And no clip was more powerful, more eloquent, than the moment when Flick sat on the bench, alone, lost in his thoughts and Raphinha consoled him, drawing him out of his dark place, roles reversed.

View image in fullscreen Fermín López, Raphinha, Lamine Yamal and Anthony Gordon celebrate their team’s third goal against Valencia. Photograph: David Ramos/Getty Images

“The coach-player relationship is the most important in football,” Raphinha says. “From the moment [Flick] arrived, we could talk to him about anything – and anything is anything. That time, I saw him, head down. At first, I didn’t really understand why. I asked what was wrong. He said he felt the team wasn’t playing well. From what I remember, I told him it was OK, we’d won and we would play well again. I prefer a thousand times to win playing badly than lose playing well. Win games, confidence and the football comes.

“What kind of leader [I am] depends on the moment. If I have to be slightly tougher, I can. But I prefer nicer moments, jokes. The last two years have been spectacular so I haven’t had to be the pesado [pain in the arse] often. I know that annoys people but someone has to do it sometimes.”

With a squad like this, especially? Four of Barcelona’s first team were born in 2007. “Buah!” Raphinha says, laughing. “That hurts: it shows I’m closer to the end than starting out at 18, 19, like them. But I’m in spectacular physical shape so [retirement] is some way off. It’s very easy with them. There are young players but they’re very responsible about their career, their lives. Once in a while, you have to [be paternal] because they’re kids. But they understand. If they get told off, they know it’s for their own good. I’ll tell them.”

View image in fullscreen Raphinha, pictured at the Barcelona training complex, is thriving in the role of captain. Photograph: Pablo Garcia/The Guardian

Is there something of the father figure in him with Lamine Yamal in particular? “No, no,” Raphinha jumps in. “Big brother, that’s better.” And Lamine Yamal is the star who should win the Ballon d’Or, he says: for his “individual numbers, collective titles, and the magic on the pitch, charisma. There’s no doubt. For me, he has to take the prize, no matter what. Even if I wasn’t Lamine’s teammate, for what he does, the numbers, the titles – and I think titles are important – he’s the candidate. One of one. Of three trophies, he won two with Barcelona. He won the World Cup with Spain.”

Only the Champions League escaped them; for two years Barcelona have come close, and it is their obsession now. “The semi-final against Inter [in 2025] hurt the most,” Raphinha says. “Against Atlético [in the quarter-final in 2026] we could have gone through, we could talk about things that could have gone differently, decisions. But against Inter, we had one foot in the final and to lose that way was hard. We’re a young team – that’s not an excuse – and sometimes you lack the maturity to manage key moments. This season we’re more mature, better prepared. If we carry on like this, with this mentality, we can compete for it all. We have everything.”

Starting from the front with the captain, the leader and the No 9.

Sports.title: Former England player Andy Carroll reveals he was sexually assaulted in 2021
Sports.content:
The former England forward Andy Carroll has revealed in his autobiography he was sexually assaulted by a man in 2021. The 37-year-old included the details in his book, Owning It. As a victim of sexual assault, Carroll was automatically granted anonymity.

Carroll revealed the incident took place at his home during a second spell at Newcastle. The offender – a friend of his former partner, who was staying away at the time – was later jailed for three years, with Carroll having testified in court.

The former Liverpool and West Ham striker, who is now a player/co-owner of the National League South club Dagenham & Redbridge, said the incident happened when he was sleeping. He then threw the man out of the house, then knocked him unconscious when he attempted to get back inside.

“I was sexually assaulted, there I said it. Scary to even think about and only a few people knew about it before now,” wrote Carroll, who had decided to include the incident in his book “at the very last minute” after discussing it with his partner, Lou Teasdale.

“Me and Lou spent a lot of time discussing whether to mention it in this book or not. I avoided my publisher for so long that they probably suspected I got cold feet.

“Scary to talk about but it’s made [me] the person I am today as much as any of the good stuff. And if me talking about it helps just one person then good, it will have been worth it.”

Carroll said testifying in court, where the attacker was found guilty of sexual offences and placed on the sex offenders register, was “humiliating and embarrassing and absolutely horrendous”.

The 37-year-old said: “What happened to me affected every facet of my life. I’d think about it every day, making it difficult to focus on anything else, including football … The trauma of what happened to me hasn’t gone away.”

Sports.title: UK Football Police Unit accused of ‘bringing Hillsborough’ into alcohol debate
Sports.content:
English football’s leading fans’ group has criticised the UK Football Policing Unit for “bringing Hillsborough into the debate” around drinking in sight of the pitch.

Talk of changing the law to allow fans to drink at their seat or in the stands has resurfaced after Andy Burnham, the prime minister, said the rules were outdated and discriminatory and should be scrapped.

The Football Supporters’ Association (FSA) immediately backed his call but the UKFPU urged caution, stating: “Following a number of football-related tragedies, changes in legislation were implemented after the Taylor Report for good reason and we are currently in the longest ever period without a significant football-related disaster.”

The UKFPU added it would be “incredibly rash to make fundamental changes without a full examination of the evidence”.

“The UKFPU would welcome a meeting with the prime minister to discuss his views and explain the challenges these proposed changes would bring to policing and the safety of staff and fans at football games.

“Other sports simply don’t see the violence and criminal behaviour from their supporters that football does, albeit a minority, with alcohol often playing a significant part in violent and disorderly behaviour. It would be irresponsible to fuel this by allowing greater alcohol consumption during games.”

The Taylor Report referenced by the UKFPU was commissioned in the wake of the 1989 Hillsborough disaster, which resulted in the deaths of 97 Liverpool fans.

The FSA published a thread on its X account setting out its position on drinking in the stands, which began: “Arguably the most important point is that the UK Football Policing Unit’s comments bringing Hillsborough into this debate have to be corrected. The disaster was not caused by alcohol. Full stop.

“Fans were ‘unlawfully killed and a catalogue of failings by police and the ambulance services contributed to their deaths’.”

The UKFPU has been contacted for comment.

Burnham’s comments have sparked social media debate in which differing views have been expressed by match-going fans.

The FSA’s post on Thursday added: “It’s unfair to criminalise fans for having a pint – especially since you can sit in the same seat drinking alcohol whilst watching an Oasis gig or rugby league. We are fundamentally sceptical of any law which is only targeted at football supporters.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“That doesn’t mean every club should be forced to serve alcohol to every seat! A club should have the choice to do what is right for its fans. Consultation is critical, some stadiums or stands might not be suitable (eg family areas) whereas it might be popular elsewhere.

“Ultimately, we think clubs, in liaison with their supporters, should be able to determine what is best for themselves, rather than relying on legislation which is decades old and was written through the prism of viewing all football fans as potential hooligans.”

The Sporting Events (Control of Alcohol) Act 1985 prohibits drinking in sight of the pitch in England and Wales in the top five men’s leagues.

Burnham said on Wednesday: “I don’t think it’s fair for football fans to be singled out in that way and I made that point. I think that legislation dates to an era where football was very different. And I do believe there is a case to remove that discrimination. There are different ways it could be done, perhaps on a trial basis.

“But I’m not going to back away from what’s been a long-held view of mine. I don’t see how it can be fair that some supporters of one sport can be treated differently from others.”

Sports.title: Infantino under pressure to include abandoned World Cup sell-off plan in external Fifa review
Sports.content:
Fifa council members will demand that Gianni Infantino include the abandoned World Cup sell-off plan and the Folarin Balogun affair in his proposed external review of Fifa’s governance.

In a letter sent to all 211 of Fifa’s member associations on Monday, Infantino said he would ask the council to commission a review of “Fifa’s current governance framework for major strategic initiatives” at its next meeting, in Zurich on 15 October, but he faces an internal battle over its terms of reference.

The Football Association’s chair, Debbie Hewitt, wrote to Infantino last week demanding the release of all documents relating to the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme that was abandoned last month, as well as the background to the global governing body’s decision to lift Balogun’s suspension during the World Cup, a request that has the support of many fellow council members.

One told the Guardian that without a retrospective analysis of FFE and Balogun, any governance review would lack credibility. Another suggested Infantino was seeking to avoid personal scrutiny by offering to look at Fifa’s governance structures moving forward rather than past controversies.

The council is made up of 28 representatives of the six confederations, eight vice-presidents, Infantino and Fifa’s secretary general, Mattias Grafström.

In the immediate aftermath of the Balogun affair, when the US striker’s suspension from the World Cup last-32 tie against Belgium was lifted after a phone call to Infantino from Donald Trump, a group of council members attempted to call an extraordinary general meeting but were unable to get the 19 votes required.

The European, Asian and North and Central American and Caribbean confederations campaigning against Infantino have 21 of the 38 council seats between them, but that includes delegates from Qatar, Saudi Arabia and Malaysia, who have issued public statements of support for the president.

The German football federation president, Bernd Neuendorf, expressed the European view clearly this week by describing Infantino’s offer of a governance review as cynical electioneering, but any vote on the matter at the council is likely to be tight.

“I regard Gianni Infantino’s letter as a transparent ploy to secure ⁠his re-election next year,” Neuendorf said. “Fundamentally, Fifa now seems to have recognised that changes are essential. However, Gianni Infantino ⁠is definitely not the right person to lead a reform ⁠process.”

Infantino said on Wednesday his letter had been well received. He was speaking while attending the opening night of the Arabian Gulf Cup in Jeddah, from where he will fly to New York for meetings at the United Nations general assembly.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“I am looking forward to receiving feedback from everyone, following my letter,” he said. “I have received positive messages about it from different parts of the world, and it is important that we keep listening to each other, here in Saudi Arabia, in any one of Fifa’s 211 member associations.

“We have a council meeting next month, so we will continue to have dialogue on these important matters. There must be a culture of dialogue, of listening to each other and respecting each other.

“This is not about generating positive headlines, it is about doing what is right for the game. And I have never been more determined and committed in doing that. Fifa is always engaged. I am always engaged and want to hear how we can continue to grow football for the benefit of everybody, everywhere.”

Sports.title: Football Daily | Pints and points: the arguments for and against booze at football matches
Sports.content:
THIRSTY WORK

Considering he is a lifelong Everton fan, it’s no surprise that Andy Burnham seems to be in favour of allowing fans to drink Tin at football matches. Bouts of boardroom turmoil, points deductions and assorted relegation battles mean the lot of an Evertonian is not always a happy one. The Prime Minister believes that if he and other fans fancy a sip or two to help ease the pain of watching Thierno Barry head wide of an open goal, then that ought to be their constitutional right as proud Englishmen. Sadly, no such right currently exists, as alcohol consumption within view of the pitch has been outlawed in the top five divisions of English football since the troubled times of the 1980s. Instead, thirsty match-goers are forced to endure an agonising wait of 45 whole minutes before rushing to the bar, joining long queues of fellow fans eager to buy pints of foaming shaft they must subsequently chug back, yard-of-ale style, in enough time to return to their seats for the start of the second half.

In a move some cynical folk have described as populist political grandstanding, Burnham has correctly pointed out that in not being allowed to enjoy a pint during games, football fans are being discriminated against compared to their counterparts in sports such as cricket, rugby and horse racing. “I don’t think it’s fair for football fans to be singled out in that way and I made that point,” he told a gaggle of reporters during a flight to New York. “That legislation dates to an era where football was very different and I do believe there is a case to remove that discrimination. There are different ways it could be done – it could happen on a trial basis. But I’m not going to back away from what’s been a long-held view of mine. I don’t see how it can be fair that some supporters of one sport can be treated differently.”

While Burnham has a point, reaction to the possibility of booze returning to football match stands has been mixed. While the sanctimonious bleating of “if you can’t last 45 minutes without a drink, then there’s something wrong with you” from the puritan brigade strikes Football Daily as reason enough for an immediate change in legislation and trebles all round, reintroducing alcohol could pose a logistical problem not previously experienced by the current generation of fans. Specifically, them being forced to repeatedly stand up and sit down again in order to make room for an endless procession of people going to and from the bars and toilets. While we’re not proud to admit it, Football Daily has attended enough rugby internationals to know exactly how annoying this can be.

The Football Supporters Association favours Burnham’s suggestion that allowing fans to bring an overpriced, flimsy receptacle of flat lager to their seats would massively enhance the matchday experience and the Premier League is obviously open to any idea that helps its members prise an extra few quid out of customers. The UK Football Policing Unit, however, is understandably less enthused. “Other sports simply don’t see the violence and criminal behaviour from their supporters that football does, albeit a minority, with alcohol often playing a significant part in violent and disorderly behaviour,” they harrumphed. “It would be irresponsible to fuel this by allowing greater alcohol consumption during games.” While alcohol consumption increases the risk of violent disorder, the recent box-park phenomenon of performative and celebratory pint-throwing almost certainly will too. Nobody wants to come home from a football match drenched in beer, even if the only alternatives are to stay at home or start supporting Spurs.

LIVE ON BIG WEBSITE

Join Daniel Harris from 7.45pm BST for hot clockwatch action in the Nations League with Netherlands 1-2 Germany, Portugal 3-1 Wales and more.

QUOTE OF THE DAY

“Whenever they say they don’t want me in the national team, I will be the first one to go. When I think I am not adding anything to the team, or that I create an atmosphere, I will be the first to go. I will take my suitcase and leave. The Portuguese count on me. That’s why I’m still here … just look at the numbers, I’m sure you can make some calculations, I’m still doing well. The day they don’t count on me, no problemo, I will leave. I will always be the No 1 fan of this federation. It would be the cherry on the top of the cake to score my 1,000th goal with the national team. It would be the culmination of a beautiful story. I said I wanted to reach that target and I will reach that target. But I don’t have an obsession. If you are obsessed with something, you won’t get it … just enjoy. Carpe diem, enjoy the day.” – Cristiano Ronaldo is completely calm and not at all obsessing over the 21 goals he needs to reach the 1,000 mark ahead of Portugal’s Nations League match against Wales today.

View image in fullscreen Cristiano Ronaldo is 21 goals away from the big 1,000. Photograph: Antonio Pedro Santos/EPA

double quotation mark Like anyone with a sense of football heritage, as soon as I read in yesterday’s Football Daily that Javier Aguirre had joined Valencia, I scrambled to see when they would play Anthony Gordon’s Barcelona. Sadly, it seems we’ll have to wait until the end of January for that particular reunion. Hey, fixture list, beep you” – Jim Hearson.

double quotation mark If Thomas Tuchel believes that 99.9% of supporters he bumps into do not talk to him about his substitutions during the Argentina game (Football Daily Tuesday), has he noticed a significant percentage of fans turning on their heels and walking in the opposite direction muttering furiously to themselves when they spot him? I would estimate that this could encompass approximately 51.8% of England supporters in his orbit. Another cohort, which I would put at around 37.6%, may break down weeping and gnashing their teeth uncontrollably at a missed opportunity to beat a limited and cynical Argentinian team, thereby missing their opportunity to congratulate Thomas effusively on England’s knockout win over Democratic Republic of Congo” – Dexter O’ Riordan.

If you have any, please send letters to the.boss@theguardian.com. Today’s letter o’ the day prize goes to … Jim Hearson, who wins a copy of Behind the Curtain by Big Website’s Jonathan Wilson.
