Sports.title: My bad TV history qualifies me to discuss Disney’s women’s football coverage | Max Rushden
Sports.content:
Disclaimer: I have made a lot of bad TV programmes. I have done quite a few below-average radio shows. Podcasts, there are millions of them – some might say too many – and I’ve done my fair share that won’t go down in history. In between those, I’ve hopefully done some pretty good ones – it’s not for me to say.

I have had good ideas and the odd great one that didn’t make it to air (attention the full-size unreferenced post-Keys and Gray elephant in the Soccer AM studio). I’ve had more awful ones. I’ve hosted shows where I’ve had almost complete editorial control, and ones where I could have been replaced by a performing monkey.

I’ve had to host TV shows at every possible height – sitting on a sofa, on a normal chair, on a normal chair behind a desk, on a bar stool in a pub, on a bar stool not in a pub, and standing up when there was somewhere comfortable to sit just out of shot. I complained a lot, but standing did actually work, Murray.

The point being, I have some experience when it comes to reviewing the opening night of the Disney+ coverage of the Women’s Champions League. The Hangout was hosted by Alex Scott with her fellow former England international Lianne Sanderson, the content creators Tyra Mills and Alex Bailess, and quite inexplicably a golden retriever called Barley Boy, who at the time of writing has 82,000 more Instagram followers than I have – I must work on my reels.

The show included a quiz about Italy, including guess the Italian name for football and what pasta the reporter in Milan is cooking. There’s an incredible still image of the panel staring at a load of farfalle on a big screen normally reserved for team lineups or key match incidents.

The immediate reaction was a mix of bewilderment and fury from seasoned lovers of the women’s game. Kathryn Batte wrote an understandable critique for the Telegraph. The broadcaster Flo Lloyd-Hughes posted on X: “Disney’s new UWCL coverage is the closest we’ve seen to CBBC football (derogatory). I wouldn’t be surprised if we see someone gunged for making a wrong prediction or perhaps Raven will make a cameo. Keep stopping to remind myself this isn’t a dream.”

Consistent with all the criticism is the truth that the men’s Champions League would never be covered in the same way. It is perhaps interesting to ask how the team arrived at the concept. Why replace former pros with content creators, why replace tactical analysis with asking what’s the biggest city in Italy? Why a dog?

The broadcaster Marva Kreel perfectly articulated one of the issues in her own X post: “I think a lot of the problem with the debates in women’s football broadcasting over analysis and punditry v content creation and gimmicky fun, is that in men’s football you can get both – and in different shows. In women’s football you get one show, and so they try to do it all.”

It’s a fair point. I’ve mainly hosted the show before the show – where a dog running around wouldn’t be regarded as a crime against the game. In fact hosting live football is significantly more straightforward than interviewing an indie band about their difficult second album or trying to come up with a three-hour radio show in the middle of the international break. The show Disney tried to make on Wednesday is technically much harder than Super Sunday – but that doesn’t mean it was the right call.

I can understand the thinking. I imagine the bosses told the producers they want to bring in a younger audience. I have been told this before. Exactly how to do that is impossible to work out. Should I stop making references to Jossy’s Giants and Aswad? And Disney could probably argue that most of the criticism didn’t come from young people. It came from people who expect the game to be covered in a certain way.

(From left) Former England international Lianne Sanderson, content creators Alex Bailess and Tyra Mills, and golden retriever Barley Boy. Photograph: Disney+

Disney may be being cynical – people are talking and writing about it. The hardcore will watch anyway. Had they produced more traditional coverage, no one would have said anything. And sometimes you have to try something different. I wouldn’t want to be too critical; Disney may give me a gig one day.

Major broadcasters have less money to make the same amount of stuff – and have had a battle over the past 20 years to work out how to harness social media. I saw it at Sky, where a Facebook livestream filmed on an iPhone in the green room would get as many views as the show itself with the costs of studio/lighting/sound/producers etc.

As a middle-aged man – whose wife accuses him of being a “boomer” – I really dislike the phrase “content creator”; perhaps I’m nervous that eventually they’ll take all my jobs. From what I saw, Bailess and Mills came across as very personable and fun – which was clearly the brief – and you can’t criticise anyone for taking a job. And they bring a following with them – quite how many followers lead to subscriptions is a different question.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

I feel for Scott, who perpetually finds herself in the middle of some sort of culture war. You are entitled to regard her as the greatest or worst broadcaster of her generation – or somewhere in between – as you are with me or anyone else. I know many listeners certainly feel the latter about my abilities.

I found the discourse around the end of Football Focus pretty troubling – people suggesting the show went woke and lost its way when she was appointed. It’s much more accurate to accuse me of turning Soccer AM woke, with my clarinet, lefty snowflake opinions and inability to flirt on live television. But then I’m not a woman and I’m white; generally people just accuse me of turning it shit.

But back to the Hangout. I imagine Scott didn’t suggest having a dog in the studio or having guess the pasta. Perhaps she has a lot of editorial control – I genuinely don’t know. But sometimes as a host you have to do what you’re told and do it with conviction.

The reality of live football coverage is that people are watching because they want to watch the game. If people want comedy, they’ll watch Curb Your Enthusiasm. If Liverpool are playing Real Madrid, the fans will watch it – and either enjoy or endure the coverage. But what you can do as a broadcaster is make it as compelling as possible, and there are different ways of being a good host or pundit.

Live football coverage hasn’t changed dramatically in 50 years. Welcome, team news, managers, bit of tactics or player focus, throw to commentators. Half-time: what did you make of that? Full time: what did you make of that?

The dog did not return for the second night of coverage. I know it would have been a strange and difficult day for everyone involved. They made a show, people didn’t like it and they had to go again the next night. Do you double down, screw the haters, or try to subtly move towards a more traditional setup? It seemed on Wednesday they went for the latter.

You can’t magic up an audience, but you can make people feel like you respect the game, you can do it in an entertaining way without introducing animals, and people will come back and watch you again.

Sports.title: Has the time come to separate home and away fans at WSL games?
Sports.content:
With interest in the Women’s Super League on the rise and more clubs playing at their main stadiums, there are questions over whether to separate supporters into stricter home and away sections, as in the men’s game, or to continue with mixed seating and optional away ends.

From the 2023-24 season, new league regulations required clubs to include an away-ticketing policy in their licensing agreements, a move backed by the Football Supporters’ Association (FSA).

The issue became a bigger talking point following the expedited growth of women’s football after Euro 2022. The SheGulls supporters’ club for Brighton Women said: “Now there are bigger and more passionate crowds with louder voices commanding more respect and attention. Put two sets of them together, and you can expect issues as we see on occasions at the moment.”

Under the policy, travelling fans wishing to sit with their own supporters can do so in a designated area, while others retain the choice of where they want to sit. Some supporters believe separation is a foregone conclusion. SheGulls added: “It would be nice to live in a world where it isn’t required, but the truth is it can be hard enough to generate an atmosphere at home from within our own fan base, never mind if they’re interspersed with Arsenal or Chelsea fans, for example. It feels inevitable.”

Dedicated away seating has been welcomed by, among others, Manchester City Women Official Supporters Club (MCWFC OSC), who cite an “increase in Manchester City supporters at away matches” as having “given a real boost to the atmosphere in stadiums”.

The FSA has taken a keen interest in developments and a spokesperson said: “The FSA and its members helped advocate for dedicated away sections, to help create community, atmosphere and allow travelling fans to connect, and to have a visible travelling fan section for away players to look towards.”

The infrastructure is already in place to segregate fan bases in most stadiums, where it is established for men’s games, but there is no stipulated away-ticket allocation owing to varying stadium sizes. Manchester United Women’s Supporters Club (MUWSC) feels supporter segregation could be a good move. “This doesn’t feel like a bad thing; segregation often results in an increased atmosphere which players regularly comment on as a positive thing,” it said.

Some experiments have taken place, with the WSL-run League Cup final using “club ends” behind the goals with mixed seating in the other stands, a model also used at FA Cup finals and at the 2025 Euros.

View image in fullscreen Brighton fans at St Andrew’s watch their team take on Birmingham in the WSL earlier this month. Photograph: Natalie Mincher/SPP/Shutterstock

The FSA added: “It is important now to look at whether home-only sections might be helpful for the same reasons: visibility, community and atmosphere. For us, this is about fan choice rather than ‘segregation’, and that choice is really important to an enjoyable matchday experience for all. It is important to consider general and neutral fans in the conversation, too, and there may not be a one-size-fits-all answer for every club.”

The current policies used in the league were developed through dialogue among the league, its member clubs and fans, through the FSA. This collaboration has enabled initiatives such as the Fan Choice trial and the Stadium Design Guidance. The belief is that the women’s game requires a distinct approach as its fanbase grows.

Tottenham, for example, have embraced the mixed home and away seating format. The club is understood to view its flexibility and family-friendly environment as a way to maintain atmosphere. It is felt an inclusive environment does not diminish the passion or noise levels of home supporters. However, it is also understood that the club may consider trialling a more segregated model if it is proven to improve the overall product and help the game grow.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

There are potential pitfalls with segregated stadiums. MCWFC OSC said separating fans often is not practical: “Even when matches are held at the main stadia, the men’s away end isn’t always used due to lower attendances. Clubs often keep fans together in just one or two stands to reduce operational costs so that traditional segregation can be impractical or simply unnecessary.”

SheGulls said: “There are some minor concerns about the way the game is going in terms of the need for segregation, but equally many think if we were segregated, or had the option of say a mixed zone, it would alleviate the angst that is sometimes caused by the current system.”

Creating a good atmosphere is key and many of the fan groups point out that supporters can still sing if they are in a mixed area. MUWSC has chants adapted for all ages, as well as a songbook where fans can look up the lyrics and join in. “There are so many positives about the environment that has been created in the women’s game, but remembering that welcoming atmospheres don’t mean you have to be quiet, and that being inclusive doesn’t mean never saying anything negative about the opposition.”

View image in fullscreen Crystal Palace fans applaud the players after their goalless draw against Arsenal at the Emirates Stadium. Photograph: COLORSPORT/Ashley Western/Shutterstock

Arsenal, meanwhile, have a separate away section for all WSL home fixtures at the Emirates, with the infrastructure already in place from men’s matches. It is felt this helps create a more competitive atmosphere and gives opposition fans a dedicated space. While Arsenal have a dedicated away end, away fans are still able to sit in “home” sections, especially families or groups with mixed loyalties.

Chelsea are staging all 13 of their home WSL matches at Stamford Bridge, which has a designated away end, this season, following consultation with players and supporter groups. The club are launching a new fan engagement project, The Blueprint, to help shape matchday culture and atmosphere. That is similar to Arsenal’s Block by Block initiative, introduced when they began playing all their WSL matches at the Emirates.

Chelsea host Arsenal in the WSL on Sunday, with the visitors selling out their allocated away tickets for the second consecutive time. Last season, Arsenal fans who missed out on away-end tickets sat in home sections alongside Chelsea supporters, raising questions around segregation.

The FSA has praised the clubs’ approach to collaborating with their fans: “We believe clubs should consult with their own fans to come up with local solutions that allow passion and vibrant support, but that keep the game welcoming and inclusive for all.”

As the league grows, so do the needs of different, growing fan bases, making it a key point of discussion among clubs, supporters and the league for the foreseeable future.

Sports.title: Have Arsenal been figured out? Three big questions after Brighton’s upset
Sports.content:
Before this past weekend, Arsenal had not lost in the Premier League since April. Nine straight league wins had been enough to crown the Gunners as champions at the end of last season and firmly establish them as the team to beat early this season.

Against Brighton on Saturday, though, the team to beat were beaten. Thoroughly.

Arsenal weren’t just pecked by the Seagulls. They were pressed to death by them. Usually so resilient, even in the face of such opposition exuberance, the Premier League champions fell apart on the south coast, losing a match by three goals for the first time in over three years. It was jarring to see Arsenal so out of sorts.

Was this simply a Control-Alt-Delete game for Arsenal, or has the manner of the Seagulls’ performance provided a template for others to use? Was Saturday merely a blip that the Gunners will quickly recover from or the first crack in their previously impenetrable armour? Let’s tackle those and some other questions from the Premier League’s big upset before the international break.

How did Brighton do it?

The most effective element of Brighton’s performance was their relentless pressing of Arsenal in periods of settled possession. While the Seagulls still had pressing triggers which prompted them to push high up the pitch at certain moments, Fabian Hürzeler also recognised the need to prevent the champions from getting to the edge of the box. They were in Arsenal’s faces for most of the match.

Brighton defensive midfielder Chema Andrés pushed up on to Martin Ødegaard whenever he could, moving Brighton into a man-to-man shape against the ball and limiting the Norwegian whenever he dropped deep. Faced with a four-on-four situation in build-out, Arsenal simply weren’t sharp enough on the ball to get around the press, forcing David Raya to go long more times than he would have liked. From there, Brighton could turn the ball over and attack at speed in the other direction.

This made the match a transition-heavy affair which suited Brighton’s attacking players. Focal point Charalampos Kostoulas was an all-round threat while Pascal Gross, Maxim De Cuyper and Diego Gómez were impactful in open space. Hürzeler’s approach never allowed the game state to shift in Arsenal’s favour. He covered all bases.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Twice weekly Sign up to Soccer Desk Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer. Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Is Brighton’s formula replicable?

Maybe, but it will be tough. Hürzeler’s team are a physical force of nature. Of the four players that covered the most distance on Saturday, three were Brighton players and it’s these legs and lungs that allows them to press so hard for so long. No Premier League team is averaging more high turnovers per 90 minutes this season. Not every team can do what Brighton do.

For all that Brighton’s approach as a team, and a club, epitomises the modern game, there was an old school quality to the way they disrupted Arsenal. “We wanted to win the small battles first,” explained Hürzeler on talkSport, revealing the instructions he gave his players. “Win the first header, win the first tackle, win the first throw-in, win the first corner.”

Should Arsenal fans be worried?

Probably not, since there were some mitigating factors that explain Arsenal’s underperformance. The trip to Brighton was their fourth away game in just 10 days, and their general lethargy reflected this. Furthermore, many of Arsenal’s best players, including Martin Ødegaard, Declan Rice and Bukayo Saka, were denied a pre-season due to their extended involvement at the World Cup.

Two of Brighton’s three goals came from low-xG shots from outside the box. Arsenal were guilty of not closing the space for the shooter quickly enough, but on another day Gross and Kostoulas would have shot over the bar rather than into the top corner. Indeed, Brighton’s three goals came from a total xG of just 1.31, less than Arsenal’s xG of 1.63.

Arsenal are also still without the injured William Saliba whose presence next to Gabriel Magalhaes surely would have steadied their defensive line. Without Ben White in the lineup, the Gunners additionally lacked the chemistry down the right wing that has been such a feature of their early-season success. Saka was a non-factor in the game.

Many predicted Arsenal would stroll this season’s title race. They still might. While Manchester City are now top of the table, Arsenal are two points better off now than they were at the same stage of last season when they went on to win the title for the first time since the Arsène Wenger era. Until Saturday, they had won seven out of seven in all competitions this season. Mikel Arteta need not panic.

You can bet, however, that the tactical analysts and data crunchers employed by Arsenal’s rivals will have closely watched Brighton’s 3-0 win more than a few times by the time club soccer resumes next month.

Sports.title: Wayne Rooney reveals the TWO clubs he couldn't refuse after four 'difficult' managerial jobs - then admits harsh truth he may never return to dugout
Sports.content:
Wayne Rooney reveals the TWO clubs he couldn't refuse after four 'difficult' managerial jobs - then admits harsh truth he may never return to dugout

Manchester United legend Wayne Rooney has revealed he would only return to football management for two clubs.

The former England captain burst onto the Premier League scene by scoring spectacular goals for his boyhood club, Everton.

Rooney was then transferred to Manchester United, where he won almost every major trophy during Sir Alex Ferguson's legendary reign at Old Trafford.

After 13 years with the Red Devils, Rooney made a sensational return to Goodison Park for one last Premier League hurrah with Everton.

Having dedicated a combined 16 years of his footballing career as a talisman for Everton and Manchester United, it came as no surprise to anyone that Rooney named the two clubs whose offers he simply could not refuse in the future.

Starring in his new family documentary – The Real Rooneys, the former Everton and Manchester United captain was asked about his managerial future on Virgin Radio.

Wayne Rooney admits Man United would be one of two jobs he would return to management for

Rooney would also return if given the chance to take charge of Everton, but admits a surprise return to the dugout is 'unlikely'

Even though Rooney described a surprise return as 'unlikely,' the 40-year-old said he could still see himself going back to United or Everton 'in any capacity'.

'I doubt it, again I know I've done four difficult jobs. The only way I'd go back in any capacity would be Everton or Manchester United. But that's very unlikely,' Rooney said.

In his glittering career at Man United, Rooney recorded 559 appearances and scored 253 goals.

After becoming the club's all-time leading scorer, Rooney returned to Everton in 2017. Show host Chris Evans then quizzed Rooney about which job he would take out of the two. Rooney responded: 'The one that comes first.'

Rooney left Plymouth Argyle by mutual consent in December 2024, which remains his last coaching role since he retired as a player in 2021.

The five-time Premier League winner also had forgettable managerial stints at Derby County, DC United and Birmingham City.

Leaving his management days behind, Rooney feels his new role as a pundit has given him 'purpose'.

Rooney acknowledged he may never manage again after several unsuccessful stints in the dugout

'I'm not doing it for money; I'm doing it for a purpose rather than just being at the house all day,' he said in the documentary.

'There's a possibility I'll never manage again moving forward. I'm enjoying Match of the Day, and it's time to learn and get better at what I'm doing.'

Speaking to the Daily Mail after undergoing an impressive transformation in recent weeks, Rooney revealed that he worked 'really hard' to lose weight in the gym.

'I've seen recently I've been taking this pen thing about me,' he said.

'It's a shame, because I'm working really hard to lose weight. Apparently I've been on the pen.'

Sports.title: I was a former NFL kicker and now coach the next generation, be warned Harry Kane - THIS is the ruthlessly cut-throat world that awaits you if you want to chase a career in Gridiron
Sports.content:
It’s not impossible for Harry Kane to become an NFL kicker one day but I’d still put it at very long odds.

I have seen guys jump from being soccer players to kickers but, even then, they’re usually in their early 20s and only make it to college football. The only real exception is the current kicker Brandon Aubrey, who was drafted by side Toronto before making the switch to NFL.

The big difference is that NFL kickers have focused on one thing for a very, very long time. They probably started specialising in kicking field goals around the age of 13, so by the time they make it to the NFL they have been at it for ten years. Just kicking field goals, nothing else. It would be like a soccer player not practising tackling, passing or even general shooting but just taking free-kicks, non-stop, for a decade.

So, even when you’ve got someone who’s athletic and is a sensational soccer player, like Harry Kane, it’s going to be hard to actually be as good as somebody who just did one thing for many years.

People often compare it to golf but, even then, you have different types of swings, different clubs, different lies. When it comes to kicking, every time you step on the field your goal is the exact same thing you have done since you were 13: hit the ball as far and as straight as possible every single time. Then go back through the video and nitpick every little detail so you can hit it farther and straighter next time and do it over and over and over again. It’s intense and it’s boring, too. This is why it’s dominated by people who have that mental strength to perfect one simple skill.

I’ve coached loads of NFL kickers, including Philadelphia Eagles’ Jake Elliott. These guys aren’t just amazing on game day. They are on it every single day. Their supreme leg strength is probably the least of all the factors to make it. You have to have the skill set and mentality to be almost 100 per cent every single day.

Harry Kane faces a difficult challenge if he wishes to make it as a professional NFL kicker

That’s not to say he can’t do it. It took Aubrey about two years of focused, intense training. If Kane put all of his mind and training into it, he could probably get to that level in a year or two if his body doesn’t give out beforehand due to age or overuse.

Even then, there's so many other kickers that he would be competing with for his job. Ones that are polished and experienced and have the knowledge of kicking in high-pressure situations.

And they have to make them. Kickers have to make above 90 per cent of their attempts to have a job, basically. If you are below 90 per cent, if you miss more than maybe three field goals over the course of a season, they are going to look to replace you.

That's a different pressure to even those experienced by elite soccer players, just from the nature of the game.

To land a spot as an NFL kicker, which is one player per team, you would have to be in the top 32 in the world at what you do. The coach that takes a chance on Harry Kane is putting their job on the line to give him a shot. If it all goes sideways, that same coach might lose their job.

There are some similarities in the technique. They can be launching it more than 60 yards and if you look at the kicks, they’re high and dead straight. There’s zero movement on the ball. In that sense, maybe, it’s more similar to a defender striking it long than a striker.

Brandon Aubrey has warned the England skipper that his job is not as simple as it may seem

There’s lots more body behind the ball because you’re striking a stationary object. You can really get your whole body behind it. In soccer, things are always moving, you’re hitting it off balance, with players around you, from different angles, everything like that. The difference is in being able to maximise getting as much body behind the ball in every strike.

If I had any piece of advice for Kane, it’s this: drills, drills, drills. Do as many as you can. A kicker’s body only has so many full-strength kicks in them in a day or a week, but at half-speed, where you can just dial it in, you can do those from sunrise to sunset. Do it.

Sports.title: Barcelona insist they are NOT interested in Man United's wantaway wonderkid JJ Gabriel, 15 - despite star flying to Spain for talks amid tug-of-war with Real Madrid
Sports.content:
Barcelona insist they are NOT interested in Man United's wantaway wonderkid JJ Gabriel, 15 - despite star flying to Spain for talks amid tug-of-war with Real Madrid

Barcelona's sporting director Deco insists the Catalan giants are not interested in signing Manchester United wonderkid JJ Gabriel.

The 15-year-old winger, who has demanded to leave United, was spotted in Barcelona last week after holding talks with their arch rivals Real Madrid.

It raised the prospect of a tug-of-war between the two Spanish clubs, but Deco has distanced Barca from a move for Gabriel.

Speaking at a football conference in Portugal on Thursday, he insisted: 'There's nothing to say about this boy. It's normal we always have players linked with us. There's a huge market for that, even when they are young.

'We are not interested in any player in his situation. I'm not sure what's happening, and if he's still a Manchester United player. We are not involved in that.

'First of all, we need to understand how the situation is before we try to do something. To speak about young, teenage players, it is not our business.'

JJ Gabriel, 15, stunned Man United bosses when he told the club he wanted to leave

United were stunned by Gabriel's request last week and have refused to rip up his registration. They still to hope to convince the youngster that his future lies at Old Trafford.

But he has not been seen at the club since scoring a hat-trick on his UEFA Youth League debut against Sabah a fortnight ago and seems determined to leave.

Gabriel turns 16 a week on Tuesday when he will be able to appoint an agent and join a foreign club using his Irish passport – meaning United would only receive around £300,000 in compensation.

Head coach Michael Carrick insisted last week that Gabriel's wellbeing is the most important thing regardless of his future at the club.

'He's a young boy, JJ,' said Carrick. 'I think the exposure and the scrutiny and everything, you've got to be careful and be sensible and think of him as much as anything.

'So the situation will work itself out, whatever way it's going to work itself out. Making sure he's okay is the important thing.'

Sports.title: Wayne Rooney reveals his Jewish roots after discovering his grandmother's Polish heritage and taking his sons to Auschwitz
Sports.content:
Wayne Rooney has revealed he has Polish-Jewish heritage in his new documentary.

The former England captain, 40, is starring in a new £10million fly-on-the-wall show, The Real Rooneys, which was filmed last year for Disney+.

'I’ve recently found out that my mum’s mum, so my nan’s, family were Polish Jews,' he says.

'I’m Catholic, but then I’ve always asked questions like why aren’t we Jewish?'

Asked whether he might investigate further and do a spin-off show, he quips: 'Roo the Jew?'

The Rooneys take a trip to Auschwitz in the documentary and Wayne tells his taxi driver: 'I've watched a lot of documentaries on it and you just wouldn't think human beings could do that to other human beings. It's crazy.

Wayne Rooney pays a trip to Auschwitz with his family in his new Disney+ documentary

Rooney reveals that he has Polish-Jewish heritage via his maternal grandmother

Rooney Pictured with his wife Coleen at the premiere for their 10-part documentary on Tuesday

'Having knowledge of what happened before our time and what people did for us to be able to enjoy the privileges we have now, we forget that sometimes.'

In a poignant scene outside the camp, his son Kit asks about the guard towers, where Rooney and their guide explain how the Nazis presented their prisoners from escaping.

He also visited with his England team-mates in 2012 during the European Championship in Poland and Ukraine.

'I’m a parent and it’s tough to see what happened there,' he said at the time.

'You’ve seen the amount of children who died. You see the children’s clothes and shoes, it’s really sad. You have to see it first hand.'

The Rooneys also take a trip to Krakow with third and fourth sons Kit, 10, and Cass, eight, due to the latter taking an interest in the Second World War from his studies.

Coleen, 40, notes that Wayne has 'a real bug for learning about different places in the world, culture, people, values'.

The Manchester United legend has opened up more about his spiritual side recently, explaining on a recent episode of Stick to United how he would like to visit the site of Jesus' baptism, the River Jordan.

'That’s where John the Baptist baptised Jesus, it would be really interesting to go.'

He used to wear a cross at training and revealed that he used to pray for his family before matches.

'I pray to God, of course. I believe in God,' he said in 2012.

'I pray in the physio room. I go in after my warm-up. I basically spend a few minutes in there on my own.

'I don’t pray to help me score goals. I pray for the health of me and everyone on the pitch.

'It is something I have always done. I pray at night. I pray for my family and friends and for the health of everyone I love.'

The new documentary is an intimate look into the life of the family, which also includes Kai, 16, and 13-year-old Klay, who both play for Manchester United's academy.

At the premiere for the show on Tuesday night, Rooney appeared to have turned back the clock as he displayed his new nose job, slimmer physique and smooth skin.

He looked smart in a crisp blue suit worn over a light-coloured shirt as he posed on the red carpet at the event, which was held at the Picturehouse in central London.

The 10-episode documentary is out today, covering a pivotal year in the Rooney household, after Wayne was sacked as Plymouth Argyle manager, swapping the touchline for school runs.

Rooney first shared the results of his nose job back in August after revealing he’d had an operation to fix it after breaking it twice during his football career.

The former forward first revealed he'd had the operation on his new podcast Stick to United, which he presents with football influencer Mark Goldbridge, a week after having surgery.

He revealed that he was feeling 'a little bit uncomfortable' following the surgery.

Coleen Rooney revealed she considered 'separating' from 'careless' husband Wayne following a series of explosive rows

It seems it's not always happy families in the Rooney household as the former England footballer and the I'm A Celebrity star admitted they can go days without talking to each other

He said: 'It's actually really lucky I've got no black eyes, but I've still got two plastic tubes up my nose, which are coming out very soon. I can't wait for them to come out.

'So, they've cut here [under my nostrils]... So, that's all stitched – a little bit uncomfortable.'

Wayne said the first time he broke his nose was during an FA Cup game against Preston North End in 2015 while playing for United.

He added that he remembered the game for 'a bit of a dive' he made to win a penalty.

Wayne continued: 'And then when I went to DC, I broke my nose again. That was a bad one then.

'So I needed surgery, but I've never had it. Put it off. And then this summer I thought get the World Cup out the way and I'll get it done. So had it done last week. Went well, but these tubes were horrible.'

The sportsman later recalled that during the same 3-1 victory against Preston at Deepdale, his former team-mate Marouane Fellaini also broke his nose.

'But he missed the next couple of games. I didn't miss any games,' he added.

Sports.title: Wayne Rooney hits out at Benjamin Sesko for wearing 'little stupid shinpads' as Man United legend questions striker's shin injury in brutal takedown
Sports.content:
Wayne Rooney hits out at Benjamin Sesko for wearing 'little stupid shinpads' as Man United legend questions striker's shin injury in brutal takedown

Wayne Rooney has questioned why Manchester United striker Benjamin Sesko sat out the club's 1-1 draw away at Fulham with a shin injury.

Rooney took to his podcast Stick to United to voice his displeasure with Sesko's absence from Sunday's game, implying that the Slovenian's shin injury was not serious enough to keep him out. 'Shin? Has he broken it?' said Rooney. 'You can hurt your shin, you can take tackles... I bet he's wearing them little stupid shinpads as well.'

The former United skipper did not stop there, later going on to say, 'If you're trying to play No9 [for Man United] and you've got a must-win game and you've got a sore shin and you're not playing... that's a big part of the problem.'

Later on in the show he reflected on his time at United, saying: 'Unless you physically can't play, you play when you're injured. I remember before games we used to get injections and the doctor used to put them in your arse.'

Two more former United players, Paul Scholes and Nicky Butt, also voiced their concern over the striker's omission from Sunday's squad.

Wayne Rooney did not mince his words when criticising the Slovenian international

Sesko has enjoyed purple patches in his short time at Old Trafford but has been unable to pick up consistent form

On their podcast, The Good, The Bad & The Football with Paddy McGuinness, Scholes aligned with his ex-teammate's view, saying: 'If it isn't broken, just wear your shinpads.' Butt then added: 'You're a player - you either break your shin or you don't play!'

As Daily Mail Sport reported yesterday, the comments by Butt and Scholes did not go down well in Slovenia, with Leeds defender Jaka Bijol backing Sesko to rise above it.

‘I hope and believe that Beni knows how to distance himself from this kind of pressure,’ he said. ‘When things aren't going your best on the pitch and you have certain doubts, reading things like this can make your confidence even worse.

‘He shouldn't pay too much attention to it, since we all know what quality he has. He himself knows what kind of footballer he is, and I think he always shows it with incredible things on the pitch.’

Another of Sesko's compatriots, Zan Vipotnik of Swansea, also spoke out in defence of the forward as he said: 'It's not easy for him. Recurring physical problems are bad, and to add to that it messes with your head... I really hope and believe his absence from the pitch will be as short as possible and that things will turn for the best very soon.'

Sports.title: Andy Burnham's football booze plot risks spoiling the experience for everybody - and if one person gets hurt, it will have been a failure, writes LUKE POWER
Sports.content:
If Andy Burnham seriously wants to reintroduce alcohol into the stands at the football, he should first be showered with Carlsberg by a rowdy gang of revellers.

He should then let the gaggle of drinkers do the same to his family or friends - or whichever politician he wants to hang out with at a match.

And then he should cram into a tight passageway for 100 minutes and let people brush past him with armfuls of beer, spilling it on his running shorts and making the floor stickier than a cheap nightclub in Freshers' Week.

Call it dramatic, but that is the fate that potentially awaits football fans if Burnham's plot to revive the reign of booze in the stands comes to fruition.

The Prime Minister is a genuine football man and means well, but is it a fate any of us really want?

The average British matchgoer is well-behaved and respectful but the truth is that all it takes is one rotten egg to spoil the experience for many others.

Andy Burnham's plan to allow booze in the stands is a risk to the safety and pleasant experience of fans

A parent taking their son or daughter to their first game, or a lifelong follower attending a match for their 80th birthday, shouldn't have to worry about sticky substances and plastic cups raining down from above.

They shouldn't have to deal with the complications that can arise from a lager lout getting rowdy, or the irritation of people shuffling past throughout the game.

The UK Football Policing Unit has warned that giving supporters easier access to alcohol would be 'irresponsible' as it could fuel more 'violent and disorderly behaviour'.

There is even the risk that players end up having booze or, worse, containers thrown at them.

And at the end of the day, it's a much mightier clean-up job for the stadium staff.

Many clubs will want it because it would allow them to generate greater revenue and you can bet your bottom dollar that particular institutions would rinse fans for all they've got.

Burnham's idea also has support from the Football Supporters' Association, who said: 'It’s unfair to criminalise fans for having a pint. We think that the legislation is outdated and deserves to be reviewed.'

It is worth thinking carefully about. Women's football and other sports make it work, but their atmospheres in general carry less edge. Perhaps, after a trial, having specific alcohol-approved sections could be welcome.

But if one person gets hurt, it will have been a failure.

Sports.title: Andy Carroll's Liverpool hell: Former star wanted to FAIL his Anfield medical and 'almost cried' at his unveiling - before his life spiralled out of control with boozy strip club and casino nights out
Sports.content:
Andy Carroll's Liverpool hell: Former star wanted to FAIL his Anfield medical and 'almost cried' at his unveiling - before his life spiralled out of control with boozy strip club and casino nights out

Andy Carroll has claimed that Newcastle held him 'over a barrel' in order to push through his mega-money move to Liverpool, as he opens up on his miserable spell on Merseyside.

Carroll, 37, became the Reds' record signing when he joined for £35million in January 2011 from Newcastle, making 58 appearances and scoring 11 goals for the club across two seasons.

However, the striker, who currently plays for Dagenham and Redbridge in the National League South – a club he co-owns with YouTuber KSI – has detailed how he never wanted to leave his boyhood club for Anfield in his new book, Owning It.

'After landing in Liverpool, we went straight to Anfield, where I had my medical,' he wrote. 'I kept thinking, "Please just fail this and you can go home." But I passed with flying colours.'

Carroll then detailed how the Magpies forced him to hand in a transfer request, otherwise he 'wouldn't play' for his beloved Geordies again.

The forward continued: 'Newcastle had me over a barrel, and I later learned that me putting in a transfer request meant that Newcastle got to keep 10% of the £35 million fee that otherwise would have gone to me.

Andy Carroll played for Liverpool between 2011 and 2013 and made 58 appearances

'The first thing I did after signing was phone my mom and dad. They were less upset that I'd left Newcastle for Liverpool than the fact I hadn't discussed it with them. "You need to pick up the cat," I said. And that was that.'

Carroll went on to describe how he 'looked like I wanted to cry' when being unveiled as a Liverpool player alongside Luis Suarez, despite forcing himself to explain that he was happy to be at the club.

Back in 2011, the story was that Carroll had forced a move away from Newcastle in order to be Liverpool's new main man after the departure of Fernando Torres to Chelsea.

But Carroll claims the rhetoric from St. James' Park was 'so far from the truth as to be almost laughable' and that then boss Alan Pardew was former owner Mike Ashley's 'puppet'.

He added: 'I was desperate to tell everyone what had really gone on in all its gory detail, but I thought it best to keep a lid on it.

Carroll opened up on how he was hoping to fail his medical at Liverpool and wanted to 'go home'

During his unveiling he describes how he looked like he 'wanted to cry' alongside fellow new signing Luis Suarez (right)

'I didn't want Liverpool and their fans to think I hated the idea of being there, especially as they'd shelled out so much for me and handed me the number 9 shirt as worn by Ian Rush, Robbie Fowler, and Torres.'

In his book, the striker also tackled his persistent problems with alcohol, which arose after he got his first big salary bump up.

'Before my weekly wage jumped to £2,500 a week, I was quite sensible,' said Carroll. 'But soon enough I was spending time in bars, strip joints and casinos. If everyone wanted a tray of shots, I'd buy a tray of shots.

'And while alcohol didn't turn me into some violent loon, a well-known footballer spending time in local establishments was bound to attract trouble.'

Carroll went on to play for a further seven clubs after leaving Liverpool, including the likes of West Ham, West Brom, Reading and even a return to Newcastle. His career also saw him take to the lower leagues of France with Bordeaux.

He continued: 'I'm not saying I could have had a career like Harry Kane but he is a great example of what kind of career you can have when you live a clean and disciplined life.

Carroll has releases a new book called Owning It where he has opened up about his career in depth

'Don't drink alcohol, eat the right things and spend hours each week in the gym and recover properly.

'Contrast, I wanted to live an everyday life. Go out at weekends with friends and go on holiday with friends in the international break. Go to music festivals and have a few too many drinks and a kebab now and again. Make mistakes without appearing in the papers.

'You could argue trying to live a normal life is incompatible with being a majorly successful sports person. But there is no point spending the rest of my days wishing I had a different mindset. I'm sure I've had more fun than your average player.'

Elsewhere in the book, the former England international also made the bombshell admission that he was sexually assaulted 'a few years ago' by a 'celebrity mate' who was later jailed for three years.

In a deeply candid passage in his new book, Carroll has told how he went through the 'traumatic' assault, which he has been unable to forget after a 'humiliating and horrendous' court case.

Carroll explained that the incident occurred one evening after he had played a game for Newcastle United when a 'celebrity mate' of his former partner invited himself round to watch a boxing match.

The striker wrote that after feeling uncomfortable during their interactions, he went to bed early and remembers feeling 'light-headed' after a 'few drinks'. He then claims he awoke to him sexually assaulting him.

Andy said he threw him out the house and 'smack[ed] him as hard as [he could]' and knocked him unconscious when he tried to re-enter. The star then called the police before sobbing in [his children's] nanny's arms.

Sports.title: Move over JJ Gabriel: With 'kid Messi' wanting out, here are three Man United wonderkids ready to replace him as the brightest young talent at Carrington - and how close they are to Michael Carrick's first team
Sports.content:
Whether JJ Gabriel is leaving Manchester United is, for now, still up in the air.

His family want his contract ripped up amid interest from Barcelona and Real Madrid, while the top executives at United, including director of football Jason Wilcox, chief executive Omar Berrada and minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe, are all in discussions about how to win them back round.

Gabriel is a generational talent, that much is obvious from watching him, and if he goes it would be a brutal blow for the club.

But he is not the only player emerging at Carrington that fans should be getting excited about.

Daily Mail Sport has picked out three academy stars who, like Gabriel, are waiting for their shot at a first-team debut in the years to come…

JJ Gabriel (pictured) wants out of Manchester United. Although his departure would be a brutal blow, there's several other talented teenagers at the club ready to fill the void

JIM THWAITES

Age: 18, Position: Midfielder

Seen as the best set-piece taker in all of academy football, Thwaites is so much more than just a corner and free-kick specialist.

The young midfielder, who has been taken under the wing of Bruno Fernandes in recent months since being elevated into first-team training sessions, is excellent as a deep-lying playmaker and has been a standout across the Under 18s and Under 21s in recent seasons.

Small in stature, many youth scouts have marvelled at what they see as a ‘Spanish’ player profile, a technical midfielder who isn’t dictating matches due to physicality, which is so often the case in the rough-and-tumble of English football.

Ruben Amorim was a big admirer and even name-checked Thwaites for his performances during United's 2025 post-season tour of Asia.

Thwaites was just 15 when he was fast-tracked into the Under 18s and later that season made his first foray into the Under 21s.

He deals well with being pressed and has a wide range of passes in his arsenal, as recently proven with a delightful chipped assist to Gabriel for his hat-trick goal against FK Sabah in the UEFA Youth League.

Jim Thwaites is regarded as the best set-piece taker United's academy - but there's so much more to him than that

Thwaites (right) has been taken under the wing of Bruno Fernandes (left) in recent months since being elevated into first-team training sessions

It's no surprise that he's a midfielder Michael Carrick has taken a shine to. The fact Thwaites did not leave on loan this summer underlined what Daily Mail Sport has reported for months – that Thwaites’ development is one of the top priorities for United.

If Gabriel heads for pastures new, Thwaites is absolutely the next academy star in line to break through.

NOAH AJAYI

Age: 17, Position: Forward

Daily Mail Sport understands Ajayi will soon ink a professional contract to commit his future to Manchester United after extensive negotiations.

All of Europe’s elite have been scouting and calling round about Ajayi – not least Bayern Munich and Barcelona – and the spectre of Gabriel has allowed his German team-mate to flourish somewhat in the shadows.

The 17-year-old already looks to have the physical frame to cope with playing against players much older than him and there is a burst to his initial acceleration that makes him a real threat playing out wide on either side.

Ajayi was strongly considered as an option to join Gabriel on the first team’s pre-season tour this summer, only for injury to curtail that.

Talented young winger Noah Ajayi is set to sign a professional contract at Old Trafford

A growth spurt to take Ajayi to 6ft 2in has pleased United staff. He has the frame to cope with facing opponents much older than him

There is also hope, as well as some expectation, that by the end of the current campaign Ajayi will have landed a first-team debut, such is his ability and trajectory now he is back fit and firing – which he proved last weekend in an electric outing for the Under 18s against Wolves.

A growth spurt to take him to 6ft 2in has pleased United staff. If Ajayi hasn’t been on your radar, start keeping an eye on the Germany Under 19s international.

JAICE DORE

Age: 15, Position: Forward

A wildcard pick to finish, and a winger that some youth football experts believe is one of the most exciting prospects in years due to his freewheeling playing style.

Dore appears to play the game much like a young Jadon Sancho did while he was at Manchester City, exciting supporters and getting them out of their seats.

During the summer, the 15-year-old made his debut for Darren Fletcher’s Under 18s and Dore, who came through grassroots side Fletcher Moss, just like Marcus Rashford did once upon a time, is an explosive dribbler who has shown an ability to score off both feet.

Some youth football experts believe Jaice Dore, 15, is one of the most exciting prospects in years due to his freewheeling playing style

Dore has not been accelerated anywhere near as much as Gabriel, and both Thwaites and Ajayi are much closer to a first team debut as of today.

But Dore is standing above the rest in every match he plays these days. A spot in the Under 18s this season, with a view to playing for the Under 21s next season if his progression continues apace, makes him the teenager to follow the progress of moving forward.

Sports.title: Alexander Isak fires back at Newcastle icon Alan Shearer - 'A bit irrelevant'
Sports.content:
Alexander Isak fires back at Newcastle icon Alan Shearer - 'A bit irrelevant'

Alan Shearer suggested that Alexander Isak should have insisted on taking Liverpool's late penalty in the 2-2 draw against Newcastle last month, having been given a hostile reception

View 2 Images Alexander Isak was criticised for not taking a penalty against Newcastle (Image: Richard Sellers/Getty Images)

Alexander Isak has shot back at Alan Shearer, calling his criticism "irrelevant" after his little dig at the Liverpool striker for not taking a penalty against former club Newcastle.

‌



Isak was bombarded with boos and abuse upon his return to St James' Park last month as Liverpool drew 2-2 with Newcastle. The away side earned a point thanks to Dominik Szoboszlai's last-gasp penalty following a foul by Lewis Hall on Victor Munoz.

‌



Isak left Newcastle for Liverpool last summer in an extremely contentious £125million transfer, which came about after he refused to play for the Magpies to force through the move. The Sweden international is not popular on Tyneside and the home fans made their feelings clear on August 23.

‌



Newcastle legend Shearer said Isak was "battered" by the fans and should have taken the late spot-kick as a way of responding.

FOLLOW OUR LIVERPOOL FB PAGE! Latest Reds news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

‌



Speaking on The Rest Is Football, he said: "I was thinking 'Go on, come and take the penalty! What have you got? Go and grab the ball and take the penalty Isak.'

"I wanted him to go and take it. I was thinking 'Come on, you've been absolutely battered. Lets see what you've got. Go and grab the ball and take the penalty.'"

But speaking to Swedish outlet Fotbollskanalen while on international duty, Isak gave his comments short shrift. "Szoboszlai was the penalty taker for that match," he said.

‌



“It’s a bit irrelevant. Those are team matters and it’s not for the media or the supporters to decide who should take a penalty.”

View 2 Images Dominik Szoboszlai rescued Liverpool a late draw at St James' Park (Image: Robbie Jay Barratt - AMA, Getty Images)

Isak also brushed off the hostile reception. "I was prepared for the atmosphere, so it was a special match," he said calmly.

‌



The 27-year-old made a slow start to life at Liverpool following his blockbuster transfer, with a lack of match fitness and a serious injury holding him back. But he has started his second campaign with four goals in five Premier League matches for the Reds and is delighted to have finally settled under Andoni Iraola's management.

“It means a lot. If you compare it to last year, I feel I’m in a much better place now physically and in every possible way," he said. "There are many matches where I feel I should and want to contribute more and be more involved. There’s nothing strange about that.

“My first feeling is that we’re more stable defensively. Then we have a lot to improve offensively. The foundations are there and the bar is high.”

Article continues below

Isak is currently away with Sweden, who face four games against Romania (twice), Poland and Bosnia and Herzegovina. Having overcome his fitness issues, the striker is confident he can contribute for both club and country without needing to be wrapped in cotton wool.

"Graham [Potter] is free to use me, but it’s four matches in a short period, so we’ll need to look at playing time for the sake of the team," he said. "If you play four lots of 90 minutes, maybe you don’t give your best, but I feel good and there shouldn’t be any problems.”
