Following his surprise pole position at another high-speed track earlier this month, Pierre Gasly put his Alpine a strong seventh, ahead of Oscar Piastri’s McLaren and Isack Hadjar’s Red Bull. Esteban Ocon completed the top 10, though his team mate was unable to set a competitive time as his engine failed when he rejoined the track following the restart.

Oliver Bearman therefore ended the session 20th ahead of the Aston Martin drivers, both of which have already picked up grid penalties for power unit parts changes. Fernando Alonso was further delayed by an oil leak in his power unit.

Sports.title: Russell fastest as hydraulic problem halts Antonelli in first practice | Formula 1
Sports.content:
George Russell led the opening practice session for the Azerbaijan Grand Prix while a technical problem delayed his team mate.

Russell’s best lap, aided by a significant slipstream from a rival car, was exactly four-tenths of a second quicker than the next-closest driver, Max Verstappen. However Russell’s session almost came to an early end when he abandoned his attempt to take turn three and swerved into the run-off area, narrowly missing the barrier as he did.

Verstappen began the session strongly. The Red Bull driver was fastest over the opening 10 minutes, running on hard tyres, before Antonelli beat his time.

Despite his stoppage, the world championship leader ended the session with the fifth-fastest time. The two Ferrari drivers also beat him, Charles Leclerc only fractionally slower than Verstappen.

Liam Lawson returned to Racing Bulls after his brief stint at Red Bull’s senior team and set the sixth-fastest time. Isack Hadjar, back in the car Lawson drove in the last three races, was only able to do eight laps before Red Bull told him to stop due to a technical problem.

Nico Hulkenberg put his heavily updated Audi seventh-fastest. He briefly came to a stop near the end of the session but was able to resume.

Oscar Piastri set the eighth-fastest time with his final lap of the session. His running in McLaren’s updated MCL40 was disrupted when the team identified a potential problem on his team mate’s car and told him to stop, though Piastri was able to rejoin the track for a final lap.

The final places in the top 10 went to Pierre Gasly and Esteban Ocon, the latter also stopping with a fault at the pit lane exit near the end of the session.

Carlos Sainz Jnr was the quickest of the two Williams drivers in their updated car. However he had to stop in the pits early in the session due to a fire on his right-rear brake, potentially related to the new duct furniture Williams has introduced as part of its extensive reworking of the FW48.

Sports.title: Social Media: Ben Sulayem defends Gasly after latest abuse from Colapinto fans | Brief
Sports.content:
FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem has condemned the online abuse directed at Pierre Gasly by supporters of his team mate.

Gasly briefly delayed Franco Colapinto during the latter stages of the Spanish Grand Prix two weeks ago. The driver and his family have since received abusive messages on social media.

“The online abuse directed at Pierre Gasly and his family is completely unacceptable,” said Ben Sulayem in a post. “Pierre has my full support, and I strongly condemn this behaviour. No driver, official, volunteer or fan should have to face this.

“Incidents like this are why I founded the United Against Online Abuse initiative. We simply cannot accept online hate within our sport and we all have a responsibility – governing bodies, teams, drivers, fans and social media platforms – to challenge this behaviour and create an environment built on respect.”

Colapinto’s supporters have been repeatedly accused of aiming abuse at drivers and other figures in the sport, including Jack Doohan last year, his own team this year and the FIA’s stewards last month.

“Competition and passion are at the heart of motorsport, but abuse has no place in it,” Ben Sulayem added. “We must continue to stand together and take meaningful action to protect everyone in our sporting community.”

Sports.title: Ocon confirms he is a “free agent” for 2027 as rumours link Camara to Haas | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Esteban Ocon looks set to leave Haas at the end of the season as the driver admitted he is a “free agent” for 2027.

The 30-year-old joined the team from Alpine last year. He was out-scored by rookie team mate Oliver Bearman last year and lies behind his team mate in the standings.

“At the moment I’m definitely a free agent for next year,” said Ocon in Baku. “[There are] all these discussions and there are certain topics in the background that are out of my control at this moment. So I’m focused on the track, trying to deliver the best I can and getting the result that this team deserves.”

Neither Haas driver has scored since Ocon’s ninth-place finish in Monaco.

Ocon said he’s been “really happy with my personal performance” lately. “I think I’ve been getting the maximum out of the car for quite a while now and we’ve never doubted about it.

“Of course, when the car is working, it helps [you] to get something better. When the inconsistencies of the cars are here, where you struggle more, you don’t look as good.

“But I know that I’m exploiting the maximum of the package that I have every single time. So that’s strong.

Ocon ran 10th at the last round in Madrid prior to his pit stop, but fell to 11th at the finish.

“I’m the last one to have scored for the team in Monaco, but it’s been a while. But we were [running] in the points in Madrid, we got both Audis at the start, and we lost it in the pit lane. So this is something we will get stronger on now. But it was a very strong weekend.

“I’m happy with my performance. So we need to keep going here, hopefully have another strong one. There’s usually things happening on this track so I’m looking forward to driving here.”

Sports.title: Antonelli has “perfect driving style” for 2026 cars – Russell | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Andrea Kimi Antonelli is enjoying an extraordinarily successful second season in Formula 1 because his driving style works perfectly with the current generation of cars, says his team mate.

George Russell is Antonelli’s closest rival at the top of the championship standings, but the second-year driver is 81 points ahead. This is a sharp contrast to last year, when Russell out-scored Antonelli by 319 points to 150.

While Russell said Antonelli’s ability was clear before this season, he believes the reduction in aerodynamic downforce and grip this year has played to his team mate’s strengths.

“Of course Kimi is extremely talented,” said Russell. “He’s an incredible driver and has been fast in his whole career.

“I think his driving style is very similar to what he had last year and I think with just how things have fallen this year, it’s kind of the perfect driving style for these cars.”

Russell believes the same is true of other drivers, including Lando Norris, who is the only driver to have won more than one round this season.

“If you look last year, there are definitely trends,” said Russell. “If you look at Brazil last year, Kimi had a really strong race and Lando won in Brazil, and they’re two drivers who are always very strong on the low grip tracks and they’re two drivers who are arguably the best-performing drivers of this season.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“He’s an amazing driver and he was of course doing extremely well last year as well. Let’s see next year if it changes or not, but certainly his natural driving style suits very well for this regulation.”

Charles Leclerc echoed Russell’s view that Antonelli’s potential was clear despite his patchy rookie campaign last year.

“I wish I knew, but clearly he’s doing something that works very well,” said Leclerc. “But to be honest, it’s not that it comes as a complete surprise.

“If I look at Kimi going through the junior ranks, I think it was quite clear for everybody that he had something very special. If you look obviously at his first year in Formula 1, I think he probably faced challenges – it is not up to me to go into detail, I don’t know, but surely he had some struggles in the first year – but this year has been extremely impressive. I mean, from the first race to now, he’s been perfect and driving at a very high level against a driver that I rate extremely high as well, which is George. So he’s doing an incredible job.”

However Leclerc said there is only so much he can tell about Antonelli’s qualities from outside the Mercedes team.

“To [tell] you exactly why he’s so fast, and why he is outstandingly fast this year compared to last year, is very difficult for me. We are all here analysing the data of everybody but we can only go up to a certain amount of detail, then you really need the data of the actual car to dig into more detail.

“So it’s difficult. But his laps look a lot on the limit but somehow he manages to do the lap when it counts and that’s been very impressive to watch.”

Sports.title: Tyson Fury vs  Anthony Joshua Finally Official: December 11 in Cardiff on Netflix
Sports.content:
The British heavyweight rivals will meet at Principality Stadium after a dispute over the venue delayed their long-awaited fight.

Tyson Fury (36-2-1, 25 KOs) and Anthony Joshua (30-4, 27 KOs) will finally fight on Friday, December 11, 2026, at Cardiff’s Principality Stadium, live on Netflix. The confirmation ends months of negotiations over where the British heavyweight clash would take place.

The venue dispute is settled. Joshua’s camp had insisted on staging the bout in Britain, while New York’s Madison Square Garden became a serious alternative.

“I can now confirm that Fury Vs Joshua will be coming to the UK, as I promised British boxing fans. The time for talking is over……..” Turki Alalshikh wrote on X.

Both fighters signed earlier this year. A date and venue remained unresolved, however, allowing the dispute to drag on despite their agreement to face each other. Fury repeatedly blamed Joshua in public and suggested he could pursue a third fight against Oleksandr Usyk.

Dana White said: “For more than a decade, boxing fans have been clamoring for the heavyweight showdown between Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua. Together, they bring 66 wins, 52 knockouts and multiple heavyweight world titles into the ring. On December 11, two of the biggest heavyweights of this generation finally collide and the winner will take a significant place in heavyweight history.”

Netflix says White and The Ring will collaborate to promote the fight, despite Eddie Hearn’s earlier insistence that White would not be its promoter.

Joshua has boxed at Principality Stadium twice before, stopping Carlos Takam and then outpointing Joseph Parker to add the WBO heavyweight belt to his collection. He returns to face the British rival whose name has followed him through years of callouts and failed negotiations.

Both men came through summer bouts.

Joshua survived two first-round knockdowns against Kristian Prenga in July before stopping him in the second. Fury stopped Mariusz Wach after seven rounds in Thailand that month, having returned in April to outpoint Aslanbek Makhmudov at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.

Those victories kept their meeting alive. Now the former heavyweight champions have a confirmed December date in Britain, with Netflix carrying the broadcast.

Sports.title: Manny Pacquiao and Shakur Stevenson Remain in Cardiff Talks
Sports.content:
Manny Pacquiao against Shakur Stevenson remains under discussion for the proposed Anthony Joshua-Tyson Fury card in Cardiff. It would give the event a second major fight, but neither Pacquiao nor Stevenson has received a bout agreement.

BoxingScene’s Lance Pugmire reports that two people connected to the talks say Netflix wants the matchup as part of a “double main event.” December 11 is the date under consideration at Principality Stadium, with December 18 also possible. Pacquiao adviser Jas Mathur told BoxingScene that Pacquiao’s financial terms are still being negotiated.

That leaves a great deal to settle before anyone can call this a fight. The Cardiff show itself has yet to be formally announced, and moving Joshua-Fury from the previously discussed Madison Square Garden setting means assembling the rest of the card around a different venue and date.

Pacquiao-Stevenson would bring two very different attractions to that card. Stevenson, 29, is coming off his January win over Teofimo Lopez and has since signed with Zuffa Boxing. Pacquiao, 47, drew with Mario Barrios in his July 2025 return. His name would draw attention far beyond the usual boxing audience, though the long layoff and age difference would become part of the conversation as soon as the fight was announced.

The proposed pairing also raises a practical question: what weight would they fight at? Pacquiao’s return came at welterweight, while Stevenson’s recent work has been at lighter weights. No weight, number of rounds, or title terms have been announced.

For now, the news is that Pacquiao-Stevenson has survived the reported switch to Cardiff and remains in Netflix’s plans, according to BoxingScene. The decisive development would be agreements reaching both fighters. Until then, it belongs on the list of fights being negotiated, rather than the Joshua-Fury undercard.

Pacquiao turns 48 on December 17. If the fight lands on December 18, Shakur would face him one day after his birthday. Pacquiao won his first world title in 1998, before Shakur turned two.

That age difference makes the matchup a hard sell as a competitive fight. If Shakur wins easily, how much credit does he get for beating a man nearly two decades older? If he boxes his way to a quiet decision, Pacquiao’s name may bring viewers to Netflix, but the fight may give them little reason to watch Shakur again.

Pacquiao’s fame can make this a major event. Turning it into a fight that helps Shakur is another matter. First, both men need to agree to terms; neither has received a bout agreement.

Sports.title: Shakur Stevenson Picks Leonard, But Ray Robinson Set The Harder Standard
Sports.content:
Shakur Stevenson prefers Sugar Ray Leonard to Sugar Ray Robinson. It is easy to see why. Leonard’s speed, movement, and command of distance resemble the qualities Shakur prizes in his own boxing. But Leonard’s finest wins also required him to fight through danger, and Robinson did that across a schedule neither man came close to matching.

“I like SRL better then I like SRR, This might make my people mad but SRL was one hellavu fighter to me his level was extremely high!!” said Shakur on X.

Stevenson posted that on X on September 22. He had previously called Robinson “buns,” then conceded Robinson was a great fighter and said he had been talking trash. His preference for Leonard is consistent with that view.

Leonard was no fighter who simply ran from trouble. He lost a hard 15 rounds to Roberto Durán, came back to beat him, and stopped Thomas Hearns late in their first fight. His footwork gave him choices; when those fights demanded more, he had offense and resolve to draw upon.

Robinson’s record makes the comparison tougher for Shakur. At age 29, Robinson was 108-1-2 with 72 knockouts. Shakur Stevenson (25-0, 11 KOs) has fought 25 times at the same age. Leonard had fought 34. Different eras produced different schedules, but Robinson’s total still speaks to his ability to win, recover, and do it again.

Shakur’s defense is exceptional. What remains unproven is how he would respond if his legs slowed and an opponent forced him to fight for long stretches at close range. Leonard showed he had answers when movement was insufficient. Robinson showed them more than a hundred times before his 29th birthday, backed by power Shakur has yet to display.

Shakur can like Leonard better. If he is judging the full range of what a fighter had to survive and deliver, Robinson deserves a closer look.

Nobody from modern eras, Leonard included, touches what Robinson accomplished by 29.

Robinson was 128-1-2 with 84 knockouts by the time he hit his 30th birthday, and that lone defeat to Jake LaMotta was avenged multiple times over. He was fighting every few weeks, traveling by car or train, taking on rugged contenders in 15-round fights with small gloves and no modern sports science. If Leonard had tried to keep that exact pace against that level of weekly attrition, his body would have broken down even sooner. Leonard had brittle hands and a detached retina by fight 28. Robinson had a jaw made of granite, brutal endurance, and lethal power in both hands.

Shakur picking Leonard makes sense purely through the lens of modern comfort. Leonard represents the blueprint Shakur relates to: the flashy television superstar, the Olympic gold medalist, the master of lateral movement, hand speed, and distance management. Leonard showed that a fighter could dictate terms, generate huge paydays, and maintain an aura without having to fight forty times a year in smoke-filled arenas.

Where Shakur’s comparison falls completely flat is what Leonard actually did when boxing finesse failed. When Leonard got pulled into absolute hell against Roberto Duran in Montreal, he stood flat-footed and fought. When he was fading and behind on the cards against Thomas Hearns, he unleashed a vicious, predatory assault to close the show. Leonard had a ruthless finishing instinct.

Shakur takes the defensive, perimeter-oriented parts of Leonard’s style and strips away the violent bite. Robinson was a destructive puncher who could knock an opponent out going backward or forward. Shakur is a pure points collector who treats contact like a disaster.

Shakur looking at Robinson and favoring Leonard sounds like modern revisionism. It is a fighter who relies on safety and low output, trying to validate his own approach, overlooking the fact that both Sugar Rays had an appetite for destruction that Shakur has never shown inside a ring.

Sports.title: Jaime Munguia May Vacate Rather Than Fight Bektemir Melikuziev
Sports.content:
Jaime Munguia may give up his WBA super middleweight title rather than defend it against Bektemir Melikuziev. Rick Glaser says Munguia’s team is considering that option. If his information is right, the decision would fit a career that has generally been managed with care. I expected Munguia’s team to have little appetite for Bek once the mandatory fight was ordered.

Glaser says Munguia’s camp is taking a “deep dive into the idea of giving up the title.” He has not said Munguia has vacated. The WBA has given the two sides until October 21 to make a deal and may call a purse bid if they fail to agree.

The Golden Boy connection makes this especially revealing. Melikuziev has fought under its banner since turning professional, and the company knows what its own fighter would bring against Munguia. Bek is a powerful southpaw with a damaging body attack. Munguia’s willingness to take punches while pressing forward would give him chances to land, but it would also give Bek chances to hurt him.

Munguia (46-2, 35 KOs) accepted the Canelo Alvarez fight for a huge payday and lost. Bruno Surace then knocked him out in a matchup Munguia was favored to win. Sergiy Derevyanchenko gave Munguia a hard fight, so his record is not free of risk. Melikuziev presents a different calculation: considerable danger with nowhere near Canelo’s commercial reward.

The WBA belt helped Munguia regain world champion status when he beat José Armando Reséndiz in May. Defending it is another matter. A purse bid could also take the choice of date, venue, and broadcaster out of his team’s hands. Vacating would leave Munguia free to pursue a bigger name at 168, though that freedom would come at Bek’s expense.

Melikuziev (17-1, 11 KOs) beat Darius Fulghum in a WBA eliminator in May 2025, then watched Munguia get the fight with Reséndiz. Bek told The Ring he had been assured he would get the next shot. If Munguia vacates, Bek may still get a chance to win the belt. He would lose the chance to win it from Munguia, a victory that would mean far more for his career.

We’re seeing the new age of belt-holders. Champions giving up their belts exposes the entire modern hustle around world titles. Fighters treat sanctioning body belts like disposable leverage tools rather than something to defend against legitimate threats. They want the belt purely to slap “world champion” on a poster, collect the promotional bump, and leverage it into an in-house payday.

The second a dangerous, low-profile puncher gets ordered as a mandatory, they drop the trinket in the trash and run. Look at the pattern playing out right now. Hamzah Sheeraz walked away from his belt rather than get in the ring with Janibek Alimkhanuly. Teofimo Lopez is on the verge of playing the same game,

Now Jaime Munguia’s camp looks ready to dump the WBA strap because Bektemir Melikuziev offers pure risk with zero casual crossover appeal. Bektemir is a nightmare matchup for a flawed fighter like Munguia. Bek is a heavy-handed, compact southpaw who specializes in cracking the ribs and punishing guys who march forward without defense.

Against Bektemir, Munguia risks getting stopped on regular DAZN for modest money, completely torpedoing his marketability for another mega-fight. Dumping the title completely strips away the pretense of championship prestige. Decades ago, winning a belt meant you took on whoever climbed the ladder, regardless of style or reward. What we’re seeing now is champions treating mandatory defenses like bad business propositions.

If Munguia vacates, Bektemir Melikuziev should get the first chance at the vacant WBA title, but the WBA would still have to choose his opponent. Its current rankings put Canelo Alvarez at No. 2 and José Armando Reséndiz at No. 3. A Canelo fight would be the biggest prize for Bek, though there is no indication Canelo wants it.

Reséndiz looks like the more realistic choice: he lost the belt to Munguia in May and would have a chance to win it back. That would give Bek a title opportunity, but it would deny him the higher-profile victory over Munguia that he has spent more than a year pursuing.

Sports.title: Cuban Boxing Greatness Crossed a Dividing Line
Sports.content:
Cuba produced professional stars before it became an Olympic boxing power. That history makes any list of its greatest fighters difficult to rank. Kid Chocolate and Kid Gavilan built their names in long professional careers; Teófilo Stevenson and Félix Savón never fought professionally. The dividing line was a political decision in 1962 that changed what a Cuban boxer could do with his talent.

Chocolate was a major New York attraction in the 1930s, admired for his speed and two-handed punching. Gavilan later won the welterweight title and made the bolo punch his signature. Luis Rodriguez added another championship to Cuba’s professional history when he beat Emile Griffith for the welterweight title in 1963. These men built their reputations in fights against the leading professionals of their day.

After Cuba banned professional boxing, a fighter who wanted that career had to pursue it abroad. José Nápoles became a welterweight champion after making his home in Mexico. José Legrá won the featherweight title while based in Spain. Later fighters such as Erislandy Lara left Cuba to compete for professional titles. Their success carried a personal cost that a list of wins and belts cannot show.

Cuba also built an amateur program under coach Alcides Sagarra that produced generations of Olympic champions. Stevenson won heavyweight gold in 1972, 1976 and 1980. Savón won the same prize in 1992, 1996 and 2000. Their medals need no imagined professional careers to give them value. But the absence of professional fights leaves one question open: how would the system’s best have performed against established champions over twelve rounds?

Guillermo Rigondeaux gave that question a partial answer. He won Olympic gold in 2000 and 2004, then left Cuba and became a professional champion. In 2013, he beat Nonito Donaire in a super bantamweight title fight, controlling distance and making a dangerous puncher miss repeatedly. Donaire was a proven champion, and Rigondeaux’s amateur schooling held up against him. One fight cannot settle how Stevenson or Savón would have fared as professionals, but it gives this comparison something firmer than speculation.

Lara’s December 2025 defense of the WBA middleweight title shows that Cuban fighters still succeed on the professional side of that divide. The strongest case for Cuba’s boxing greatness comes from looking at both sides: champions who proved themselves over long professional careers, Olympic greats whose careers took another course, and Rigondeaux, who crossed between them and beat one of the best.

Sports.title: Ben Whittaker Faces Conor Wallace With Little Buzz
Sports.content:
Matchroom’s countdown poster for the October 3 fight puts Ben Whittaker front and center in gold gloves, treating Conor Wallace like an afterthought tucked near the bottom. That tells you everything about how this IBF final eliminator is being sold. Matchroom wants the spectacle, yet they are hiding the very man brought in to provide a test at Birmingham’s Utilita Arena on DAZN.

The sanctioning body slapped a number two ranking on Wallace, dangling a mandatory shot at Dmitry Bivol for the victor. Matchroom calls this Whittaker’s most demanding fight to date, yet their own promotional material treats Wallace like a ghost.

Wallace is a heavy-handed southpaw who thrives on forward pressure, precisely the style that gave Whittaker fits against Liam Cameron. Cameron refused to play along with the showboating, got right in Whittaker’s chest, took away his operating room, and forced a difficult inside brawl that ended in a bizarre technical draw. That fight exposed the cracks in Whittaker’s viral persona.

Whittaker loves dropping his hands, leaning back, and relying on pure reflexes against timid opposition. A southpaw stepping outside the lead foot and drilling straight left hands down the pipe shatters that rhythm instantly. If Wallace gets past the jab, cuts off the ring, and forces Whittaker into the ropes, the fancy footwork disappears, leaving a grueling night of trench warfare.

Wallace built that top ranking touring the regional Australian circuit, highlighted by a narrow split decision win over Jerome Pampellone. Whittaker, despite his Olympic silver medal pedigree, spent his recent dates clowning against Richard Rivera, Braian Nahuel Suarez, and Benjamin Gavazi. Both fighters avoided the domestic shark tank of Joshua Buatsi, Willy Hutchinson, or Anthony Yarde to land in this position.

Taking an open sanctioning door is standard boxing business, but Dmitry Bivol waits on the other side. Bivol dismantles loose showmen with relentless robotic fundamentals, punishing anyone who drops their hands. Wallace is the final chance to discover if Whittaker has actual substance when an opponent fires back with bad intentions, and Matchroom is foolish to hide the danger.

Eddie Hearn labels Ben Whittaker a generational talent, but Matchroom matches him like an unpolished novice they are terrified of getting touched. If a promoter genuinely believes an Olympic silver medalist is that caliber of fighter, you do not keep him in bubble wrap for four years. Look at genuine generational fighters or top-tier Olympians: Vasiliy Lomachenko was fighting for a world title in his second professional bout. Sugar Ray Leonard, Floyd Mayweather Jr., and Andre Ward were dismantling legitimate, battle-tested contenders by their thirteenth fight.

Whittaker is 29 years old. He is not a 20-year-old kid who needs physical maturation or time to grow into his man strength. At his age, an elite fighter should be in his prime, yet Matchroom is treating this October 3 date with Conor Wallace like a massive hurdle rather than what it actually is: an exercise in matchmaking self-preservation.

Wallace is an eight-year pro whose record looks manufactured in a lab. He racked up wins on the Australian circuit against obscure opposition, barely edged Jerome Pampellone by split decision, and somehow landed the IBF number two ranking because the sanctioning bodies operate on regional belt accumulation rather than quality. S

erious boxing fans know Wallace is not a top ten light heavyweight in the world. He is a convenient mark with an inflated ranking.The fact that Matchroom selected Wallace for an IBF final eliminator instead of testing Whittaker against domestic threats tells the whole story. Why hasn’t Whittaker been matched against Joshua Buatsi, Anthony Yarde, Willy Hutchinson, or Dan Azeez? Those are the domestic names that would force Whittaker to prove he belongs.

Matchroom deliberately avoided that gauntlet because they know what happens when someone refuses to buy into the showmanship. The Liam Cameron fight gave away the game. When Cameron got inside, roughed Whittaker up, and took away his operating space, the flashy reflex defense fell apart. Whittaker looked ordinary, rattled, and completely out of ideas before that bizarre ring fall ended things in a technical draw. That reveals what Hearn and his team likely see behind closed doors in sparring. If a fighter looks unbeatable in the gym against world-class work, a promoter moves him fast to cash in.

When a promoter slow walks a 29-year-old Olympic medalist against handpicked opposition, it means the gym reports are raising red flags: leaks in the defensive fundamentals, getting clipped when trading on the inside, or an engine that cannot handle a relentless twelve-round pace.

It appears that Matchroom is trying to sneak Whittaker through an open back door to a massive payday against Dmitry Bivol without having him run a real gauntlet. Wallace was brought in to provide the illusion of a world-level eliminator without the actual danger. If Whittaker were the transcendent force Hearn claims, the training wheels would have come off years ago.

AI-improved.

Sports.title: Gerrie Coetzee’s Bionic Hand Ends Michael Dokes’s Reign
Sports.content:
Michael Dokes had the faster hands and a title defense close to home on September 23, 1983. Gerrie Coetzee had two failed title bids and a reputation for fading late. Ten rounds later, Dokes was on the canvas, and Coetzee was the WBA heavyweight champion.

Don King billed the fight at Richfield Coliseum as “The Buckeye Homecoming,” though the crowd was about 7,000 in an arena that held 22,000. Dokes (26-0-2, 15 KOs), from nearby Akron, was a 5-1 favorite over Coetzee (28-3-1, 17 KOs). His title reign had begun with a disputed first-round stoppage of Mike Weaver, followed by a draw in their rematch.

Coetzee knew how a strong start could go wrong. John Tate had outlasted him over 15 rounds, and Weaver had stopped him in the 13th. Dokes showed his speed early and cut the challenger near the right eye in round two. Coetzee took the punches and kept coming.

His rebuilt right hand had earned him the nickname “The Bionic Hand,” and it remained one of his best weapons. Dokes had another punch to consider that night, though: Coetzee used his left hook more often than he had in earlier title bids. The hook made his attack less predictable while he pressed the quicker champion.

In the fifth, a short left-right combination put Dokes down on one knee. He rose quickly and fought back, but the knockdown changed the terms of the fight. Coetzee did not slow down as he had against Tate and Weaver. He stayed close enough to make Dokes work and reached the tenth ahead on all three official cards. Dokes still had good moments, particularly in the eighth; this was no uncontested march to the finish.

Coetzee landed two heavy rights past the midpoint of the tenth and followed Dokes into a corner. Dokes tied him up, but after referee Tony Perez separated them, Coetzee attacked again. A left-right combination sent Dokes down. The bell rang during the count, and Perez counted him out at the official time of 3:08.

The right hand helped Coetzee win the title on his third attempt. It also broke again, requiring surgery and keeping him out of the ring for more than a year. He lost the belt to Greg Page in his first defense. Dokes later admitted that cocaine and Jack Daniel’s had been part of his preparation, but that admission does not account for Coetzee’s work over ten rounds. On a night built to celebrate Dokes, the fighter everyone thought would fade was still throwing with force at the end.

Sports.title: Richardson Hitchins Accepts Keyshawn Davis Fight
Sports.content:
Richardson Hitchins agreeing to face Keyshawn Davis at welterweight exposes a massive tactical gamble that could backfire on both men. Hitchins cannot survive by running all night, while Keyshawn faces an agonizing dilemma: turn into a relentless pressure fighter or get picked apart from long range for twelve miserable rounds.

Keith Connolly admitted the cold truth to his man: this is a coin flip, yet the financial payout justifies the danger.

“We’ve accepted the fight. We’re waiting for a couple of commercial things to come through, so to speak, a date to be set. I told Hitchins, it’s a 50-50 fight. But I said, ‘This is the type of fight that if you take it, it’s worth the risk because of the money we’d be receiving, but also the opportunity of two guys fighting in their prime,’” Connolly said to Brian Custer.

Gustavo Lemos already provided the blueprint to rip Hitchins apart by refusing to let him settle into a rhythm. Keyshawn brings sharper reflexes and slicker counterpunches than Lemos, yet patience will ruin him here. Hitchins wants a slow, sleepy track meet where he can flick out light jabs and steal rounds without getting hit.

Keyshawn must trap Hitchins on the ropes, rip shots to the ribs, and fight through the inevitable clinches. Stepping into that pocket comes with severe danger. Hitchins excels at leaning on opponents, tying up arms, and forcing resets that drain an attacker’s stamina. Keyshawn cannot afford to reset every time Hitchins grabs him.

The jump to 147 pounds favors Hitchins physically. Keyshawn built his career down at lightweight, while Hitchins carries natural length and leverage that will look massive inside the ring. Keyshawn will not overpower Hitchins with size. He has to take punches to land his own, risking exhaustion against a rangy spoiler who knows how to make opponents miss.

Placing this fight on a massive Tyson Fury vs. Anthony Joshua stadium event or a David Benavidez vs. Michal Cieslak bill is the only way promoters can afford both purses. Neither man draws enough single ticket buyers to headline on their own. Once the money is guaranteed, Keyshawn must decide if he truly has the engine to chase Hitchins down.

Ghana News.title: Democracy must not be for sale: Who pays for Ghana’s politics, and how do we confront money, influence and accountability?
Ghana News.content:
Ghana has come a long way in the practice of constitutional democracy. But our democratic journey has never been a straight line. From colonial constitutional reforms to independence, military interventions, civilian governments and successive constitutional experiments, Ghana’s political history has been shaped by both democratic aspirations and interruptions.

Understanding that history is important because it reminds us that democratic governance is not something we inherit permanently; it is something each generation must protect, strengthen and improve.

The 1951 Constitution introduced a Legislative Assembly made up predominantly of elected African representatives. The 1954 Constitution further expanded African participation and strengthened representative government. These developments contributed to the attainment of self-government and, ultimately, independence.

Ghana became independent in 1957 under a parliamentary system. The Governor-General represented the British Monarch, while executive authority was exercised through a Cabinet answerable to Parliament. Universal adult suffrage provided the basis for electing the National Assembly.

In 1960, Ghana became a republic. The office of Governor-General was replaced by that of President, and Kwame Nkrumah became the country’s first President. The First Republic subsequently moved towards a one-party system.

On 24 February 1966, President Nkrumah was overthrown in a military coup. The National Liberation Council (NLC) suspended the Constitution and governed through decrees. The country returned to constitutional civilian rule under the 1969 Constitution, establishing the Second Republic. That Republic was, however, overthrown on 13 January 1972.

The National Redemption Council (NRC), later transformed into the Supreme Military Council (SMC), ruled until another military intervention in 1979. The Armed Forces Revolutionary Council (AFRC) subsequently transferred power to an elected civilian government, ushering in the Third Republic.

That Republic lasted only about two years. On 31 December 1981, Flight Lieutenant Jerry John Rawlings led another military takeover, establishing the Provisional National Defence Council (PNDC), which ruled until the return to constitutional democracy.

The adoption of the 1992 Constitution after a referendum marked another defining moment. Multiparty elections were held in December 1992, and the Fourth Republic formally began on 7 January 1993.

The 1992 Constitution established Ghana as a democratic constitutional state in which sovereignty resides in the people. It provides for constitutional government, separation of powers, fundamental rights, democratic elections, checks and balances and the rule of law. Most importantly, it established elections, not military intervention as the legitimate means of changing governments.

The Fourth Republic has now outlived all previous constitutional republics in Ghana. That achievement deserves recognition and, more importantly, protection.

Democracy Is Working, But It Is Not Perfect:

Ghana’s democratic resilience should not be confused with democratic perfection.

Our democracy continues to face interconnected challenges: weak institutional enforcement, excessive partisanship, misinformation, gender inequality in political representation, youth exclusion, winner-takes-all politics, patronage, weak accountability, the high cost of political participation, vote buying, electoral inducement, political financing gaps and public apathy.

Of particular concern is the growing influence of money in political competition.

So the question must be asked plainly:

Who really pays for Ghana’s elections?

Political parties may finance their activities from party resources. Candidates may finance campaigns directly or mobilise support through personal and professional networks. Individuals, businesses and other private actors may also contribute.

There is nothing inherently wrong with political fundraising. The danger begins when financial support creates expectations of preferential treatment, access to public contracts, influence over policy, political appointments or other private benefits.

When money enters politics with an invisible price tag, the relationship can move from legitimate political support to patronage, clientelism and potentially corruption. That is where democracy becomes vulnerable.

The Price of Political Participation:

The cost of entering Ghanaian politics has become a serious democratic concern.

A CDD-Ghana and Westminster Foundation for Democracy study estimated that the cost of running for Parliament had risen to approximately GH¢4 million, with about GH¢2 million associated with nurturing a constituency and running in party primaries, and another GH¢2 million associated with the general election campaign. The study also linked the rising cost of politics to the growing presence of opaque and potentially illicit money in campaign financing.

This means Ghana’s political-financing problem begins long before the general election. Internal party contests can themselves be expensive.

The consequence is obvious: when political competition becomes excessively expensive, capable citizens without substantial personal wealth or wealthy networks may be pushed out before voters ever get the opportunity to assess their ideas and competence.

That is not merely a political-party problem. It is a democratic problem.

Savannah: Poverty Must Never Become a Political Currency:

The Savannah Region provides an important context for this conversation. According to Ghana Statistical Service data from the 2021 Population and Housing Census, multidimensional poverty in Savannah stood at 49.5 per cent, compared with 24.3 percent nationally. The same census recorded a 28.4 percent unemployment rate among persons aged 15–35 in Savannah, compared with 19.7 per cent nationally. These figures should not be interpreted as evidence that Savannah voters are inherently susceptible to inducement.

They tell a different story. They tell us that poverty, unemployment and limited economic opportunity can create vulnerabilities that political actors may exploit.

The answer, therefore, is not to blame citizens for accepting short-term assistance. The answer is to build an economy and social system in which citizens are sufficiently secure to make political choices without survival becoming the price of their vote.

Savannah does not need politics that puts a price on poverty.

It needs politics that invests in people.

What Does the Law Say?

Ghana already has important constitutional and statutory safeguards.

Article 55 of the 1992 Constitution provides a framework for political parties, including requirements relating to democratic organisation and political-finance disclosure. Political parties are required to declare their revenues, assets and sources of funding and publish audited accounts annually. The Political Parties Act, 2000 (Act 574), also contains requirements concerning political-party financing, disclosures and reporting.

The legal framework further restricts political-party funding to permissible Ghanaian sources, including qualifying Ghanaian-controlled corporate bodies.

However, important gaps remain, particularly concerning candidate financing, expenditure ceilings, third-party financing, disclosure and enforcement.

The Representation of the People Law, 1992 (PNDCL 284) criminalises electoral bribery, treating and undue influence. Its provisions make clear that giving money or something of value to induce a voter to vote in a particular way can constitute bribery. The Constitution also contains broader integrity safeguards. Article 284 addresses conflicts of interest by public officers, Article 286 provides for asset declarations by specified public officers, while Article 296 requires constitutional and statutory discretionary powers to be exercised fairly and candidly and without arbitrariness, caprice or bias.

The problem, therefore, is not simply the absence of laws. It is also the gap between law, detection, investigation, evidence, enforcement and credible sanctions.

A law that exists only on paper cannot adequately protect democracy.

The Delegate System and the Meaning of Internal Democracy:

A significant recent development has brought the question of money, participation and internal party democracy into sharper focus.

On 29 July 2026, the Supreme Court, by a 5 - 2 majority, declared the delegate-based system used by political parties to select presidential and parliamentary candidates unconstitutional. The case was Prof. Kwabena Frimpong-Boateng & 2 Others v. New Patriotic Party & 4 Others.

The Court held that political parties must organise their candidate-selection processes in accordance with the democratic principles required by Article 55(5) of the Constitution. The ruling requires political parties, within one year, to establish systems that enable all registered members in good standing, as determined by their party constitutions, to participate directly in selecting presidential and parliamentary candidates.

The significance of the judgment goes beyond the delegate system itself.

When political power is concentrated in a relatively small electoral college, the cost of influencing that smaller group can become a democratic concern.

CDD-Ghana has noted that its research on the cost and monetisation of party primaries was among the evidence considered by the Supreme Court.

The broader lesson is simple:

Democracy must not merely exist at the national ballot box. It must also be practised within the institutions that produce candidates for public office.

Money Is Not the Enemy. Hidden Influence Is. It is important not to demonise money itself. Elections cost money. Political parties need resources to communicate ideas, organise supporters, travel, produce campaign materials and participate effectively in democratic competition.

The issue is not whether money should exist in politics. The issue is what money does in politics. Money should facilitate participation, not purchase political power. It should support ideas, not secure public contracts. It should not create secret obligations between financiers and future office holders. It should not turn public office into an investment whose returns are collected through patronage.

The objective of reform, therefore, should not be a politics without money. It should be a politics in which money is visible, lawful, proportionate and accountable.

What Must Ghana Do?

Ghana needs a comprehensive political-finance framework that matches the realities of modern politics.

First, political-finance laws should cover political parties, individual candidates, campaign expenditure, fundraising and third-party financing.

Second, Ghana should introduce realistic and evidence-based contribution and campaign-expenditure ceilings that can actually be monitored and enforced.

Third, political parties and candidates should be required to make timely, itemised and searchable financial disclosures. Citizens should be able to know who financed political campaigns, how much was contributed and whether the required accounts have been audited.

Fourth, the Electoral Commission and other relevant institutions need stronger investigative, auditing and data-analysis capacity to detect suspicious political financing.

Fifth, there should be credible and enforceable sanctions for violations. Enforcement must be sufficiently independent to apply regardless of political affiliation.

Sixth, whistleblowers, journalists and civil-society actors who expose illicit political financing need effective protection and safe reporting channels.

Seventh, sustained public education is necessary. The Electoral Commission, NCCE, media, schools, civil society and political parties all have roles to play in helping citizens understand electoral offences and the dangers of political inducement.

Finally, Ghana must confront the economic conditions that make vote buying attractive. Jobs, skills development, enterprise support, social protection and inclusive economic growth are not separate from electoral reform. They are part of it.

Should the State Fund Political Parties?

Whether Ghana should introduce direct state funding for political parties remains a policy question, not an automatic solution.

If adopted, any such system would have to be transparent, rules-based, audited and designed to reduce unhealthy dependence on wealthy private financiers without creating new avenues for political patronage.

At the same time, private political contributions cannot simply be criminalised. What matters is that their source, amount, purpose and legality are transparent and consistent with Ghanaian law.

The objective must be to prevent money from becoming invisible political debt.

From Transactional Politics to Transformational Politics:

The responsibility for protecting Ghana’s democracy does not belong only to politicians.

Citizens, too, have a role.

But citizens cannot be expected to resist economic pressures indefinitely while the cost of living, unemployment and poverty remain serious concerns.

This is why electoral reform must go hand in hand with economic empowerment. Savannah should not be described merely as a region where voters are vulnerable to inducement. It should be recognised as a region with enormous democratic potential and a young population that deserves opportunity, dignity and meaningful participation.

The 49.5 percent multidimensional poverty rate and 28.4 percent youth unemployment rate are not arguments for buying votes. They are arguments for stronger development, decent jobs, skills, enterprise and social protection.

Ghana has already paid a high price for political instability in its history. We should not wait until public confidence is exhausted before reforming the weaknesses within our democratic system.

Let us move from transactional politics to transformational politics. Let the politician come with a plan, not a price Let the voter come with a conscience, not a bill. Let public office be won through ideas, integrity, competence and service - not the deepest pocket. Our democracy belongs to all of us.

We are citizens and participants, not spectators. And perhaps the most important question for our generation is not simply who wins an election, but what kind of political system are we building for those who will come after us?

A vote is small in the hand, but enormous in its consequence. When money buys political choice, the immediate beneficiary may be one person; when democracy is weakened, the cost is eventually paid by an entire generation.

Ghana's democratic future must therefore be one in which citizens can choose freely, young people can enter public life without becoming indebted to wealthy patrons, political competition remains reasonably accessible, and public office creates an obligation to serve the public; not to repay hidden financial networks.

Democracy is a public trust. It must never become a private transaction.

***********

Author: Ananpansah Bartholomew Abraham(AB)

(DBE, LL.B, BSc, MSc)

Ghana News.title: Aburi Amanfrom landowners appeal for government support for Atwapim development project
Ghana News.content:
The allodial landowners of Aburi Amanfrom in the Atwapim area have appealed to the government to support the ongoing multimillion-dollar Atwapim land development project being undertaken by Ghanaian construction firm Royal Kingdom Estates.

The landowners say the 60-hectare development has the potential to transform Aburi Amanfrom into a modern residential and hospitality destination while creating jobs and stimulating economic activity in the area.

Speaking to journalists at Aburi Atwapim on Friday, September 18, 2026, Head of the Royal Agona Clan, Abusuapanyin Seth Adu Ansah, also called on the security agencies to prioritise the safety of workers and visitors at the project site.

He said ensuring security around the project would help create a conducive environment for the development to proceed and be completed on schedule.

According to him, the project would serve as a premium residential community and hospitality hub, bringing significant economic benefits to Aburi Amanfrom and surrounding communities.

Abusuapanyin Seth Adu Ansah dismissed what he described as claims by some individuals that they owned portions of the land earmarked for the development.

He challenged anyone with a legitimate claim to pursue the matter through the appropriate legal channels.

“If anyone believes they have a legitimate claim to the land, they should seek redress through the courts,” he said.

The traditional authorities and landowners also expressed their appreciation to Royal Kingdom Estates for what they described as its corporate social responsibility initiatives in the community.

They said the company's investment was already contributing to employment opportunities for young people in the area.

The landowners described the development as an important opportunity for the growth of Aburi Amanfrom and its surrounding communities.

They said they remained committed to supporting efforts to transform the area into a modern and economically vibrant community.

They subsequently urged all stakeholders to work together to protect the project and create an environment that would support further investment and employment opportunities for young people.

Ghana News.title: Cargill Ghana and International Cocoa Initiative celebrate 111 young graduates building skills for the future
Ghana News.content:
Cargill Ghana, in collaboration with the International Cocoa Initiative (ICI), has celebrated 111 young graduates who successfully completed various vocational apprenticeship training programs between 2023 and 2026.

The graduation ceremony, held in Debiso in the Western North Region of Ghana, marked another significant milestone in efforts to provide young people with practical skills and economic opportunities.

“At Cargill, we believe that the future of cocoa is closely connected to the wellbeing and prosperity of the communities where cocoa is grown,” said Max Essoh Latte, Managing Director of Cargill Ghana.

“By equipping young people with practical skills and creating opportunities for them to build more sustainable livelihoods, we are addressing some of the underlying factors that can contribute to child labour while helping young people realize their potential.”

The program aims to support young people who face limited opportunities for further education or skills development and provides them with practical training in various vocational trades.

The goal is to support program beneficiaries to acquire skills that can enable them to establish their own business and contribute to the economic wellbeing of their families and communities.

Following the program’s first graduating cohort of 60 young people in April 2025 in Sefwi Bekwai, Western North Region, this latest graduation brings the total to 171 young people have now acquired practical skills in various vocational trades, including auto mechanics, carpentry, tailoring, baking, welding, dressmaking and glass fabrication, among others.

“This initiative is an example of how we can help reduce child labour and poverty in cocoa-growing communities,” noted Mike Arthur, Country Director for ICI.

“When young people have access to vocational skills and opportunities within their communities, it can provide stronger pathways towards economic independence,” he said. “Initiatives such as this can contribute to reducing vulnerability to child labour, while helping young people build livelihoods, support their families and contribute positively to their communities.”

The ceremony brought together representatives from Cargill Ghana, ICI, government institutions, traditional leaders, community leaders, parents, master craftspersons, development partners and other stakeholders committed to the protection and empowerment of children and young people in cocoa-growing communities.

In a speech during the ceremony, Samuel Apana, Sustainability Operations Manager at Cargill Ghana, emphasized that the initiative reflects Cargill’s investment in people and communities as part of building a more resilient cocoa sector.

He noted that providing young people with practical skills and opportunities can help strengthen families and communities while contributing to broader efforts to prevent child labour.

He encouraged the graduates to make good use of the skills and to use their newly acquired skills to build livelihoods, create opportunities for others and contribute positively to their communities.

Commenting on the event, the Deputy Chief Executive in charge of Operations at COCOBOD, Dr. James Kofi Kutsoati, noted that the intervention complements COCOBOD's broader efforts under the Cocoa Sector Child Labour Monitoring System (CS-CLMS), which is designed to eliminate child labour in cocoa-growing communities.

“Over the years, through the implementation of the Cocoa Sector Child Labour Monitoring System, COCOBOD has made significant progress in addressing this challenge.

"It is in light of this progress that I call on all stakeholders to work collaboratively to eliminate child labour and secure a brighter future for our children and the cocoa industry,” he stated.

As part of the initiative, all 111 graduates, comprising 75 females and 36 males, received start-up tools to support them as they begin the next chapter of their lives and put their newly acquired vocational skills into practice.

The provision of the tools was intended to help the graduates transition from training into employment and entrepreneurship, enabling them to begin applying their skills to contribute to the economic wellbeing of their families and communities.

International Cocoa Initiative (ICI) is a leading non-profit organization tackling child labour and forced labour in the cocoa sector in West Africa, while Cargill is committed to providing food and agricultural solutions to nourish the world in a safe, responsible, and sustainable way.

Ghana News.title: Hunnyboy reveals how social media landed him Shatta Wale feature
Ghana News.content:
Ghanaian singer Hunnyboy has revealed how a social media campaign led to his collaboration with Shatta Wale and changed the course of his career.

Fast-rising Ghanaian singer Hunnyboy has finally revealed the story behind how he landed a feature from legendary musician Shatta Wale.

Speaking on Joy Prime’s Changes show, the Afro-fusion artiste, born Edward Tagoe, said the collaboration that changed his life did not come through industry connections, but through consistent grinding.

According to Hunnyboy, Shatta Wale noticed him after he tagged him in one of his songs on social media while he was constantly promoting his music on the platform.

“Through social media. I wasn’t fond of TikTok at the time because I had like 100 followers and the engagement wasn’t that huge. So my focus was on Instagram and Twitter. One evening, I posted one of my videos and captioned it ‘imagine Shatta Wale’s voice on this.’ The next morning, my friend called me and said a lot of comments were tagging Shatta Wale and so he requested that we push the agenda. So we kept posting videos with the song and tagged Shatta Wale on all the posts. One morning, I saw one comment under one old video of mine and he was like this is fire, just contact Sammy Flex and let’s do this. I was very happy.”

Initially, he thought it was one of the numerous fake accounts impersonating Shatta Wale, but it turned out to be his real account. The two eventually met and worked on a song together.

That message led to their hit single Winning in February 2025, produced by Skantybeats, a song Shatta Wale benevolently jumped on without any label politics.

The song became an instant street anthem, celebrating resilience and victory, and opened massive doors for him. Shatta Wale also mounted him on the biggest stage of his career so far, the record-breaking ShattaFest, which pulled over 600,000 fans.

Hunnyboy, known for blending authentic Highlife and traditional Ghanaian sounds with Afrobeats and Dancehall, is now gearing up for his debut album, with Peace of Mind as one of the lead singles.

Ghana News.title: I am a perfectionist – Actor William Lamptey
Ghana News.content:
Ghanaian actor William Lamptey says winning the 2026 Africa Monologue Challenge has made him realise he is a perfectionist.

The winner of the 2026 Africa Monologue Challenge (AMC) opened up about how monologues have shaped his creative journey and helped project African stories.

In an interview with Nikki Samonas on Joy Prime’s Changes show, Lamptey said winning the recently concluded 2026 Africa Monologue Challenge, which took place in Ghana, made him realise that he is a perfectionist.

Asked whether he would consider himself a perfectionist after winning the competition, he said, “Yes,” adding that criticism is not new to him, as he often criticises himself to ensure perfection in his craft.

This, he said, has led him to believe that he is a perfectionist in his artistry.

“Regardless of what I do, I strive to make sure that it’s the best of what I’m doing. Even if it’s something that I’m playing with, I make sure that I’m doing it well and take it seriously,” he said.

Speaking about how he won the 13th edition of the AMC, he shared that his final two monologues were the breakthrough performances that paved the way for his success.

The actor said his monologues, titled Down Syndrome and Truth, caught the attention of both viewers and the judges. This boosted his confidence and strengthened his belief in himself, motivating him to push harder and ultimately win the competition.

“My last two monologues because they made it to the judges’ favourite and I won the viewers’ favourite. That was phase eight and nine. The eighth one was ‘Down Syndrome’ and the ninth one was ‘The Truth’ which I won the judges’ and viewers’ favourite. Those two I feel gave me a very strong footing because I got motivated after my ‘Down Syndrome’ monologue won the viewers’ favourite. That’s why I was able to make it to the next phase.”

Reflecting on the journey, the actor said he does not consider himself exceptionally more talented than the other competitors in the challenge but believes his victory was by favour.

With a heart full of gratitude, he expressed his thankfulness to God for how far he has come in the industry and for granting him the opportunity to win the competition.

“I’m thankful to God for everything because there are certain things that I feel he just blessed me with. I don’t know why and how he does it but I’m truly grateful. I feel it’s been a long journey and it hasn’t been easy at all. I’m just casting my mind back and thinking of how anxious I was and how fierce the competition got because all my friends are so talented but out of two thousand, I made it to number one. How? Why?” he questioned rhetorically.

Lamptey also expressed his appreciation to Ghanaians and his fans for the unwavering support they showed him throughout the competition.

He said he did not expect to win, particularly because of how competitive the voting became at a point during the challenge.

“I started this thing with the intention that I wanted to keep myself busy. I got 70,823 votes and the voting ended two days before the performance and I was really mesmerized because my Kenyan brother made the competition very fierce for me. At a point he was like 2,000 votes ahead of me and I didn’t know how I was going to get there. But to know that I wasn’t standing alone and Ghanaians and people around the world had pulled out to help me get to that point of toping the polls before the night of the performance. So it was a fulfilling moment because I knew we won two sides of the coin. The audience helped me, God helped me, and I helped myself as well.”

Ghana News.title: No room for another false start as Ghana begin AFCON qualifying campaign
Ghana News.content:
Two years ago, Ghana began its quest to qualify for the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations with what appeared to be a straightforward opening assignment.

Angola and Niger stood in the way of the Black Stars in their first two fixtures. Angola were due at the Baba Yara Sports Stadium, a venue where Ghana had not lost since 2000, while Niger were to host the Black Stars at a neutral venue in Morocco because they did not have a CAF-approved stadium.

On paper, Ghana were clear favourites to collect maximum points from the two games.

But what followed was the beginning of one of the most disappointing AFCON qualifying campaigns in the country’s history.

Late goals in both matches denied Ghana victory. Angola ended the Black Stars’ 24-year unbeaten run in Kumasi, while Niger fought back to secure a 1-1 draw, leaving Ghana with just one point from their opening two games.

That disastrous start ultimately set the tone for the entire campaign.

Ghana went on to finish the six-match qualification series without a single victory, scoring just three goals in the process. For the first time in two decades, the Black Stars failed to qualify for the AFCON.

For a nation with Ghana’s football pedigree, it was a campaign that represented a spectacular failure.

There has not been a dramatic turnaround since. Qualifying for the 2026 FIFA World Cup remains arguably the biggest positive during that period, but the Black Stars now find themselves at the beginning of another AFCON qualifying campaign - with the prospect of another failure already an uncomfortable thought.

And if anything, the opening assignment looks even more difficult this time.

Ghana travel to face Côte d’Ivoire before returning home to take on The Gambia. On paper, that is a significantly tougher start than the one they had two years ago.

Back in the 2021 AFCON qualifying campaign, Ghana collected maximum points from their opening two matches and eventually finished top of their group. This time, the Black Stars must negotiate an away trip to the reigning African champions before facing The Gambia just five days later.

For new head coach Carlos Queiroz, however, the objective is straightforward: qualification.

The Portuguese coach has even described qualifying for the tournament as a trophy in itself, a reflection of the importance he places on getting through the campaign.

“We are here to play, to have a specific competition. All national teams at this moment today have one specific competition called qualification. That’s the first cup that we have to win,” Queiroz said.

“This game is just one step on our journey to that dream.”

The optics, however, are far from ideal.

Ghana will begin the campaign without a number of their most influential players. Captain Jordan Ayew, Mohammed Kudus, Antoine Semenyo and vice-captain Thomas Partey have all been ruled out of the opening two matches through injury.

Côte d’Ivoire, meanwhile, have built a formidable record at home and have gone more than two and a half years without defeat on their own soil.

Ghana also enter the fixture having not won an AFCON qualifier since September 2023.

Tough is an understatement.

But the Black Stars have to find a way to produce a decent start.

The events of the previous qualifying campaign serve as a painful reminder of how quickly a poor opening can derail an entire journey. Ghana cannot afford to repeat that mistake.

And then there is one more statistic that should provide plenty of motivation.

Ghana have never beaten Côte d’Ivoire in an AFCON qualifier.

More remarkably, the Black Stars are yet to score a goal against the Ivorians in an AFCON qualifying fixture.

History, form, injuries and the quality of the opposition all appear to be stacked against Ghana.

Queiroz has made qualification the first trophy he wants to win.

Now, his team must find a way to take the first step.

The President of the Association of Ghana Industries (AGI), Dr Kofi Nsiah-Poku, has commended Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Forson for the progress made in stabilising Ghana’s economy.

He made the remarks during a meeting between the Finance Minister, the leadership of the AGI and leading captains of industry.

“We are grateful for what you have achieved so far. We now know that we have achieved stability, and it is time for us to grow so that we can create jobs,” Dr Nsiah-Poku said.

He noted that the progress made provides a strong foundation for the country’s next phase of economic development, with attention now turning to industrial expansion, exports and job creation.

Dr Forson explained that the meeting formed part of the Government’s stakeholder engagements towards the preparation of the 2027 Budget.

“We are preparing a new direction for the country. I called this meeting to engage you on what will help you expand, export more and create more jobs,” the Finance Minister said.

The meeting underscored the Government’s commitment to working closely with industry to consolidate economic stability and translate it into stronger growth, increased exports and sustainable jobs for Ghanaians.

World.title: Trump pleads not guilty to 34 felony counts
World.content:
News outlets will not be allowed to broadcast former President Donald Trump’s arraignment on Tuesday in a New York state court, a judge said Monday night, but he will allow some photographers to take pictures in the courtroom before the proceedings formally begin.

Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan rejected the request by several media organizations, including CNN, for permission to broadcast the historic proceedings. Trump’s arraignment — like most arraignments in the Manhattan courthouse — is a public proceeding, but news cameras are not usually allowed to broadcast from inside the courtroom.

However, the judge is allowing five pool photographers to take still photos at the beginning of the proceedings “until such time as they are directed to vacate the jury box by court personnel.”

Earlier on Monday, Trump’s lawyers urged the judge to reject the media’s request for live cameras in the courtroom. The Manhattan District Attorney’s office told the judge they didn’t have a position.

The media outlets that tried to get cameras into the courtroom argued that “the gravity of this proceeding … and, consequently, the need for the broadest possible public access, cannot be overstated.”

Trump is now in Manhattan ahead of the arraignment. A grand jury indicted the former president last week.

The arraignment is also expected to bring the unsealing of the criminal charges against Trump, which have not yet been seen by his lawyers or the public.

The indictment stems from Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s investigation into hush-money payments, made during the 2016 presidential campaign, to women who claimed they had extramarital affairs with Trump, which he denies.

Trump denies all wrongdoing and his lawyers said last week that they’ll fight to get the charges dropped.

World.title: Russian authorities detain suspect over St. Petersburg cafe blast
World.content:
A Ukrainian tank is seen near the frontline area amid the Russia-Ukraine war, in Bakhmut, Ukraine, on April 02. (Muhammed Enes Yildirim/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images)

The Ukrainian military has reported little change to the front lines but heavy fire from Russian forces at various parts of the front line in the Donetsk region.

The General Staff said that more than 45 enemy attacks had been repelled over the past day, with the focus on Lyman, Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Mariinka.

It said there were 17 air strikes and more than 20 strikes by multiple launch rocket systems.

“In the Bakhmut direction, the enemy is trying to take full control over the city of Bakhmut and continues to storm it,” the General Staff said.

West of the city, Ukrainian defense forces repelled about 20 enemy attacks, according to the General Staff.

Oleksandr Syrskyi, commander of Ukrainian Land Forces, posted on Telegram that in Bakhmut he had met with “soldiers and commanders who destroyed the myth of invincibility of the Wagner fighters and Russian paratroopers.”

“The enemy is weakening and trying to cover up its failures with new fakes about the capture of Bakhmut,” Syrskyi said.

Syrskyi referenced the possibility of a future counter-offensive, saying that “the forward movement of our entire army depends on what every soldier is doing right now on their section of the front.”

Some of the most intense fighting is to the northwest and west of the city of Donetsk – as the Russians continue months-long efforts to dislodge Ukrainian defenses in Avdiivka and Mariinka. The General Staff said that some 20 assaults had been repelled.

“There are also some operational successes of our military in the Donetsk area. Our military have taken some positions. They have taken a more strategic and favourable position,” said Oleksii Dmytrashkivskyi, spokesperson for the military in that zone.

He also noted that Russian special forces had been introduced in the area.

“The enemy is trying to attack our positions between Avdiivka and Marinka. These attempts do not stop. It should be noted that the enemy has suffered quite significant losses,” Dmytrashkivskyi said.

He also claimed that the Russians “don’t have the same amount of equipment and, as they themselves say, they are on a ‘diet’ of ammunition for assaults.”

Social media video showed both sides engaged in heavy fire in the Avdiivka area, which the Russians have surrounded on three sides.

Denis Pushilin, the leader of the self-declared Donetsk People’s Republic, claimed that Russian forces were still advancing in the Avdiivka direction.

“It is still premature to speak of encirclement, but the situation is being created, if not critical, then extremely difficult for the enemy… After clearing Kamianka, our units are moving further. There are difficulties both with the terrain, which must also be overcome, and there are also similarities with weather conditions. But these difficulties are mutual — both for the enemy and for us,” Pushilin said.
