World.title: Macklemore announces Free Palestine Tour
World.content:
Macklemore announced he will launch the Free Palestine Tour this fall after being removed from Ed Sheeran’s tour this month over his pro-Palestinian performance.

The “Thrift Shop” rapper took to Instagram on Monday and jokingly said that his “schedule freed up a bit,” announcing three performance dates in Dublin, London and Paris next month.

“What happened to me is bigger than one artist or one stage,” he wrote. “When the billionaire class can decide which voices are allowed on stage and which ones are too dangerous to hear, everyone should be paying attention.”

The performances are part of what Macklemore named the “Free Palestine” tour and the poster said it would be him “and friends.” He said he spent the last week reaching out to other artists to work out scheduling, but no other names have been announced as of Monday.

He wrote that there has been a “been a collective awakening around Palestinian liberation” and the expectations of artists.

“It’s 2026. Being apolitical during a genocide doesn’t work anymore,” Macklemore said. “People are asking artists to show up, educate themselves and be in community.”

All proceeds from the performances would benefit organizations supporting Palestinians, he said.

Robert Kraft intervenes

Macklemore, whose real name is Ben Haggerty, announced earlier this month that U.S. venues gave Sheeran an ultimatum to remove him from the tour or face show cancelations. Macklemore said that New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft “rallied” other stadium owners after taking issue with his “Free Palestine” remarks during a show.

Sheeran confirmed that Kraft was among those who called him after Macklemore performed his anti-war song and the speech that preceded it at Metlife Stadium circulated online.

The situation surrounding Macklemore, Sheeran and Kraft made international headlines this month as many debated not just Macklemore’s speech regarding the Israel-Gaza war, but also the rights for artists to express their views.

It began when Macklemore joined Sheeran’s “Loop” tour in New Jersey and performed “Hind’s Hall,” his song inspired by the anti-war protests at Columbia University in 2024. Macklemore made a speech prior to the performance that called for a “Free Palestine” and also told Jewish members of the audience that his comments regarding the Israeli government was in no way about them. The performance of “Hind’s Hall” also had related images from pro-Palestinian demonstrations and the situation in Gaza.

The “Thrift Shop” rapper took to Instagram on Monday and jokingly said that his “schedule freed up a bit,” announcing three performance dates in Dublin, London and Paris next month. Debbie Hickey / Getty Images file

Kraft did not deny allegations made by Macklemore in his own statement earlier this month, but said Gillette Stadium — which his entertainment group owns — seeks to create a welcoming environment for everyone. He took issue with Macklemore’s actions at the New Jersey show and “and a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery that we believe has been deeply offensive and hurtful to the Jewish community.”

“Much of my time and attention for the last decade has been focused on the fight against antisemitism and hate of all kinds, and I feel a responsibility to stand up when I believe that line has been crossed,” Kraft said.

The Patriots owner also said he was not trying to stifle Palestinian advocacy or diminish the suffering of Palestinians.

Kraft did not specifically reference past actions of concern from Macklemore, but many online brought up a 2014 incident in which Macklemore wore a costume that appeared to play on antisemitic tropes: a wig, a fake beard and a hooked nose. He wore it to the Grammys that year, saying at the time that he thought it would be fun to dress in disguise to talk to fans.

Macklemore apologized after the antisemitic stereotype was pointed out, saying he had been in touch with the Anti-Defamation League, an organization founded to combat antisemitism. The ADL accepted the apology at the time, saying it took him “at his word that he did not have any ill intent,” according to The Guardian.

Ed Sheeran backlash

Sheeran faced a wave of backlash over his role in the situation as some commenters felt that the singer should have taken a stance on the war or at least Macklemore’s right to speak on his opinion. All of Sheeran’s opening acts, as well as his house band, dropped out of their scheduled U.S. tour dates in solidarity with Macklemore and the Palestinian people.

The “Perfect” singer initially released a statement explaining his side of the situation and clarifying that it was not his choice to drop Macklemore. Sheeran said that his promoters, who held the contract with Macklemore, made the decision as he attempted to build bridges with venue owners.

Sheeran went on with his scheduled concert in Philadelphia on Saturday, tearfully addressing the crowd who showed up in spite of the criticism he faced.

“I’ve never wanted to be an activist musician,” Sheeran said. “But this has put me in the middle of an important and passionate argument about freedom of speech and the most complex political issue on the planet.”

Israel launched its offensive in the Gaza Strip after the Hamas-led attacks on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and roughly 250 others were taken hostage. More than 73,000 people have been killed in Gaza during Israel’s military campaign, including at least 1,200 since a fragile ceasefire took effect in October, according to the Palestinian Health Ministry.

Sheeran acknowledged the “horrific” Oct. 7 attack on Israel by Hamas which started the war, but went on to say what has happened in Gaza as a result is “catastrophic and unjustifiable and disproportionate.”

“This is a humanitarian issue and I cannot hide how I feel about it anymore,” he said.

World.title: These young quarterbacks were supposed to break out. Now they’re hurt.
World.content:
The New York Giants were one of the NFL’s pleasant surprises in Week 1, beginning the John Harbaugh era with an impressive win over the Dallas Cowboys thanks in large part to the play of second-year quarterback Jaxson Dart.

The Giants’ dreams of a turnaround season quickly hit a roadblock on Monday, however, as Dart became the latest upstart QB to be sidelined with an injury. And now Dart may miss the rest of the regular season after imaging on Tuesday revealed his knee was hurt worse than the team initially feared, according to multiple reports.

Only two weeks into the NFL season, several of the game’s young stars are seeing their seasons upended due to varying degrees of injuries.

Dart joined the Chicago Bears’ Caleb Williams and the Washington Commanders’ Jayden Daniels as signal callers who had to leave the field early in Week 2. That trio joined a list of sidelined quarterbacks that also includes the Minnesota Vikings’ Kyler Murray and the defending Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks’ Sam Darnold.

All five of those players are former first-round draft picks — and all are under the age of 30.

Dart left in the first quarter of New York’s 28-6 loss to the Los Angeles Rams. On a third-and-8 pass attempt, Dart was sandwiched by multiple players as the pocket collapsed around him, and he took a substantial hit to his left knee from a Rams linebacker.

Dart limped off the field and was taken back to the locker room. After initially being ruled questionable to return, he was ruled out for good in the second half.

“He’s going to be OK,” Giants general manager Joe Schoen told ESPN’s Laura Rutledge during the “Monday Night Football” broadcast, adding that Dart would undergo X-rays at the stadium.

Dart’s hard-charging play style raised eyebrows during his rookie season, when he missed time due to a concussion but seemingly refused to tone down his aggressiveness when he returned.

Jaxson Dart lays on the field after being injured during the first quarter of a game against the Los Angeles Rams at SoFi Stadium on Monday. Logan Bowles / Getty Images

During the preseason, Dart even expressed confusion at why he so often is required to enter the blue medical tent on the sidelines.

“I really respect the rules, and the thought behind, you know, the NFL has of keeping players healthy and reviewing things,” Dart said in August after a big hit required he undergo a mandatory medical evaluation. “But at the same time, I’m still puzzled by just feeling like every time that I get hit, you know, I just find my way in there.”

Dart’s injury Monday, though, came on a relatively routine pass play, highlighting how no quarterback is ever truly safe.

The same can be said of the Commanders’ Daniels, who dislocated his left elbow while trying to regain his balance after he was tripped by one of his own lineman in a 37-20 loss to the Cowboys. Daniels, the 2024 Offensive Rookie of the Year, dislocated the same elbow last season, in which he appeared in only seven games due to multiple injuries.

“It sucks for him,” Washington coach Dan Quinn told reporters Monday. “I know how much these guys put into it. So, when there are setbacks like this, you just want to stand by them.”

A little before Daniels’ exit, the Bears’ Williams was carted off the field with a hamstring strain in a 9-3 loss to the Vikings. While Williams’ emotional exit from the game quickly became a social media meme, it also cut short what had been an exciting start to the season. Chicago was coming off a Week 1 in which it had scored 59 points.

“He’s right now working through every avenue that he’s got available to get back on track here. We’ll see what that looks like,” Bears coach Ben Johnson told reporters Monday.

Johnson added that Williams has an ability to recover quickly, and his injury is considered week-to-week.

While the Bears, Giants and the Commanders all lost after their starters went down, their seasons are far from over.

The Vikings lost Murray in Week 1 but still managed a 2-0 start to the season with Carson Wentz at the helm. And now Murray is expected to start in Week 3 after recovering from a concussion.

The Seahawks are also 2-0 with Drew Lock playing in place of Darnold, and even exploded for 31 points on Sunday. Darnold is expected to return to practice this week, though his starting status is up in the air.

For now, the Bears will turn to Tyler Bagent, the Giants to Jameis Winston, and the Commanders to Marcus Mariota as the three clubs try to keep their seasons afloat without their young leaders.

And Dart, Williams and Daniels — all three of whom have flashed potential to not only be great players but stewards for the league because of their exciting style of play — will have to wait a little longer to cement their star turns.

World.title: Russia forced a Ukrainian soldier to make a propaganda video. His village refused to bury him.
World.content:
Since his return, Shybalov and Duman relocated from Kyiv to the small town of Mykolaiv in Ukraine’s western Lviv region, where Duman is from. The couple keeps to themselves.

Shybalov had heard about Volodymyr Srebrodolskyy, whose village denied him a final resting place on the land where he was born. It enraged him.

“Russian propaganda — it’s an industry,” he said. “They facilitate this as an industry with the needed volume of basic raw materials, which are interrogations and interviews with prisoners of war.”

All of the former prisoners Shybalov keeps in touch with have had to film them, he said.

“They really perceive media as a weapon, culture as a weapon, language as a weapon and religion as a weapon,” he said. “Thus, they treat it as a proper weapon. They invest big resources to produce it. They design sophisticated and smart tactics how to use it. And they have thousands of people engaged in it.”

A cell in Donetsk

Volodymyr Srebrodolskyy’s captors placed him in a detention facility in Chystiakove, a city known as Torez until 2016, occupied by the Russian army since 2014. Located behind a double fence, the prison complex was built to hold 1,200 prisoners.

Among them was Mykola Shustrov, an army medic captured in the southern city of Mariupol while Russia brutally besieged it in the spring of 2022. Shustrov spent nearly three years in Russian captivity being moved between holding facilities.

“They came to our cell,” Shustrov remembered of one prison, “they hung up Putin’s portrait, the anthem of the Russian Federation and told us to learn it.”

After forcing the prisoners to learn the words from the anthem lyrics posted in the cell, their captors told them to sing individual couplets and questioned them about how many lines it contained. If they could not answer, the prisoners would be beaten.

By the time he got to Chystiakove, Shustrov’s teeth had been knocked out from repeated beatings and interrogations, and he lost a lot of weight because of the meager food rations.

About a year into his captivity, a video crew arrived. Shustrov and others were brought to a room where one man questioned him while another sat off camera in a balaclava and military gear. When he entered the room, Shustrov was punched in the gut. “If you don’t want that repeated,” his captors said, “answer.”

Shustrov’s interviewers were looking for compromising information on the Ukrainian army. Shustrov sat at the table, looking down, stuttering and trying to respond as neutrally as he could. The chance to show their families they’re alive was the main motivation for prisoners to cooperate with the propagandists, Shustrov said.

“You will say anything to show yourself,” he said.

Srebrodolskyy arrived in Shustrov’s cell in late 2024, in agony. He was badly beaten after failing to recite the Russian anthem, he told Shustrov and other cellmates. Srebrodolskyy’s stomach was swollen and tender from the assault, Shustrov remembered. His medical training made it clear how acute the situation was. “I can’t even drink water,” Srebrodolskyy told him.

The men asked for a doctor, but the guards said he would have to wait until morning. Shustrov spent all night speaking with the 55-year-old to distract him from the pain.

“I could not help him,” Shustrov said. “In our barracks, all I had was two hands and cold water from the tap. That’s it.”

An ambulance took him away in the morning, but it was too late to save Srebrodolskyy’s life. He was not the first man Shustrov watched die in captivity.

“He was in prison for the rest of his life,” Shustrov said, “and you begin to think, ‘Why am I enduring all of this?’”

Shustrov, who was released in a February 2025 exchange, was indignant about the village’s reaction to Srebrodolskyy’s video. The only fact to be taken from it, he said, was that the person was alive at the time of filming. Nobody can know what the captive endured, he said.

“You’re a prisoner there,” Shustrov said. “You’re not a person.”

World.title: Bodies of teacher and 10-year-old student recovered from water following incident during Iowa field trip
World.content:
The bodies of a 5th-grade student and teacher were recovered from the water at Lake MacBride State Park in Iowa following an incident during a field trip.

The Johnson County Sheriff’s Office was called to the park Tuesday afternoon for reports of people in the water near Coralville Reservoir, a news release states.

The body of Hannah Jorgensen, 24, of Tiffin, was pulled from the water around 12:43 p.m., and a search was launched for a missing 10-year-old boy.

The child, Ahmed Osman, of Iowa City, was found dead Wednesday, authorities said in an update.

Fifth-grade students from Borlaug Elementary School were on a “School of the Wild Field Trip,” NBC affiliate KWWL of Waterloo, Iowa, reported.

Iowa City Community School District confirmed the deaths in a Facebook post on Thursday.

“Our hearts are shattered by the loss of two beloved members of our Borlaug Elementary family, fifth-grade teacher Hannah Jorgensen and fifth-grade student Ahmed Osman. There are simply no words that can adequately express the depth of this loss,” the district said.

“Hannah and Ahmed were so much more than members of our school community. They were a teacher and student, a colleague and classmate, a friend, and most importantly, deeply loved members of their families.”

The district said “their absence will be felt in the classrooms and hallways of Borlaug, in the lives of those who loved them, and throughout our entire school district community.”

“We will remember Hannah. We will remember Ahmed. And we will carry their memory with us,” the statement read.

Norman Borlaug Elementary School thanked the community for its support.

“Our building is hurting right now, and so are our hearts. But knowing that you are all here for us, standing beside us, checking in, and, lifting us up. It means more than we can put into words,” the school said.

The sheriff’s office said the incident remains under investigation.

World.title: Man wounded during 2024 Trump rally shooting in Butler County dies
World.content:
One of the men who was wounded in the attempted assassination of President Trump in Butler in 2024 has died.

According to the House Republicans' social media feeds, Jim Copenhaver has died.

"We are deeply saddened by the passing of Jim Copenhaver, who was gravely wounded in the horrific shooting in Butler, Pennsylvania," the tweet from the House GOP account read. "Jim endured unimaginable hardship with strength and perseverance. We join his family and loved ones in mourning his loss and praying for them during this difficult time."

Copenhaver was one of two people injured during the shooting on July 13, 2024, at the rally. One bullet hit him in the triceps, and another was lodged in his body after it took chunks of his colon, which left him with nerve damage.

About a week after he was hospitalized, Copenhaver was discharged from the hospital.

"Jim would like to especially thank the first responders, medics, and hospital staff who have provided him with initial and continuing care," the family said in a statement released by Allegheny Health Network.

David Dutch of New Kensington was another one of the people injured in the shooting.

Corey Comperatore was killed on that day.

Both Copenhaver and Dutch spoke with KDKA-TV nearly a year after the assassination attempt and recalled the terror of being shot at during a campaign rally.

"I was standing up looking at the Jumbotron behind me, and next thing I know my sleeve has been yanked," Copenhaver said. "I could see a portion of it going by pretty fast, and I heard 'pew.' I heard it, and I didn't realize at the time that I had gotten shot. But I turned around, and that's when I got the second shot. So, the second shot didn't hit bone. Mine went into all soft material. It was like a jolt. It didn't knock me over, but I didn't want to stand anymore."

World.title: Mortgage rates are back above 7%. How much higher could they climb?
World.content:
House hunters are facing a fresh affordability crunch as mortgage rates hit 7% this week, marking their highest level in almost two years. The coming weeks aren't likely to offer any relief, with some experts telling CBS News that borrowing costs could continue to rise.

Rates are "far more likely to go up than down by the end of the year or in the next month or two," Jake Krimmel, senior economist at Realtor.com, told CBS News.

Data from Freddie Mac released on Thursday shows that the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage is now 7.03%, the highest since January 2025. Rates have increased by more than a full percentage point since the end of February, when they briefly dipped below 5%.

Separate data from the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA), issued on Thursday, shows that the 30-year fixed-rate mortgage hit 7.12% the week ending Sept. 18.

"Higher inflation, the prospect of tighter monetary policy, potentially stronger economic growth and ballooning federal debt have pushed up mortgage rates," Joel Kan, vice president and deputy chief economist for the MBA, said in an email.

The 30-year fixed-rate mortgage tends to follow the 10-year Treasury yield, which has spiked in recent months as the war in Iran fuels inflation and pushes up borrowing costs. Bond market investors are seeking higher yields to compensate for what they view as riskier investments as they grapple with the longer-term impact of the war overseas and rising government debt.

Volatility has increased in recent days, with the 10-year Treasury yield hitting 5.1% on Thursday, the highest level in around two decades and the largest single-day increase since April 2025, Zillow Home Loans senior economist Kara Ng noted.

"That kind of bond market move introduces real upside risk to mortgage rates," she said in an email.

How much higher could rates go?

Experts are divided, with some forecasting the potential for higher rates over the next few months. Yet Zillow predicts mortgage rates could dip to 6.7% by the end of the year and 6.3% by the end of 2027, offering modest relief to buyers.

Volatility in the bond market is "a reminder that the path down is not guaranteed to be smooth," Ng said.

The direction of mortgage rates will depend on the inflationary impact of the Iran war, Lawrence Yun, chief economist for the National Association of Realtors, told CBS News in an email. If a deal is reached to end the war, oil prices and mortgage rates could tumble, he said.

But if the war continues to disrupt oil flows, it could have a greater impact on rates, he added.

Inflation in August stood at 3.4% on an annual basis, up one percentage point since the war started. Stubborn inflation prompted the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates at its meeting earlier this month. Another rate increase could be in store before the end of the year, with interest rate traders pricing in a 66% likelihood for the Fed's next meeting in October, according to CME Group.

Expectations of additional rate hikes could add more pressure to an already expensive housing market. Investors often anticipate rate decisions, and their expectations can drive up the bond yields that influence mortgage rates, Krimmel said.

To be sure, even if inflationary pressures from the war subside, other factors could still keep mortgage rates elevated.

"Over the longer term, budget deficit pressures and economic growth driven by AI and data center investment will prevent mortgage rates from falling meaningfully," Yun said.

Where buyers can save

Home buyers may still have some forces working in their favor, despite the current rise in borrowing costs, experts note.

Home buying activity tends to slow after the peak summer season, giving house hunters access to more inventory and the chance to secure a lower price.

"Less competition means more negotiating power, and the ability to be more selective and deliberate about the right home," Ng said.

Home prices are already showing signs of softening. In August, for example, more than one in five homes in the market saw their price cut, according to Krimmel.

"Price cuts and the gains on your monthly budget can be greater than the gains from what you might get on saving 10 or 12 points on your interest rate," he said.

World.title: Journalists regain access to White House after judge blocks Trump's media ban
World.content:
Washington — Reporters whose White House access was revoked after President Trump barred CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the grounds were allowed to enter the complex again Thursday, hours after a federal judge ordered senior Trump administration officials to restore their press credentials.

Footage from MS NOW and CNN showed their reporters regaining access to the White House and broadcasting from inside the gates hours after U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly issued his order granting the outlets temporary relief. Politico also reported its reporter was allowed to reenter the grounds.

Journalists from all three outlets were initially denied entry earlier Thursday morning, which prompted their attorneys to ask the court for an "immediate" hearing. The lawyers said top White House officials had "repeatedly violated" Kelly's order by continuing to turn away journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico. They began getting back onto the complex around noon. The judge eventually said a hearing wasn't needed since the reporters' press passes were restored.

CNN senior reporter Betsy Klein walks to the press area on the North Lawn of the White House after being allowed back on the grounds on Sept. 24, 2026. Andrew Harnik / Getty Images

In a sworn declaration with the court that became public soon after the journalists began trickling back in, director of White House press operations Micah Stopperich said his office was notified at 7:10 a.m. to restore access to reporters impacted by the ban and started that process 15 minutes later. Secret Service then indicated at 9:07 a.m. that the press badges for those journalists were reactivated, and the credentials that had been confiscated were delivered to White House Operations staff at 9:45 a.m.

The reporters' badges were then left at the designated White House entry gate for members of the press just before 10 a.m, and Secret Service said those press passes could be picked up "as soon as they were delivered," Stopperich said.

The standoff over the banned outlets coincided with Mr. Trump welcoming Chinese President Xi Jinping to the White House for a state visit, complete with elaborate ceremonies that were not broadcast by major U.S. television networks. The outlets had suspended most coverage of White House events in solidarity with CNN, which is a part of the five-member collaborative television "pool" that documents the president's activities.

The judge's ruling

In his decision issued after midnight Thursday, Kelly granted a request from the three news outlets to immediately reinstate their access to the White House grounds while they challenge Mr. Trump's move to ban them from the complex because of their coverage of his administration.

Lawyers for CNN, MS NOW and Politico have argued that the restriction violates the First Amendment and their right to due process.

In an eight-page ruling, Kelly said the three news outlets are likely to succeed in showing that their due process rights were likely violated, writing that the journalists were not given prior notice of the bans or an opportunity to challenge them. And he noted that some of the CNN, MS NOW and Politico stories that the White House cited as justification for the bans were "routine" and, in certain cases, months old.

Kelly also said he is "skeptical" of the Trump administration's claim that the bans were motivated by national security concerns.

"[Nothing] in the record that predates this suit suggests that the revocation of Plaintiffs' hard passes was motivated by national security concerns," said the judge, who was nominated by Mr. Trump during his first term. "Certainly, that is not what President Trump said when he announced that he was 'banning' Plaintiffs from the White House—instead, he focused on the alleged lack of truthfulness and negativity of Plaintiffs' reporting."

Kelly's temporary restraining order will remain in place for 14 days while he weighs granting longer-lasting relief.

"This is a strong ruling vindicating freedom of the press, due process and the rule of law. We greatly appreciate the court's swift action," Theodore Boutrous, a lawyer for CNN, MS NOW and Politico, said in response to the decision.

The Justice Department is expected to swiftly appeal the decision. Mr. Trump said on Truth Social earlier this week his administration would turn to the appeals court if Kelly ruled in favor of the news outlets.

On Thursday morning, Mr. Trump criticized CNN and MS NOW, and alleged a recent report from MS NOW was "FAKE NEWS."

"The Dumocrats make up lie after lie," he wrote on Truth Social. "The new one is that I want Ford's Theater named after me. That's where Abraham Lincoln was assassinated. Who would want that? I don't! It is FAKE NEWS started by MSDNC AND CNN."

Trump's ban

Mr. Trump announced Friday that "effective immediately," he was banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House because of their "constant 'reporting' FAKE NEWS." On Saturday morning, reporters from the three outlets who attempted to enter the White House complex were turned away and had their press credentials taken by the Secret Service.

The news organizations filed a lawsuit challenging Mr. Trump's ban on Monday. Lawyers for the journalists said the ban amounted to unconstitutional retaliation for their coverage of the president and violated the Constitution's Due Process Clause because their reporters did not receive notice that the president would deny them access because of reporting he dislikes or an opportunity to respond to the decision.

"The President's statements make clear he implemented the ban to coerce more favorable coverage of the administration from CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO, and to deter other journalists and news organizations from reporting that the President might view as unfavorable," lawyers for the outlets wrote.

CBS News and dozens of other news organizations submitted a friend-of-the-court brief in support of the three outlets, arguing that the Trump administration's reasons for banning them "are transparently viewpoint discriminatory."

The Justice Department has defended the president's ban, arguing in a filing that the news organizations' reporting raises national security concerns. They also said journalists for the three outlets failed to act with "professionalism and decorum."

"Access to the White House is a privilege, not a right," government lawyers wrote in a filing.

They argued that the White House has "compelling reasons" for restricting the reporters' access to the White House, including enforcing "minimum standards" of professionalism for the press and protecting classified information.

The Justice Department also revealed that the White House Press Office sent letters to each of the news organizations Tuesday notifying them that the president decided to revoke their journalists' hard passes.

The letters claim that the news outlets have "exhibited behavior in violation of the standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex, including by trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues, and publishing sensitive or classified information."

The White House gave CNN, MS NOW and Politico a deadline of 5 p.m. Friday to respond to its claims.

The letters appear designed to address the news outlets' claims that the ban deprived them of due process.

But Kelly wrote in his decision that one of the standards of conduct cited by the White House in justifying the bans "is so vague it hardly does the trick."

In response to the Justice Department's argument that the outlets' reporting endangered national security, the judge said that so far, administration officials "offer little to back up their asserted national security interest to justify revocation of Plaintiffs' hard passes."

"[E]ven the justifications provided to Plaintiffs after this case was filed are ambiguous about the true purpose of the revocations: while Defendants' letters to Plaintiffs mention national security concerns, they purport to identify reporting that 'threatened national security and/or spread falsehoods,' leaving open the possibility that all the stories fall into the lat[t]er bucket, rather than the former," Kelly wrote.

Mr. Trump's ban had an immediate impact not only on each outlet's ability to access the White House grounds, but also CNN's participation in the White House television pool, which also includes four other outlets: CBS News, ABC News, NBC News and Fox News.

CNN was supposed to travel with Mr. Trump to New York on Monday for the United Nations General Assembly as part of the press pool, but was removed from the trip because of the ban. As a result, the four other networks suspended the television pool altogether in support of CNN.

Kelly's order came just hours before Mr. Trump was set to host China's Xi at the White House for bilateral meetings and a state dinner later Thursday.

The five-network television pool captures footage of the president that is then distributed to the other members of the TV pool and their affiliates and subscribers. Only those networks have set up and maintained the physical infrastructure to transmit to affiliates footage from the White House and when traveling with the president.

During a hearing on Wednesday, Kelly appeared skeptical of the Trump administration's ban. The judge pointed to two appellate court cases that established the precedent that the Fifth Amendment's right to due process applies when the White House tries to revoke a journalist's access.

"I think it is fair to say" that the process laid out in those two cases "wasn't followed here," Kelly said.

World.title: Hurricane Polo is a powerful Category 4 storm off Mexico. See its path.
World.content:
Hurricane Polo's intensity oscillated between Category 4 and Category 5 on Thursday as its path started moving away from Mexico's southwestern coast. The storm was expected to remain offshore, while its outer rainbands spread across southwestern Mexico, the U.S. National Hurricane Center said.

"Some near-term strengthening is possible, and Polo is expected to remain a powerful major hurricane for the next few days," the Miami-based center said.

Elsewhere in the Pacific, Tropical Storm Nolo formed on Wednesday, triggering a hurricane watch for Hawaii's Big Island. Nolo is expected to become a hurricane sometime Thursday.

Maps show Hurricane Polo's path

As of early Thursday, Polo's core was about 195 miles off the coast of Zihuatanejo, a coastal resort city in the Mexican state of Guerrero.

Hurricane Polo's forecast path as of Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026. CBS News

It was sending hurricane-force winds outward up to 40 miles from its center and tropical storm-force winds some 125 miles out. Polo was heading northwest at 9 mph.

Polo was forecast to bring tropical storm conditions to parts of the coastline on Thursday. In some areas, heavy rainfall "may produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain," the hurricane center warned.

Although the storm has remained far south of Baja California, the center said Polo could still impact the peninsula this weekend, as forecast models suggested it would likely change directions Friday night and travel back toward land. But Polo will have weakened significantly by then.

The Mexican government issued a tropical storm warning for a stretch of the Mexican coast from Tecpan de Galeana, in Guerrero, to Manzanillo in Colima. A tropical storm watch was in effect from Punta San Telmo to Playa Perula, in the state of Jalisco. Tropical storm warnings are issued when forecasts indicate tropical storm conditions will develop in a particular area, while tropical storm watches are issued when those conditions are possible, but not imminent.

Parts of the states of Michoacán, Colima, Jalisco and Nayarit may still see 2 to 4 more inches of rain, with up to 6 additional inches possible in certain areas, the hurricane center said Thursday. Between 1 and 2 more inches of rain could also fall in coastal parts of Jalisco and Guerrero.

Along with rain, Polo was also expected to cause life-threatening surf conditions, including rip currents, along the southwestern Mexican coast and parts of Baja California. The surf conditions could also contribute to flooding.

Mexican leaders have ordered evacuations, opened shelters and deployed military troops to areas that could be affected by the storm.

Classes were suspended Thursday at schools across the city of Acapulco, along the coast of Guerrero, its municipal government announced. Shelters across the state remained open, and officials said they were coordinating with local and national authorities to prepare for additional impacts of the hurricane.

Michoacán authorities also canceled classes through Friday in municipalities along the coast, urging residents of those areas not to leave their homes unless it was essential.

Polo's extreme rapid intensification

Polo underwent what's called extreme rapid intensification, in which a storm's wind speeds increase by 58 mph or more over the course of 24 hours, between Monday and Tuesday.

Its intensification was dramatic even by those standards, with winds that skyrocketed from 45 mph early Monday morning to 150 mph at around the same time the following day. The hurricane center described its transformation as "truly remarkable."

Its maximum sustained winds climbed as high as 180 mph at one point, far exceeding the 157 mph threshold for Category 5, the strongest on the hurricane scale.

Polo's central pressure — an indicator of its strength and potential destructiveness — made it the second-strongest hurricane on record in the Eastern Pacific, behind 2015's Hurricane Patricia. The storm's wind speeds tied 2009's Hurricane Rick as the third-strongest on record for the region.

Unusually strong El Niño conditions this year have been amping up tropical cyclone activity in the Pacific, with warmer waters, moist air and less wind shear enabling storm formation.

World.title: U.K. prime minister teases possible return of booze to soccer matches
World.content:
London — British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has called the ban on alcohol in the stands at high-level men's soccer matches in the U.K. "discrimination," teasing fellow fans with a possible reversal of a more than 40-year-old ban.

"I don't think it's fair for football fans to be singled out," Burnham told reporters in New York on Wednesday, where he is attending the United Nations General Assembly.

He hinted at a trial to reintroduce alcohol consumption in stadium seating.

The U.K. government, under then-Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher, banned alcohol in the bleachers at men's soccer games in England and Wales in 1985.

Home Secretary Leon Brittan said at the time that booze was a "major contributory factor in violent and disorderly behavior" in soccer stadiums.

Since then, fans attending men's soccer games in the top five divisions have not been allowed to drink alcohol in view of the pitch. People can still buy and drink alcohol in the concourse before games and during halftime, but they cannot carry it back to their seats.

No other sports are subject to such a ban in the U.K.

At some older, less well-equipped soccer grounds, lines for pints of beer can get so long during halftime that fans will leave their seats before the referee blows the whistle.

In a statement, the Football Supporters' Association said Thursday that it has "always argued that it's unfair to criminalize football fans for having a pint while watching the match," and it argued that many clubs are in favor of a reintroduction of alcohol, adding: "We welcome the prime minister's comments and totally agree that the legislation is outdated."

After a successful pilot run in the Women's Super League, the highest level of English women's soccer, fans of the women's game have been allowed to drink in the stands since the beginning of the current season.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham (center) sits in the stands during a Premier League match between Everton and Crystal Palace FC, at Hill Dickinson Stadium, Aug. 22, 2026, in Liverpool, England. Simon Stacpoole/Offside/Offside/Getty

Burnham, who's a season ticket holder at Premier League club Everton, criticized the restriction shortly before becoming prime minister.

Asked Wednesday if he still held the same view, he said: "I think that legislation dates to an era where football was very different … And I do believe there is a case to remove that discrimination. There are different ways it could be done. It could happen on a trial basis."

"I'm not going to back away from what's been a long-held view of mine," he said. "I don't see how it can be fair that some supporters of one sport can be treated differently."

Prime Minister Andy Burnham reacts while holding a pint of beer as he visits the Hare Inn in Harlow, Essex, England, in a July 23, 2026, file photo. Richard Pohle-WPA Pool/Getty

The ban was imposed with reason, however.

Soccer hooliganism in 1970s and 1980s England — sometimes referred to as the "English Disease" — involved fans in rival gangs linked to soccer clubs fighting each other and vandalizing areas in and around stadiums.

Several high-profile deaths linked to hooliganism, including that of a 14-year-old boy who died when fans were pushed into a wall by police after violence between Birmingham City and Leeds United fans, led to the alcohol ban.

Police have long supported the legislation.

"Other sports simply don't see the violence and criminal behavior from their supporters that football does, albeit a minority, with alcohol often playing a significant part in violent and disorderly behavior," a spokesperson for the U.K.'s Football Policing Unit said, according to CBS News' U.K. partner network the BBC.

"It would be irresponsible to fuel this by allowing greater alcohol consumption during games," they said, adding that it would be "incredibly rash to make fundamental changes without a full examination of the evidence and meaningful consultation with police practitioners who have the expertise in this area."

A fan-led review of U.K. laws around soccer in 2021 called for the legislation to be reviewed, however.

In Scotland, which also has a history of soccer-related violence, alcohol has been banned from soccer stadiums since 1981, but recent trials have seen it reintroduced, and fans can now buy booze at games at Hampden Park, the country's national soccer stadium.

World.title: Why David Eby is seemingly running for re-election against Donald Trump
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

If his first speeches are any indication, B.C. NDP Leader David Eby is running for re-election against one main opponent.

And it’s not B.C. Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson.

"There are big challenges out there for our province, challenges that are impacted by Trump's actions in positive and negative ways," said Eby at his day one campaign rally at the Canada-U.S. border, the unmistakable outline of the Peace Arch right behind him for the benefit of the cameras.

"I have a clear preference about which direction we should go: build up our province, strengthen our people, shoulder-to-shoulder across the country, standing up to Trump."

Overall, Eby said U.S. President Donald Trump’s name 18 times during Wednesday’s event. He said Trump’s name 19 times at his first public appearance to announce an election call. He said Doerkson’s name four times on Wednesday, and not once the day before.

For an indication as to why, look to both current events — but also the polls.

WATCH | NDP Leader David Eby seeking re-election: Why the B.C. NDP's David Eby seems to be running for re-election against Donald Trump | Duration closed caption 2:34 There have been plenty of announcements and news conferences on the first full day of the provincial election campaign. But as Justin McElroy explains, it’s already clear that U.S. President Donald Trump is what the B.C. NDP and Leader David Eby will be focusing on.

Constitutional, but is it honourable?

Since his re-election in 2024, Eby’s approval rating in the quarterly polls of all Canadian premiers done by the Angus Reid Institute has declined from a high of 53 per cent in March 2025 to 31 per cent in June of this year.

Whether it’s because of going back and forth on changes to the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act, drug decriminalization, or the announcement of record deficits, the number of people inclined to voice their support for Eby in polls had been going down over the past 18 months.

And that was before any possible backlash of calling a snap election in the first place, which seems to have riled even mild mannered political scientists.

"A number of people would say, look, you may have the constitutional authority, but you shouldn’t do it," said Philippe Lagassé, a Carleton University professor and frequently cited expert on the Canadian constitutional system.

"It’s not very fair, it’s not very honourable, it’s not the right thing to do, it’s not very good for democracy. And I think there, I would agree," he said.

However, Eby’s high point of 53 per cent happened in the weeks after Trump kickstarted the current tensions with his threat of tariffs and 51st state rhetoric, which Eby responded to by removing American booze from government liquor stores.

Perhaps that previous boost in popularity informed Eby’s rhetoric, perhaps not. But with a seeming lack of enthusiasm towards Eby, many political experts are saying it makes sense for the NDP leader to pivot to Trump.

"Eby benefits from this issue where he can now try to reposition the NDP as not a social democratic party, but a party that is pragmatic and following … Mark Carney's rhetoric, especially when it comes to trade and economic development," said Simon Fraser University political scientist Sanjay Jeram.

Newest poll shows slight NDP lead

And that pivot, combined with all the uncertainty with the Conservative Party in the last year, may well work in Eby’s favour.

Liaison Strategies conducted a poll on Tuesday — the day Eby called the election — surveying 1,000 British Columbians with a margin of error of +/- 3.1 percentage points. And it showed the NDP with 41 per cent support, compared to the Conservatives with 36 per cent, the Greens at 12 per cent, and CentreBC and OneBC at four per cent each.

If that result held, it would likely give Eby the clear majority he argued is needed to build what he called a Trump firewall.

Which is why many see logic in the NDP’s approach, especially when one considers the state of the Conservative Party in the week leading up to the call.

"Up until a day ago, the Conservatives seemed to be in disarray without a leader, and prior to that, a leader who seemed to be doing more harm than good, actively sowing chaos throughout the party," said University of British Columbia political scientist Stewart Prest.

But of course, in a single day, the Conservatives did remove Kerry-Lynne Findlay as leader, and replaced her with Doerksen.

In a single day, a snap election was called, and seven of eight CentreBC MLAs moved back to the Conservative caucus.

In a single 24-hour period, four NDP cabinet ministers announced they won’t be running again: Ravi Kahlon, Brenda Bailey, Kelly Greene, and Lana Popham.

A lot can change in a single day, especially in B.C. politics.

And while the last two days showed a clear message from the NDP, there are 31 left to go.

World.title: CEO who posted about wearing 'Lake America' sweatshirts to Halifax is no longer CEO
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Michigan tourist who recently went viral over a Facebook photo where she and three family members appeared to be wearing "Lake America" sweatshirts has parted ways with her employer.

Jane Smith, the former CEO of Family First Credit Union in Saginaw, is no longer employed there, according to a statement posted on Wednesday to the company's website.

"We are reaching out to inform you that Jane Smith is no longer an employee of Family First Credit Union, effective immediately," reads the statement addressed to "Family First Credit Union Members and Community" and signed by the chair of the board of directors.

The statement continues to say that chief operations officer Jason Acosta is now serving as interim CEO. It does not provide any further information about why Smith is no longer employed, or whether the decision to leave the company was hers.

CBC News has reached out to Smith, Acosta and the credit union's marketing team, and not yet heard back. But the company apologized in a statement posted to the Family First Credit Union Facebook page on Wednesday.

"We sincerely apologize for the concern, disappointment and pain this situation has caused our members and community," the post reads.

"We understand that members of our community may hold different perspectives about this decision. Our responsibility is to act in the best interest of the Credit Union, uphold the trust of our members and continue putting our community first."

A screen grab of an Instagram post by Breaking News Canada from Sept. 13 shows the since-deleted Facebook post by Jane Smith that went viral. (@breakingnews.ca/Instagram)

'Like our sweatshirts?'

The news comes in the wake of the backlash over a photo Smith had posted to Facebook on her way to Halifax, in which she and three family members pose wearing "Lake America" sweatshirts that Smith later said were AI-generated.

"Like our sweatshirts? Not sure Canada will," said the Sept. 11 photo originally posted by Smith, and later shared by her sister, followed by "lol lol."

Judging by the reaction online, just weeks after U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario "Lake America" amid the trade war between the two countries, Canadians were not lol-ing.

In a previous interview with ABC12 News in Michigan, Smith said the image was AI-generated and meant to be a joke.

WATCH | Republican mayor rejects Lake Ontario name change: Republican mayor rejects Trump's Lake Ontario name change | Duration closed caption 5:09 Robert Corradino is the Republican mayor of Oswego, N.Y., a city on the southeastern shore of Lake Ontario. He says the body of water is central to his community's identity and the city's decision not to follow U.S. President Donald Trump's directive to rename the lake 'Lake America' is one his constituents 'overwhelmingly' support.

"We weren't trying to make a political statement," Smith told the news outlet.

"However, we were, you know, kind of poking fun at the fact that, you know, one of the Great Lakes's names were getting changed."

She further explained that the sweatshirts weren't real, saying she ran a photo of them through ChatGPT to add the "Lake America" gear, then posted it to her private Facebook page with an AI label.

When they arrived in Halifax, it was her sister who reposted it publicly, added the comment and didn't include the AI warning, Smith said.

"We never had actual sweatshirts. We never wore sweatshirts."

There's been ongoing backlash over Trump's proposed name-change on both sides of the border. Prime Minister Mark Carney has said Canadians will call it Lake Ontario "now and always." In the U.S., three members of Congress have introduced a bill aimed at stopping Trump's renaming, titled "Hands off our Great Lakes."

World.title: Trump pursues deals with China while scolding Canada for doing the same
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results. U.S. President Donald Trump rolled out the red carpet for Xi Jinping this week, heralding the Chinese president as a "great leader" while looking to expand or extend a deal both countries reached last year to stave off some tariffs and carve out something of a trade truce. Trump has previously said he’s made "fantastic trade deals" with Beijing and, recently, even mused about inviting Chinese auto manufacturers to set up factories in the U.S. "If China wanted to come in and open a plant to build their cars here, I'd be OK with that," he said on the Fox News program The Ingraham Angle. Trump also reportedly got that extension with China late on Wednesday. And yet, Trump and many in his administration have repeatedly scolded Prime Minister Mark Carney for reaching a vastly smaller trade deal — agreeing in January to let in 49,000 Chinese electric vehicles with a tariff rate of 6.1 per cent (down from 100 per cent), while China lowered tariffs on Canadian products including canola, peas, lobsters and crabs. "They'll look back at this decision and surely regret it," U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said of the EVs at the time. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick took a more bellicose approach, accusing Canada of turning its back on the U.S. "We are a $30 trillion economy, we are the consumer of the world. Carney has a problem with us, he gets on a plane and goes to China? Does he think the Chinese economy is going to buy his stuff?" he said to Bloomberg. WATCH | Carney mocked for China trip: Lutnick's insults to Canada represent 'real frustration in Washington' | Duration closed caption 9:42 U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick blasted Canada's trade strategy on Friday, saying Prime Minister Mark Carney 'has a problem with us' and mocking Carney's recent trade visit to China. The journalist who asked Lutnick about Canadian trade, Semafor editor-in-chief Ben Smith, weighed in on Power & Politics. Jia Wang, senior fellow with the China Institute at the University of Alberta, says this highlights the way the U.S. demands one thing of its trading partners, while doing another itself. "The hypocrisy in the way the U.S. treats its trading partners is palpable," she said. Canada’s trade with China did pick up steam in 2025 as businesses sought to diversify in the face of U.S. tariffs. At the same time, American importers purchased fewer products made in China. But Canada would have to increase its China trade by more than 380 per cent to catch up to the amount of imports the U.S. still brings in every year. The U.S. imported more than $434 billion worth of Chinese goods in 2025. By contrast, Canada imported just $90 billion from China. And yet Sen. Rick Scott, a Florida Republican and Trump loyalist, highlighted what he saw as Canada’s risk in increasing trade with China, in a lengthy essay posted on X. Prime Minister Carney is facing a big decision: should he trade with Communist China or the U.S.? His choice will have serious consequences for Canada's future ⬇️

Choosing Communist China as a trading partner over the U.S. isn't just a bad idea – it's a trap. Xi doesn't do… —SenRickScott "Choosing Communist China as a trading partner over the U.S. isn't just a bad idea — it's a trap," he wrote in early September. As many commenters pointed out, Florida buys more goods from China than from Canada. In fact, it is one of four U.S. states that list China as their top source of imports. (California, South Carolina, Tennessee are the others.) But Wang says that sort of nuance is lost in Trump’s zero-sum world where everything is about power. WATCH | What to expect from Xi Jinping's meetings with Trump: What to expect from Xi Jinping's meetings with Trump | Hanomansing Tonight | Duration closed caption 4:17 Chinese President Xi Jinping was welcomed with a rare planeside greeting from U.S. President Donald Trump upon his arrival in Washington Wednesday. Jinping's state visit comes when tensions between the two geopolitical rivals are high over trade, artificial intelligence, Trump's war with Iran and China's designs on Taiwan. Trump "is more than happy to receive Chinese investment, to do more with China economically, to further strengthen the relationship with Xi, while being very critical and very harsh on Canada," she said. Mark Manger, a professor with the Munk School of Global Affairs & Public Policy at the University of Toronto agrees there is an element of hypocrisy in an American policy that tries to strike deals with China while discouraging countries like Canada from doing the same thing. "But we also have to take everything the U.S. president says with a grain of salt. What great deals is he striking with China? I don’t see anything there," he said in an interview. Manger says China remains the world’s biggest exporter, and is closing in on the American lead on artificial intelligence. And more to the point, he says, China knows it can outlast Trump. "The Chinese are playing a longer game," said Manger. And both Manger and Wang say Canada needs to play the long game as well. "We have to deal with both economies. We can’t wish them away," said Wang. And, she says, dealing with both economies will require leadership, strategic thinking and deft decision making as smaller countries like Canada navigate the two biggest economies in the world.

World.title: Sobeys' parent Empire agrees to end property controls after battle with Competition Bureau
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canada's Competition Bureau has reached an agreement with Sobey's parent company to have the grocery giant strictly limit or stop using property controls after the agency found the practice to be anti-competitive.

Property controls are clauses written into the land title that can prevent rival grocery stores from opening new stores nearby (exclusivity clauses), or can ban food products from being sold at nearby pet stores, dollar stores, gyms or other retailers and restrict what future leaseholders can sell on the land (restrictive covenants).

Empire Company Limited — which owns Sobeys, Farm Boy, Safeway, Freshco, IGA and others — has been under pressure from the consumer watchdog for months to get rid of their property controls after it found the practice to be anti-competitive.

"This all started with an investigation that we started in 2024 about the use of property controls by Loblaw and Sobeys and their impact in the grocery sector," said Anthony Durocher, acting senior deputy commissioner of the Competition Bureau.

"Loblaw has made commitments to curb its use," he told CBC News. "Now we have an agreement with Sobey's as well."

Win for consumers, economist says

The investigation into the Canadian grocery giants' use of property controls came off the back of federal committee hearings held in 2023 that were meant to get to the bottom of rising grocery prices.

"Sobeys, in a way, has been the hardest nut to crack," said economist Jim Stanford, who testified at those hearings. "They denied that these things were wrong and initially pledged to continue doing it."

The new deal is a win for the bureau — and for consumers, he said.

"I think this is a recognition that these practices are wrong — economically wrong and morally wrong — and the Competition Bureau is taking them seriously."

Land title documents obtained by the CBC's Marketplace earlier this year found stores within a radius of up to five kilometres from a grocery giant were restricted from selling perishable food items, like "fresh or frozen food, including meats, fruits, vegetables, fish, poultry, bakery, pre-packaged bread, delicatessen, bulk food or dairy products."

WATCH | Why property controls mean you might be paying more for groceries: One reason why you might be paying more for groceries | Duration 3:15 Why are grocery prices so high? One factor may be property controls — a powerful tool that big groceries can use to block competition and control local markets across Canada. Marketplace breaks down how it works and why it can take a toll on your wallet.

Some restrictions also prevented nearby retailers, such as dollar stores, from offering steep discounts on big national brands like Kraft, Coca-Cola and Evian.

A spokesperson for Sobey's parent company, Empire, told CBC News in a statement that the company is "pleased to have resolved the matter of property controls with the Competition Bureau," adding that they continue to invest in their network of stores across Canada.

Empire Company Limited is the second-largest grocery network in Canada after George Weston Limited, which owns Loblaws, No Frills, Superstore, Zehrs, Dominion, Fortinos, Freshmart and others.

Loblaws committed to cease enforcing its own restrictive covenants and to limit its exclusivity clauses in 2025, after the Competition Bureau's initial probe. The watchdog says it continues to monitor that commitment.

'Exclusivity clauses' still permitted

While the new agreement legally requires Empire to refrain from using new or existing restrictive covenants, it does allow "limited" use of exclusivity clauses.

This means that while the company can no longer restrict what other businesses can sell, they can still prevent direct competitors from opening locations on a shared development.

"There are some cases where it's justified in specific circumstances," said Durocher, pointing to Competition Bureau's public guidance for retailers.

The guidance says a "limited" exclusivity clause can be pro-competitive in a scenario where "no retailer would otherwise make the necessary investments to become a key tenant in a new shopping plaza." It further states that in such a case, no retailers of a particular type would risk opening up in the shopping plaza without the exclusivity clause, "and so the clause increased competition."

Produce is shown at a Sobeys store in Toronto in this 2023 file photo. Canada's Competition Bureau launched an examination into the country's entire food supply chain earlier this year in a bid to address high grocery prices. (Graeme Roy/The Canadian Press)

The bureau is prepared to make case-by-case judgements in these instances, Durocher said, having identified 19 such scenarios on land occupied by Empire-owned grocery stores in the course of their investigation.

The federal government granted the Competition Bureau increased authority to enforce their property control rules earlier this year.

Ultimately, Durocher said, this makes it easier for grocers, butchers and bakeries to open up and to compete. "More competition means lower prices, more choice, more innovation," he said.

Durocher said he intends to pursue similar, legally binding deals with other grocers, while simultaneously moving forward with the consumer watchdog's formal examination of the industry's barriers to competition launched in June.

This includes investigations into production and processing, transportation and distribution, and retail pricing across Canada's food supply chain.

As the examination continues, the Competition Bureau might be somewhat "hamstrung" by their limited powers, said Stanford, adding he would like to see more done to "stop these companies from getting so big in the first place."

"I'm encouraged by this, but I don't know if it means a whole new era of cracking down on food oligopolies or not," he said. "That remains to be seen."

World.title: RCMP allege 24-year-old Quebec man researched chemical weapons, planned attack for ISIS
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A 24-year-old Quebec City man has been charged with terrorism-related offences, according to federal police. The RCMP say Louay Angoud intended to carry out an attack on behalf of the Islamic State.

He is alleged to have communicated online with members of a terrorist group and gathered information to build a chemical weapon that could be used to poison Canadians.

His charges are the following:

Using or possessing property for terrorist purposes.

Commission of offence for terrorist group.

Participating in activity of a terrorist group.

Possession of weapon for dangerous purpose.

Angoud appeared at a Quebec City courthouse Thursday via video link from an RCMP station.

The Crown opposed his release.

He is scheduled to return to court in Quebec City on Sept. 28 for his bail hearing.

He is being defended by legal aid.

World.title: White House reporters from outlets banned by Trump regain access after hours-long delay
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Reporters from three news outlets banned from the White House by U.S. President Donald Trump were back on its grounds on Thursday afternoon, hours after a federal judge ordered the administration to reinstate their access.

CNN, MS NOW and Politico journalists were allowed back after being shut out throughout the morning despite an overnight ruling from a U.S. district judge — the latest development in an extraordinary showdown between Trump and media outlets whose coverage he dislikes.

The news outlets had asked in a court filing Thursday for an immediate hearing to address their inability to access the White House grounds earlier in the day. The filing said a Secret Service agent had confiscated the journalists' credentials.

In a statement, the White House later confirmed access had been restored and said that Secret Service had indicated the passes were available for pick up at the press gate around 9:45 a.m. ET.

But the delay caused speculation that the Trump administration was defying a court order, which it has been accused of doing in several cases.

WATCH | 3 U.S. media outlets sue Trump administration : 3 U.S. media outlets sue Trump administration | Duration closed caption 2:42 CNN, Politico and MS NOW are suing the Trump administration after being barred from the White House. Major U.S. networks are also suspending pooled coverage, escalating the fight over press access.

The news organizations are seeking to cover the state visit of China's Xi Jinping, where press freedoms have been curtailed on the mainland and in Hong Kong.

Trump announced he was banning the outlets last week, assailing what he called "fake news," and later arguing that their reporting was a risk to national security. The outlets argued they were singled out because of the content of their coverage, calling the ban a blatant First Amendment violation.

The ban prompted other media outlets to take action in solidarity. The U.S. network press pool — consisting of five major networks, including CNN — has suspended coverage of Trump pool events pending further notice.

In an order that was filed overnight, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly said the media outlets had met the legal thresholds to obtain a temporary restraining order, in effect for 14 days. He said they were likely to succeed in showing that their White House press passes were revoked without due process.

"This is a high bar, but plaintiffs have met it," he wrote.

The ruling did not address that rotating pool. After Wednesday's hearing, the networks continued to refuse to air footage of Trump without assurances that CNN would be permitted into the White House pool.

White House argues access 'a privilege, not a right'

Kelly said the government must have clear standards for conduct that would lead to revoking a press pass. He called the standard of objectionable reporting outlined in letters that the White House sent the outlets "so vague it hardly does the trick."

Kelly — nominated to the bench by Trump in 2017 — heard arguments on Wednesday from the opposing sides.

Temporary restraining orders are typically designed to preserve the status quo pending a closer review of the case by the court.

Kelly rejected the White House's claim that revoking the press passes was necessary for national security.

"Nothing in the record... suggests that the revocation of plaintiffs' hard passes was motivated by national security concerns," he wrote.

"The court is skeptical … that defendants' interest in safeguarding national security is the actual motivation for, or is even advanced by, the revocation of plaintiffs' hard passes."

WATCH | Did Trump just silence himself? Did Trump just silence himself? | About That | Duration 2:55 After the U.S. president revoked White House media access for CNN, MS NOW and Politico, other major U.S. networks including Fox News pulled out of the TV pool coverage in solidarity. Andrew Chang breaks down what the coverage boycott could mean for Trump's media reach. (Photo credits: The Canadian Press, Reuters, Adobe Stock, De Nederlandsche Bank and Getty Images)

Ted Boutrous, the lawyer for the plaintiffs, argued in the hearing that there was an urgent need for renewed access, saying that the ban caused irreparable harm to the outlets at a time of momentous news events.

Justice Department attorney Michael Velchik, in his argument, had reiterated the administration's point that the president had the right to choose who gets into the White House.

"Access to the White House is a privilege, not a right," Velchik said.

Velchik added that the U.S. president had criticized other news organizations even more harshly — such as calling ABC "the worst" — but hadn't banned them.

In response, Boutrous said, "Suddenly it's a national security case," arguing that the president brought up that point only after the lawsuit was filed.

Trump "keeps proving our point," Boutrous said, describing how the president has consistently used negative coverage of him as justification for the ban.

Trump also loses Iowa case

Trump, who as a private businessman earned a reputation for being litigious, has sued a number of news outlets since becoming a political figure, making various claims of harm to his reputation.

On Wednesday, an Iowa judge dismissed Trump's lawsuit accusing the Des Moines Register and its former pollster of misrepresenting the state of the 2024 presidential race, rejecting the president's claim that the newspaper's poll coverage violated Iowa's consumer fraud law.

Calling the case extraordinary, Iowa District Judge Scott J. Beattie said that allowing the lawsuit and its "faulty" claims to proceed could have a chilling effect that "can discourage others from reporting on and debating public affairs."

The White House said it would appeal the ruling to the Iowa Supreme Court.

Among the other press-related cases winding through the courts are a multibillion-dollar defamation suit Trump has filed against the BBC concerning a 2024 documentary, and a suit against the Wall Street Journal regarding an article connecting Trump to a 2003 birthday for his one-time friend Jeffrey Epstein, who was later indicted for child sex-trafficking offences.

World.title: ACSN extends lockdown of Colombia’s Caribbean coast to Friday morning
World.content:
Santa Marta-based organized crime group ACSN said Wednesday that the lockdown it has imposed on parts of Colombia’s Caribbean coast will be lifted on Friday morning.

In its first formal statement, the ACSN said that “the armed strike announced for 72 hours will end at 7:00AM on Friday 25 September 2026.”

The lockdown, which was initially called for 48 hours on Monday, has devastated the legal economy in the port city, particularly after ACSN assassins uploaded videos of them opening fire at stores that ignored the order to social media.

The online videos and half a dozen burnt buses and taxis all but cleared the streets of Santa Marta, which became a ghost town on Tuesday.

“We have never seen anything like this,” one Santa Marta resident told news program El Reporte Coronell.

President Abelardo de la Espriella announced the militarization of Santa Marta, but this was barely visible in the city’s downtown area and in the majority of Santa Marta’s neighborhoods.

“There are no police or soldiers in the streets, the people feel unprotected and are in panic,” said journalist Javier Manjarres on social media platform X.

“The current situation is a consequence of the behavior of the security forces and the decisions taken by the National Government in regards to our organization,” the organized crime group said in their statement.

The ACSN admitted that the clandestine lockdown was the result of the killing of Jose Luis Perez, a.k.a. “Cholo,” one of its commanders in the region around the Sierra Nevada mountain range just outside the city.

According to the group, security forces executed Cholo in front of his wife after his arrest.

An 18-year-old farmhand with no ties to the organization was also executed by the security, his family told media.

The lockdown has been imposed throughout the Magdalena and La Guajira provinces, a region where the group dominates organized crime and controls drug trafficking route to the Caribbean.

World.title: Colombia withdraws support for ICJ genocide case against Israel
World.content:
Colombia has withdrawn its participation in South Africa’s genocide case against Israel, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) said Tuesday.

In a statement, the court in The Hague said that Colombia’s government “decided to withdraw the Declaration of intervention that it had filed… on 5 April 2024 in the case concerning Application of the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide in the Gaza Strip.”

The decision of the administration of President Abelardo De la Espriella is part of a wider attempt to restore ties with Israel and its main sponsor, the United States, and appease its Evangelical Christian support base.

In response to the ongoing genocide in Palestine, former President Gustavo Petro took a leading role in diplomatic efforts that sought to isolate Israel and seek justice for Israel’s victims through the world court.

In a response, the US Government put Petro on a blacklist and actively campaigned for the election of De la Espriella to prevent another leftist victory in elections earlier this year.

The new president, who took office in August, immediately restored diplomatic ties to Israel and lifted a ban on coal exports to the country in West Asia.

World.title: ACSN crime group shuts down parts of Colombia’s Caribbean coast
World.content:
Santa Marta-based crime group ACSN shut down parts of the city and the surrounding region after Colombia’s armed forces killed one of their commanders.

Jose Luis Perez, a.k.a. “Cholo,” and six of his comrades were killed during an offensive on Monday.

The son of Fredy Castillo, a.k.a. “Pinocho,” who is one of the alleged bosses of the crime group, was reportedly among those killed during the operation.

Shortly after, a pamphlet that was signed by the ACSN ordered an “armed strike” of 48 hours because of the “the fierce attacks that the government has been launching against our organization in the Sierra Nevada since this afternoon.”

Multiple buses were incinerated in the region around Santa Marta.

We hereby declare a 48-hour armed strike throughout the province of Magdalena, particularly along the Troncal del Caribe highway, in the city of Santa Marta, and in the banana-growing region. We do not want any businesses to remain open for a period of 48 hours. ACSN

According to President Abelardo de la Espriella, who traveled to the city, “they are trying to intimidate the public by promoting an armed strike.”

“I will not allow any criminal organization to subjugate citizens through threats and terror,” the president added.

Notwithstanding, multiple shop owners in Santa Marta and along the highway kept their shops closed on Tuesday, afraid to challenge the authority of the local crime bosses.

The district government closed public schools in neighborhoods where the ACSN is believed to have a strong presence. Public transport was suspended as videos of armed men opening fire on shops that failed to close voluntarily were posted on social media.

The ACSN control much of drug trafficking to the port of Santa Marta and to the coastline of the neighboring La Guajira province.

De la Espriella ended attempts to negotiate the group’s surrender and ordered a military approach after taking office in August.

World.title: Colombia’s war crimes tribunal warns ICC that De la Espriella supports “worst attack in history”
World.content:
Colombia’s war crimes tribunal JEP said that it would warn the United Nations and the International Criminal Court about plans of President Abelardo de la Espriella to cut its budget.

In a statement, JEP president Alejandro Ramelli raised the alarm warned about a pending proposal by far-right Senator Enrique Gomez (National Salvation) to reduce the tribunal’s budget by COP100 billion ($31.6 million), which received De la Espriella’s support.

A second proposal by another far-right party, the Democratic Center, sought to push all sentences against members of the security forces to military justice for revision.

According to Ramelli, the two bill proposals “prove the existence of a strategy to block the JEP’s functioning” and called on the international community to “put a stop to this effort to dismantle our financial system and calls for the essential resources needed for our operations to be guaranteed.”

These initiatives constitute a combined strategy of economic strangulation and the subjugation of the JEP to military criminal justice. It is the most serious attack we have ever faced against our independence and autonomy. JEP president Alejandro Ramelli

The president , who vowed to get rid of the JEP on campaign, said that the 2027 national budget “does not constitute any threat to any judge, it’s the Constitution at work.”

I do not have a policy of retaliation against the JEP. I have a duty to manage spending, demand results, and allocate the State’s limited resources to a justice system that serves everyone, not to a court that part of the country perceives—for reasons debated in Congress and in public opinion—as a system of privileges rather than an effective end to impunity. President Abelardo de la Espriella

Since March of 2018, the JEP has played a key role in clarifying crimes committed during the armed conflict that erupted in response to the insurgency of the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC.

Among other things, the JEP found that the guerrillas recruited more than 18,000 children and that the security forces assassinated more than 7,800 civilians to inflate their combat kills.

Hundreds of former guerrillas and former members of the armed forces are taking part in a transitional justice system that seeks to solve as many as possible of the hundreds of thousands of crimes committed during the decades-long armed conflict.

World.title: Colombia pulls out of international LGBT coalition
World.content:
The government of President Abelardo de la Espriella pulled Colombia out of the international Equal Rights Coalition, which promotes the rights of sexual and gender minorities around the world.

The Foreign Ministry announced its departure from the coalition in a letter addressed to the organization of which Colombia was co-president until February next year.

According to Caribe Afirmativa, a gay rights NGO that was part of the international initiative, warned that the decision was “a serious setback in foreign policy and commitments to LGBTIQ+ rights.”

We also view this action as a snub to the international community, a break from the leadership role Colombia had established, and an unequivocal political signal regarding the place the current government is willing to grant to the rights of LGBTIQ+ people. Caribe Afirmativa

De la Espriella has appointed multiple prominent far-right figures in his government and has vowed to wage a “Culture War” against what it considers “gender ideology.”

On top of this, De la Espriella and multiple of his cabinet members oppose the right of gay couples to adopt children and reportedly sacked the newly appointed planning chief because he and his gay partner had adopted a child.
