A medical emergency authority is being established in 2026 to unify the service, though the government’s own documents disagree about its budget by a factor of a thousand.

The interior. Malaria is endemic away from the coast, and first responders are generally unable to reach areas outside the main cities (Photo: Amanda, CC BY 2.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Sources: Hospital capacity and services from the Georgetown Public Hospital Corporation’s own pages, policy and the voucher scheme from the Ministry of Health, budget lines from the Ministry of Finance, growth and oil output from the International Monetary Fund’s July 2026 mission statement, the list of private facilities from the British foreign office, and the warnings from the United States, British and Canadian advisories.

What Is Not Known

What medical evacuation from Guyana costs. No operator publishes a price and no independent source gives one. The ranges circulating online trace to marketing and automatically generated content. The only credible published figure is regional: an insurance trade journal noting that an ambulance flight from the Caribbean can easily cost US$15,000.

Where evacuated patients actually go. Suriname is confirmed for brachytherapy and India for visiting paediatric cardiac teams. The Trinidad, Barbados and Miami routes repeated throughout expat content could not be confirmed from any source, and are therefore not stated here.

What private treatment costs. No Guyanese hospital publishes a current price list. The one page that appears to is almost certainly unedited website template data, on a site whose other pages still carry placeholder text. The only genuine published schedule found dates from 2017.

What health insurance costs. No insurer in Guyana publishes premium rates. The single published figure located was an accident expense rider rather than a health plan. Quotes are issued individually.

How many people live in Guyana. The Bureau of Statistics gives 878,674 at the 2022 census and 956,044 at the end of 2024, the International Monetary Fund works with 1.024 million and the World Bank with 835,986 for 2025, a spread of roughly 23 percent. The final census report is still unpublished. Every per capita health figure inherits that uncertainty.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is healthcare free in Guyana?

Yes in the public system, and the constitution treats health as a fundamental right. The health minister has stated that the government delivers care at its facilities regardless of a patient’s immigration status, noting that Brazilians cross the border for surgery at Lethem, while adding that the policy might be revisited if demand grew too heavy.

What is the main hospital in Guyana?

Georgetown Public Hospital Corporation, founded in 1838, which is the national referral hospital, the teaching hospital and the research centre. Its own figures give 558 inpatient beds, 456 doctors, eleven operating theatres and eight critical care units, though its accident and emergency department has only 19 beds.

Are there private hospitals in Guyana?

Yes, concentrated in Georgetown: Woodlands Hospital, Dr Balwant Singh’s Hospital, St Joseph Mercy Hospital and Davis Memorial are the main ones. None holds international hospital accreditation, and only laboratory-level certifications could be verified.

Do I need medical evacuation insurance for Guyana?

Every major Western government says so. The British foreign office advises arranging an evacuation for any serious or invasive treatment, the State Department tells travellers to buy evacuation cover in advance, and Canada advises trekkers to include helicopter rescue. No operator publishes a price, so get the named operator and trigger conditions in writing from your insurer.

Can I get cancer treatment in Guyana?

Partly. Chemotherapy, targeted therapy and palliative care are provided at the national referral hospital, and radiotherapy at exactly one site in the country, the Cancer Institute of Guyana. Brachytherapy is not available at all, and patients travel to Suriname for it with the health ministry subsidising the cost.

Will I need malaria precautions in Guyana?

In the interior, yes. Malaria is endemic away from the coast, concentrated in Regions 1, 7, 8 and 9, and driven largely by gold mining and cross-border labour movement. The State Department recommends chemoprophylaxis for all travellers even on short stays, and notes that tap water is not potable in many areas.

World.title: Costa Rica Pauses School Rebuild Over Possible Archaeological Site
World.content:
Costa Rica’s National Museum sent an archaeologist to a rural high school in Pérez Zeledón yesterday after construction crews rebuilding the campus turned up materials that may be of archaeological value. The materials surfaced during reconstruction of the Liceo Rural Buena Vista.

The Ministry of Public Education (MEP) and the National Commission for Risk Prevention and Emergency Response (CNE) tightened security around the site and reported the situation to the Ministry of Culture and Youth (MCJ), according to a statement the ministry released on Sept. 19.

The Culture Ministry said the National Museum’s specialist would examine the extent, characteristics and dispersion of the evidence found in the ground. That assessment is meant to establish the nature and scope of the materials and determine, on technical grounds, what happens next.

Culture Minister Jorge Rodríguez Vives said Costa Rica has enormous archaeological wealth that must be protected, and that a find of this kind requires authorities to act responsibly under technical criteria and the country’s laws. He credited the MEP with acting immediately to secure the site and said it now falls to the National Museum to carry out the inspection and define the steps that follow.

Officials outlined two possible outcomes. If the inspection confirms the evidence is limited and clearly defined, the National Museum could carry out a targeted rescue, recovering the materials so work can move ahead. If the materials cover a larger area or require a broader intervention, the museum will set a work plan matched to the site’s characteristics, coordinating with the MEP and the CNE according to each institution’s responsibilities.

Any action falls under Law 6703 on National Archaeological Heritage, which protects movable and immovable objects produced by Indigenous cultures that existed before or at the time of Spanish settlement in Costa Rica, along with remains associated with them.

The school’s reconstruction is funded through the Emergency Program for Comprehensive and Resilient Infrastructure Reconstruction (PROERI), carried out under a CNE emergency declaration. Within that program the CNE acts as coordinating executing body, while the MEP serves as executing unit with responsibility for technical oversight, coordination and supervision of the works.

The Culture Ministry has not described the materials publicly or said when the inspection results will be released. It said it would report its findings once the on-site evaluation concludes, along with the measures needed to protect any heritage and the route the school project will follow.

Costa Rica’s southern region is one of the richest archaeological zones. The nearby Diquís Delta is home to the pre-Columbian stone spheres, whose settlements were declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2014, and earlier excavations in Pérez Zeledón have documented Indigenous ceremonial and burial sites.

World.title: International News: Mexico-US trade talks delayed as tariff negotiations move toward October
World.content:
International News: Mexico-US trade talks delayed as tariff negotiations move toward October

By Zoila Palma: The fourth round of trade talks between Mexico and the United States will not take place next week and could instead be held in October, according to Mexico’s Deputy Economy Minister for Foreign Trade Luis Rosendo Gutierrez.

Gutierrez said the postponement is linked to scheduling conflicts, including Chinese President Xi Jinping’s planned visit to the United States and the upcoming G20 summit. Despite the delay in formal negotiations, he said technical coordination with the US Trade Representative’s Office continues on a daily basis.

The talks are aimed at reaching an interim bilateral agreement that could provide Mexico with relief from some US tariffs while addressing Washington’s concerns over automotive content and Chinese investment.

Gutierrez said Mexico’s priority is reducing Section 232 tariffs on steel, aluminum and automobiles.

World.title: Tropical Storm Fay strengthens over Central Atlantic
World.content:
Tropical Storm Fay strengthens over Central Atlantic

By Zoila Palma: Tropical Storm Fay has strengthened while moving westward over the central Atlantic, with maximum sustained winds increasing to near 50 mph (85 km/h), according to the National Hurricane Center.

Forecasters expect a generally westward motion over the next few days, with some additional strengthening possible through tonight before gradual weakening begins Friday.

Meanwhile, a broad area of low pressure south-southeast of the Cabo Verde Islands has a 70% chance of developing into a short-lived tropical depression or tropical storm within the next 48 hours.

The system is expected to move northwestward to northward, while gusty winds, heavy rain and flash flooding could affect the Cabo Verde Islands by Friday.

World.title: Belize Marine Rescue and Education Center nears completion in Gales Point
World.content:
Belize Marine Rescue and Education Center nears completion in Gales Point

By Zoila Palma: Minister of Tourism Anthony Mahler and Belize’s “Manatee Man,” Jamal Galves, visited the Belize Marine Rescue and Education Center in Gales Point Manatee to observe progress on the facility.

The visit highlighted the continued development of the center, which is nearing completion after efforts by the project team and supporters.

The center is envisioned as a space dedicated to marine rescue, education and conservation, particularly involving Belize’s manatees.

World.title: International News: Hawaii braces for up to 35 Inches of rain as Nolo strengthens in Pacific
World.content:
International News: Hawaii braces for up to 35 Inches of rain as Nolo strengthens in Pacific

By Zoila Palma: Three storms are currently active in the Pacific, with Category 5 Hurricane Polo affecting Mexico and Tropical Storm Nolo threatening Hawaii with potentially catastrophic flooding.

Polo is producing heavy rain and strong winds along Mexico’s southwestern coast and is expected to remain a powerful major hurricane over the coming days.

The National Hurricane Center says parts of Guerrero could receive up to eight inches of rain, increasing the risk of life-threatening flooding and mudslides. Meanwhile, Hurricane Odalys is moving over open waters far from land.

Nolo is forecast to strengthen into a hurricane before approaching Hawaii’s Big Island on Friday or Saturday.

The National Hurricane Center warns that some areas could receive up to 35 inches of rain, while the National Weather Service says hurricane conditions could begin as early as Friday night.

Meteorologist John Bravender warned that the rainfall could cause “catastrophic flooding,” particularly because the ground has already been saturated by months of intermittent rain.

The heightened Pacific activity is being fueled by a powerful El Niño climate pattern.

World.title: International News: Australia investigates OpenAI agent breach of Government Health portal
World.content:
International News: Australia investigates OpenAI agent breach of Government Health portal

By Zoila Palma: Australia is investigating after an artificial intelligence agent developed by OpenAI gained unauthorized access to a government health statistics portal in June, in what researchers describe as the first reported instance of an AI agent breaching a government website.

The incident involved the Medicare Statistics Reporting Service portal administered by Services Australia, Reuters report.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the agent accessed both public and non-public files while conducting research on public medical spending. However, officials said there is no evidence that individual Medicare or personal health information was accessed.

OpenAI said its review found no evidence that patient records were accessed.

The company said its models interacted with several Australian government websites during an internal evaluation and acknowledged that the models took actions that were not intended.

World.title: PM Briceño joins Small States Leaders meeting at UN General Assembly
World.content:
PM Briceño joins Small States Leaders meeting at UN General Assembly

By Zoila Palma: Prime Minister John Briceño participated in a meeting of Small States leaders in New York during the 81st United Nations General Assembly.

The meeting focused on strengthening cooperation among Small States and addressing the unique vulnerabilities they face while working toward better development outcomes.

Prime Minister Briceño shared Belize’s perspective on building resilience among Small States and highlighted the importance of stronger cooperation in responding to shared challenges.

World.title: Prime Minister attends 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly
World.content:
Prime Minister attends 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly

The Office of the Prime Minister informed that Prime Minister John Briceño departed the country on September 23, 2026, for New York City, New York, U.S.A., to attend the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly.

Leaders will convene at the United Nations Headquarters to discuss solutions to the world’s pressing global issues, from climate change to global health, peace, security, and humanitarian response.

The Prime Minister is scheduled to return to Belize on Monday, September 28, 2026.

During the Prime Minister’s absence, Cordel Hyde, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Natural Resources, Petroleum and Mining, will act as Prime Minister.

World.title: Bradley warns political frustration could lead Belize toward ‘mass political violence’
World.content:
Bradley warns political frustration could lead Belize toward ‘mass political violence’

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Former Belize City Mayor Darrell Bradley has issued a stark warning that continued public frustration with Belize’s political system could eventually result in chaos and political violence if meaningful reforms are not undertaken.

During an appearance on Channel 7’s Uncut, Bradley argued that Belizeans are becoming increasingly frustrated with what he described as a lack of meritocracy, corruption, money politics and limited opportunities for qualified people to enter public life.

“Before we have chaos, and before we have mass political violence, because that’s where we’re headed,” Bradley said, while also warning about continued emigration by educated and qualified Belizeans frustrated with the system.

Bradley did not point to any specific threat or imminent act of political violence. His comments were made as part of a broader argument that Belize’s political institutions and parties need reform and that the country requires a strong and functioning opposition.

He also argued that prolonged political dominance by one party could weaken democratic accountability, saying Belize needs an opposition capable of challenging the Government and offering voters an alternative.

The UDP enters the 2027 municipal election cycle from a weak municipal position. In the March 2024 municipal elections, the PUP won 61 of the country’s 67 municipal seats, while the UDP won six, all in San Ignacio and Santa Elena.

World.title: ‘I did not trip’: Dr Gabrielle Henry speaks on terrifying fall in new interview
World.content:
Miss Universe Jamaica 2025 Dr Gabrielle Henry .

Former Miss Universe Jamaica Dr Gabrielle Henry says moments before her serious and traumatic fall during the Miss Universe 2025 competition, she had simply been following instructions given to her by organisers.

“I stopped when I was told to stop, I looked at the cameras and then when I was instructed to go I turned to the left, which I was instructed to do,” she told Good Morning America (GMA), recalling the November 19, 2025 incident publicly for the first time, almost a year later.

At home, the video of her tumble generated shock and concern for the pageant queen, with Jamaicans offering prayers and well wishes.

The fall upended Henry’s life, shattering her dreams of representing Jamaica, she explained.

Henry’s disappointment was shared by her countrymen and was compounded by a series of prior shocks, including the Reggae Boyz’ failure to qualify for the World Cup and the passage of Hurricane Melissa.

“The devil may try to sabotage, but God’s purpose prevails! Get well soon, Gabby! We’re rooting for you to come back stronger and conquer the finals,” one user had posted under the Miss Universe Jamaica statement on Instagram.

Henry told GMA that after the fall, she was completely confused and disoriented, repeatedly blacking out for days.

“I have no recollection of the fall; I just know that the bottom of that hole was a concrete base, the first memory I have is that of waking up to my mother who was looking down on me. It was the first time I have ever seen my mother look so concerned, as soon as I saw my mom I blacked out again.” she shared.

When she regained consciousness fully, she was told she had received an intracranial haemorrhage and facial and back injuries.

“[A] brain injury is one of the most traumatising things; I would not wish it on my worst enemy. There is almost an out-of-body experience… it took me so long to get back to that place where I said, ‘This is MY body,’” Henry said in the report.

The doctor described the road to recovery as long and challenging, marked by sleepless nights and severe pain.

When asked who was to blame for the accident, she emphasised that she had not tripped and the fall could absolutely have been avoided.

“Proper measures should have and could have been put in place, it was the responsibility of those who had organised the stage who had put in the lighting to ensure that the protective mechanisms were also there,” she stressed.

Her comments align with allegations in a lawsuit she has filed against Miss Universe Organisation alleging that she was following rehearsed choreography when she fell into the unmarked hole.

READ: Dr Gabrielle Henry sues Miss Universe organisation over 2025 fall

The organisation in the wake of the lawsuit, has said they covered all of Gabrielle’s medical expenses in Thailand and “stood by her”.

The doctor confirmed that the pageant organisers had indeed supported her in the initial stages, including in Thailand however: “Following my return to Jamaica, I have not had much feedback from them as it pertains to covering my medical expenses which are still ongoing.”

The doctor is hoping to get back to practising ophthalmology eventually but noted that she has a long recovery ahead of her.

World.title: MINING MESS
World.content:
Mining and quarrying operation in progress Stock photo

THREE mining companies owed the Government penalties to the tune of US$13.7 million (approximately $2.2 billion) at the end of 2025 after they failed to rehabilitate 264.14 hectares of mined-out land as required by law.

At the same time, the March 2026 Schedule of the Mines and Geology Division (MGD) of the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries identified US$828,000 in royalty principal and US$2.58 million in interest and penalties outstanding from two operators.

These are among the key findings of a performance audit by the Auditor General’s Department (AGD) dated July 2026, of the licensing, monitoring and enforcement actions of the MGD.

The audit report was tabled in the House of Representatives on Tuesday.

Auditor General Pamela Monroe Ellis noted in her overview that the MGD is responsible for regulating the sector under the Mining Act of 1947 and the Quarries Control Act 1984, to ensure that mining and quarrying operations are properly authorised, monitored, and enforced in keeping with the law and the public interest.

The audit found that one lessee accounted for 169.68 hectares (64 per cent of the area not rehabilitated) and US$9.89 million (72 per cent of the total monetary exposure).

“The weaknesses in enforcement were linked to the absence of a single, auditable, rehabilitation register; non-use of the security deposit mechanism during the review period, and the absence of finalised rehabilitation guidelines for quarries.

“Consequently, MGD could not demonstrate that all lease renewals were supported by the required information, reducing assurance that operators had the financial capacity to meet their obligations, and that Government had adequate protection, through the security deposit, against future rehabilitation or restoration costs,” said Monroe Ellis.

She added, “The long-outstanding rehabilitation obligations remained unresolved, and MGD could not demonstrate that the polluter-pays principle embedded in Sections 53A–55 of the Mining Regulations was being effectively enforced.”

Monroe Ellis said the audit assessed whether MGD’s licensing, monitoring, and enforcement arrangements were effective in supporting orderly and compliant mining and quarrying operations for the period 2019-2020 to 2023-2024.

“In particular, the audit examined whether applications were properly assessed before approval, inspection activities were adequately planned and targeted, breaches were followed up in a timely and consistent manner, and whether MGD maintained reliable records to support regulatory decisions,” she explained.

Among the other key findings was that one operator continued mining for six years after its licence had expired, in breach of Sections 25 and 31 of the Mining Act and Section 8 of the Quarries Control Act.

Monroe Ellis also found that six quarry operators continued operations after their quarry licences had expired. Five of them submitted renewal applications between 30 and approximately 607 days after expiry, while one submitted no renewal application.

“MGD also did not consistently issue reminder notices before licences ended, or take timely enforcement action after expiry. Continued operation beyond the authorised licence period weakened the licensing regime; reduced the deterrent effect of enforcement; and increased risks related to revenue collection, environmental oversight, and public confidence in the regulatory system,” said Monroe Ellis.

She also pointed out that mining leases were renewed without key documents, and the resulting risk materialised in unenforced rehabilitation obligations.

The auditor general explained that the Mining Act, and the Mining Regulations, require that lease renewals be supported by current financial statements, evidence of public notice to allow objections, and security deposits or letters of guarantee sufficient to protect the Government against rehabilitation or restoration costs.

“The regulations also require mined-out lands to be rehabilitated within the prescribed time frame; with statutory tools such as security deposits, restoration bonds, and penalty assessments to be used to enforce rehabilitation obligations.”

According to the audit, of the eight active operators reviewed, only four submitted up to date financial statements, two submitted none, and two submitted outdated statements.

“Further, there was evidence of public notice being issued for only four of the eight leases. In addition, four of the operators that were non-bauxite entities did not provide the required security deposits.”

Monroe Ellis said MGD advised that the security deposit requirement had been relaxed to promote investment but did not provide documented approval for this concession.

The audit also found that quarry inspections were not guided by a documented risk-based approach.

Said Monroe Ellis: “Good practice for regulatory oversight requires that inspection activities be guided by a documented, risk-based methodology. MGD’s own operational plans and the Quarries Control Act envisage inspection frequency and priorities being determined by risk factors such as size of operation, environmental sensitivity, compliance history and complaints, with inspection targets assigned and monitored.”

Yet, MGD did not have a documented method for prioritising quarry inspections, and managed only 243 inspections in fiscal year 2022/23 against a target of 400.

According to the audit, royalty arrears and quarry tax obligations were not systematically tracked.

It said MGD did not maintain accurate records on the status of royalty payments and quarry taxes, and the records were not reconciled in a timely manner.

Alarmingly, the audit also found that enforcement records were incomplete, even while MGD’s standard operating procedures require the maintenance of complete and reliable records of enforcement action, including reported breaches, investigations, referrals, corrective action, and outcomes.

“We could not confirm that enforcement action was consistently pursued for 14 of the 15 illegal quarrying cases recorded in MGD’s complaints register,” said Monroe Ellis. She outlined that nine police reports were reviewed; however, only one matched an entry in the register and showed evidence of follow-up actions.

World.title: Chuck to meet with protesting lawyers over Firearms Act discontent
World.content:
Several members of the Jamaican Bar Association and the Advocates’ Association in association with bar associations across the island armed with placards outside the Supreme Court on King Street in downtown Kingston Wednesday morning demanding that their concerns about the Firearms (Prohibition, Restriction and Regulation) Act, 2022 be addressed through meaningful reforms. (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

JUSTICE Minister Delroy Chuck on Wednesday voiced disappointment with the protest action taken by members of the defence bar to show discontent with the 2022 Firearms Act, but said it is hoped that a meeting scheduled for 2:00 pm today will help stave off further plans by the attorneys to abandon the courts all of next week if their demands are not met.

“I am really disappointed that members of the Jamaican Bar Association and the Advocates’ Association have taken the action today by demonstrating around the Supreme Court. On Sunday, September 13 during the Assize service I indicated that the matter was under consideration and told the association that I was prepared to meet with them,” the justice minister said.

In referencing the pending meeting today, he said the “government is very concerned about the prevalence of gun crimes and the need to protect law-abiding citizens of this country but remains open to dialogue on the Firearms Act 2022”.

Wednesday, members of the Jamaican Bar Association and the Advocates’ Association in association with bar associations across the island, armed with placards, demanded that their concerns about the Firearms (Prohibition, Restriction and Regulation) Act, 2022 and its impact on “justice, due process, and the rule of law” be taken on board for reform.

The protest came just over a week after the justice minister’s comments at the annual Assize Service of the judiciary. Chuck, in his statements which evoked inflamed commentary from several quarters, said while the mandatory minimum sentences contained in the provision were being reviewed because of widespread concerns, “the security forces and a number of my colleagues feel that the Act is working and it is bringing down murders and shootings”.

“It is under consideration, but firearms are a major problem in our country, and that is why we don’t want to send a signal that we are going to relent on the enforcement to condemn the possession and the use of firearms. But it is under consideration,” the justice minister said then.

A week later, Saturday, September 19, members of Jamaica’s legal profession met to consider what they described as “the operation and impact of the Firearms (Prohibition, Restriction and Regulation) Act, 2022, particularly its mandatory sentencing provisions and the restrictions placed on judicial discretion”.

In a statement issued following that meeting, the attorneys said, “The legal profession supports strong and effective laws to combat gun violence and punish those who use illegal firearms to murder, rob, terrorise and intimidate our citizens. Our concern is not with strong penalties. Our concern is with a sentencing regime that does not adequately allow judges to distinguish between offenders, offences, and individual circumstances.”

The Firearms (Prohibition, Restriction and Regulation) Act, 2022, which prescribes a mandatory 15-year sentence for violations, took effect in November 2022 and, among other things, provides penalties ranging from 15 years to life imprisonment for possession of illegal weapons, and establishes a dual regime — distinguishing between prohibited weapons or unregulated firearms and connected activities and firearms that are duly authorised or registered.

According to the advocates, their meeting on Saturday “identified several areas of serious concern, including the restriction of judicial discretion; the proportionality of mandatory minimum sentences in individual cases; the diminished incentive for early guilty pleas; the resulting increase in matters proceeding to trial and pressure on an already burdened criminal justice system; the treatment of imitation firearms; and the consequences of certain provisions for licensed firearm holders”.

“The legal profession is calling for urgent amendments to the Act, including consideration of an ‘exceptional circumstances’ provision allowing judges appropriate discretion in deserving cases, meaningful sentencing incentives for early guilty pleas, reform of the certificate regime, and a review of the provisions governing imitation firearms and licensed firearm holders. The profession also calls for urgent, structured consultation with the Government, Opposition, Parliament, judiciary, and other relevant stakeholders on the proposed amendments,” the attorneys said in that statement.

Noting that the “concerns are not new” as members of the legal profession and civil society have “written, spoken publicly and proposed amendments”, the professionals said “the time has now come for action”.

They said following those extensive discussions, the meeting resolved to pursue collective action, including a silent protest outside the Supreme Court on Wednesday, September 23 followed by the withdrawal of legal services from criminal courts for one week commencing Monday, September 28.

Wednesday’s protest action was, however, not sanctioned by all segments of the defence bar, with some attorneys voicing discontent over the method employed.

One attorney, in a biting commentary on a social media platform, said while he understood the reason for the concern, professional associations are expected to maintain a high level of discourse without resorting to making public spectacles.

Yesterday, attorney Tamika Harris, a member of the Bar Council of the Jamaican Bar Association and chair of its Criminal Practice and Procedure Subcommittee who was a key figure behind the protest, said the meeting this afternoon will inform the posture of defence attorneys in the island’s courts next week.

World.title: ‘Do not sleep on Jamaican talent’
World.content:
Delroy Lindo.

For veteran actor Delroy Lindo, Jabari’s People is more than another film project. It is an opportunity to give back to the country of his parents and tell a Jamaican story that he believes deserves to be seen by the world.

The 73-year-old British-born American actor, who recently earned his first Academy Award nomination for his performance in Ryan Coogler’s Sinners, is currently in Jamaica wrapping production on Jabari’s People, his feature directorial début, in which he also stars.

Lindo, who was born in London to Jamaican parents, and whose family has roots in Ocho Rios, St Ann, said he has long searched for a meaningful way to contribute to the island.

The opportunity to contribute eventually came through film when the screenplay for Jabari’s People came his way more than a decade ago.

“This script came to me in 2015,” he said. “This is potentially an opportunity for me to substantively contribute to Jamaica, to make a creative gesture that I feel enhances and contributes to Jamaican culture and also to export Jamaica globally in terms of presenting a story about Jamaica that is an affirmation of the people, the spirituality and the culture.”

Jabari’s People follows a troubled New York teenager grappling with the death of his mother who is sent to Jamaica to live with his grandfather.

For Lindo, the film also presents an opportunity to show an image of Jamaica that he believes has too often been overlooked on-screen.

“It’s not about gangsters, it’s not about ganja, and there’s nothing wrong with ganja, but it is a very different presentation of Jamaica… It is wholesome and it is investigating who we are as Jamaicans,” he explained.

That approach, however, has presented challenges in attracting financing, with Lindo saying some potential Hollywood investors were hesitant to support a Jamaican film that did not lean into familiar stereotypes.

The production has instead received backing from private investors, including Sue Rockefeller, Regina K Scully, Melony Lewis, and Adam Lewis.

The project has also sought support through the Jamaica Screen Development Initiative, the Government’s financing programme aimed at strengthening the local screen industry.

Beyond telling a different Jamaican story, Lindo said one of his priorities from the outset was ensuring Jamaicans played a significant role in bringing it to life.

“From the beginning it was my objective to employ as many Jamaicans as we could, and that’s what we have done,” Lindo shared. “Do not sleep on the talent that is here. As far as the Jamaican Government is concerned, wealthy individuals, who have the capacity to support the growth of Jamaican film, please do so.”

He acknowledged that some of the talent on the island remains underdeveloped, but argued that greater investment and opportunities could change that.

“Some of that talent is raw, no question, but what it needs is the nurturing, the support, because in the final analysis the talent that is here can have global impact,” he charged.

Jamaican-Canadian costume designer Antoinette Messam, whose credits include The Harder They Fall, Creed, and The Book of Clarence, echoed Lindo’s call for greater investment in Jamaica’s film ecosystem.

Messam said building a sustainable industry requires productions to deliberately spend locally and, equally, requires Jamaican businesses to position themselves to supply the needs of those productions.

“We want to spend the money locally. We want to keep the money in Jamaica. It is nothing for me to have the buyer in Miami ship me clothes because it is actually easier. But, if we are going to fund, finance, and create with local actors, local talent, local hair and make-up… if I want to keep the money here, I need you as a vendor to support me,” she said.

Messam, who previously worked with Lindo on The Harder They Fall, said her connection to Jabari’s People was also deeply personal.

“I love the heart of the story. I recognise that story. That story we have heard many times during our lives — if not from our family, through someone else’s family.”

The production has also tapped the experience of Jamaican Canadian producer Lena Cordina, whose credits include television productions such as Reasonable Doubt, The Hot Zone, and Hemlock Grove.

Cordina said she was particularly interested in the project because it offered a Jamaican story outside of the portrayals that have frequently dominated international screens, while acknowledging that securing investment for films outside established commercial formula remains difficult.

For Cordina, the value of productions such as Jabari’s People extends beyond what eventually appears on screen. She pointed to the wider economic activity generated when an international-standard production operates locally and employs Jamaican workers and businesses.

“From the parking lots, to the hotels, to the waiters that get tips in the restaurant, it helps the whole economy,” she said.

For Lindo, however, the ambition remains both economic and cultural, to demonstrate that Jamaica possesses the people, stories, and creative capacity to produce work capable of reaching audiences far beyond its shores.

And, after decades of searching for the right way to give something back to the country that shaped his family, Jabari’s People appears to have provided him with that opportunity.

World.title: ‘I felt like a fool’
World.content:
File photo shows Pastor Kevin Smith in worship. A witness on the stand in the Home Circuit Court said Wednesday that he was responsible for shearing the pastor’s head, helping him get dressed for church services, and carrying his Bible to the pulpit.

A witness huffed and puffed on Wednesday in the Home Circuit Court murder trial of Andre Ruddock in Kingston as defence attorney Anthony Williams cross-examined him about how he felt when his now-deceased pastor, Dr Kevin Smith, pushed his fingers into gunshot wounds he received in his back that were allegedly inflicted by the preacher.

Ruddock is on trial for murder in relation to the October 17, 2021 killing of Taneka Gardner at the Kingdom Restoration Ministries International in Albion, St James. Smith was the pastor of the church and the witness who is on the stand said he was responsible for shearing the pastor’s head, helping him get dressed for church services, and carrying his Bible to the pulpit. Ruddock’s duties surrounded providing security for Smith.

After trying to avoid the question about how he felt at the time of the incident, the witness eventually told the court that he felt like a fool. He told the court previously that Smith shot him twice in the back and assured him that he was immortal and could not die. He said that while he was in pain on the ground after being shot, Smith walked over to him and stuffed his fingers into the gunshot wounds. The witness also claimed that he was stabbed in the back by another member of the church, who was acting on Smith’s orders.

Williams asked the witness to confirm that he told prosecutors during the trial which began last week, that he was shot in the back by Smith.

“That is correct,” the witness responded.

Williams then prompted him to explain again what he told prosecutors took place after he was shot twice in the back by Smith.

“You said he also used his hands to do what?” Smith asked.

“He pushed his fingers in the wound. I am more than positive [that happened]. I know for a fact, sir,” the witness said.

The attorney asked him how long the pastor had his fingers in his wounds.

The witness, who had a perturbed look on his face, told Williams that he did not know.

It was at the point when Williams began to ask the witness to explain how he felt while Smith was pushing his fingers in his wounds, that the witness started huffing and puffing.

That caused an angry look on his face and a piercing and penetrating gaze at the attorney. He appeared very uncomfortable.

The witness asked the attorney if he could please “move forward from that question”.

Williams expressed to him that that was not how it worked in court and pressed him to answer the question. The witness’ refusal to comply sparked the intervention of Judge Leighton Pusey who called his name, trying to get his attention. It was only after Pusey called his name a few times, that the witness decided to look at the judge.

Instead of scolding the witness, Pusey asked Williams if it was possible to come back to the question at another time during the cross-examination to get the witness to compose himself.

However, Williams expressed to the judge that the questions that were to follow had the potential of making the witness even more uncomfortable and recommended that it was better if the witness simply answered the question.

Pusey instructed the witness that he should try his best to answer the questions that Williams was posing.

The attorney then made another attempt.

“How did you feel?” Williams asked.

“I felt like a fool,” the witness answered.

Williams probed whether he said anything to the pastor while he was pushing his fingers in his wounds.

He told the attorney that he did not, and explained that he was in pain.

Williams asked the witness about the reasons for him not making mention in any of his four statements to the police that Smith had stuck his fingers in the wound.

“You gave four statements to the police. I am suggesting to you that you never told the police in any of those statements that the pastor used his finger and stick in the wound. Do you agree?” Williams asked.

“I don’t remember if I did or not,” the witness said.

He told the attorney that the events which unfolded at the church happened five years ago and that he didn’t carry thoughts about it in his head.

“I don’t want to remember. These were very traumatic events that unfolded in my life,” he said.

The attorney found it difficult to understand why even after telling the police on different occasions that he had amendments made to his multiple statements, he failed to mention anything about the pastor’s fingers in his wounds.

“My suggestion is that the reason why you did not mention it in your first statement about the pastor sticking his fingers in your wounds was because that never happened. You agree?” Williams asked.

“I disagree,” the witness said.

“I am suggesting to you that you are lying,” Williams told the witness, prompting an objection from lead prosecutor LaToya Bernard.

Williams further suggested to the witness that he was not shot by Smith, but by members of the security forces.

The witness disagreed.

“I am suggesting to you that you went to your bus and took out an illegal gun that you had in your bus and came back to where the pastor was and fired shots at the police,” Williams said, to which the witness responded in disagreement.

Williams continued, “I am suggesting to you that it was the police in carrying out their lawful duties, returned fire and shot you. It wasn’t the pastor man who shot you”.

Again, the witness disagreed.

“I suggest that not only were you firing at the police, you fired as a faithful servant to your pastor who was also firing at the police,” the attorney said.

Again, the witness disagreed.

The trial continues today.

World.title: RICKETTS’S COUNTER-ATTACK
World.content:
Jamaica’s U-14 Reggae Boyz engage in light drills before their Caribbean Football Union U-14 Challenge Series game against Aruba in Punta Cana, Dominican Republic, on Tuesday, August 18.Jamaica’s U-14 Reggae Boyz engage in light drills before their Caribbean Football Union U-14 Challenge Series game against Aruba in Punta Cana, Dominican Republic, on Tuesday, August 18.

JAMAICA Football Federation (JFF) President Michael Ricketts says he’s unfazed by criticism of his Administration’s handling of football development, insisting that it has been executing the best grass roots programme in the country’s history.

With the Reggae Boyz failing to qualify for the FIFA World Cup for a seventh-straight campaign, long-standing criticism around the governing of local football by various stakeholders and the public have intensified over the past year.

One of the main concerns has been the lack of investment in youth football, which many believe has contributed to the senior team’s struggles.

However Ricketts, who has served as JFF president since 2017, told the Jamaica Observer that the current Administration has placed more focus on youth initiatives than ever before.

He pointed to the national under-17 team that qualified for the FIFA World Cup next month, the national under-20 team that narrowly missed out on World Cup qualification, and the under-15 and under-14 programmes that have won several regional titles over the last two years. Ricketts also spoke of the improvements made at the youth level for the girls’ programmes, which was inactive for years.

Ricketts believes the criticism has been unfair, and says his and the JFF’s work can speak for itself.

“Honestly, we have done well,” he said. “Three World Cup qualifications in eight years — and we’re looking for a fourth; a governance structure that is second to none.”

“I always use Christ as an example. He was crucified, and when he was being crucified they asked, ‘Who should we crucify?’ And some people shouted, ‘Crucify Jesus!’ who would[n’t]have done anything wrong, and [they demanded they] release the criminal, who was Barabbas.

“It’s just the nature of people. Sometimes people are objective and make the proper, fair comments; sometimes they are not. I’ve become immune to these negative comments. [All] I want [is] to ensure that my conscience sets me free and I do what I think is right. And I think I am blessed to have some real good people around me, people who really support the process, and people who are loyal and committed to growing the sport of football.”

Ricketts says along with the JFF’s own initiatives, FIFA’s Talent Development Scheme (TDS) has helped to strengthen the work being done at the grass roots level.

“We would have gotten some support from FIFA in the development process and that would have paid huge dividends, because what that permits us to do is to go around and harness young talent, get them into an organised setting at the [UWI-] JFF Captain [Horace] Burrell Centre of Excellence, and then we do some training there,” he said.

“We deliberately exclude overseas-based players from the under-14s because we thought that we do have enough talent at that level, and we were intent on ensuring that we give the opportunity to all the local under-14s who were good enough to be part of this programme. But we have benefited tremendously from the TDS programme.”

Ricketts says the grass roots programmes are on the right track and will produce greater results in the years ahead.

“I must commend the [under-14] coaching staff, headed by Vassell [Reynolds] and the entire management team,” he said. “Two years agonthe under-14 unit would have won the CFU Challenge Series. The following year, they won their group at the Concacaf level, and then the following year we qualified for the U-17 World Cup.

“So we are evolving, and I really want to commend the technical committee, the technical staff. The show is on its way and the sky is the limit, and we want to again qualify for the U-17 for next year. I think our youth programme is in good and competent hands, and we just want to ensure that there is a high level of consistency and competence from our coaching staff, and we are excited at the prospects.”

World.title: Succulent Lamb Chops
World.content:
(Photo: Alan Smith)

These grilled lamb chops are packed with flavour but still incredibly simple to prepare. I marinate the lamb in red wine, garlic, rosemary, salt and black pepper before grilling them over high heat for a beautiful char. Once off the grill, I finish the chops with fresh garlic, parsley and Scotch bonnet sauce and serve with creamy garlic mashed potatoes and sautéed bok choy.

Serves 4

Ingredients:

For the Lamb Chops

10-12 lamb chops

½ cup dry red wine

2 tablespoons olive oil

4 cloves garlic, finely minced

1 tablespoon dried rosemary

1 teaspoon salt, or to taste

1 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper

For the Fresh Garlic & Herb Sauce

¼ cup fresh parsley, finely chopped

2 cloves garlic, finely minced

¼ Scotch bonnet pepper, finely minced, or to taste

3 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil

1 tablespoon freshly squeezed lemon juice

½ teaspoon lemon zest

Salt, to taste

Freshly ground black pepper, to taste

Method

1. Marinate the lamb: Place lamb chops in a large bowl or shallow dish. Add the red wine, olive oil, garlic, rosemary, salt and black pepper. Turn the chops several times, making sure they are well coated in the marinade.

2. Cover and refrigerate for at least 1 hour, or for a few hours if time allows, allowing the red wine, garlic and rosemary to flavour the lamb.

3. Remove the lamb from the refrigerator approximately 20-30 minutes before grilling. Lift the chops from the marinade and allow excess liquid to drip off. Discard remaining marinade.

4. Make the fresh garlic and herb sauce: Combine the parsley, garlic, Scotch bonnet, olive oil, lemon juice and lemon zest in a small bowl. Season with salt and black pepper, then stir well. Let the sauce sit for about 10 minutes to allow the flavours to come together.

5. Preheat a grill or grill pan over medium-high to high heat. Once the grill is hot, add the lamb chops in a single layer, leaving a little space between each one.

6. Grill for approximately 3-4 minutes on the first side, then turn and cook for another 2-4 minutes, depending on the thickness of the chops and your preferred doneness. The lamb should develop a beautiful char on the outside while remaining tender inside.

7. Transfer the grilled lamb chops to a serving platter and allow them to rest for 5 minutes.

8. Spoon the fresh garlic and herb sauce over the warm lamb chops just before serving.

9. Serve with creamy garlic mashed potatoes and sautéed bok choy.

Shan’s Tip

After removing the lamb from the red wine marinade, let the excess marinade drip off before placing the chops on the hot grill. Too much liquid can prevent the lamb from getting that beautiful char. And give the chops a few minutes to rest after grilling before adding the fresh herb sauce — it keeps the lamb juicy while the warm meat brings out all the flavour of the garlic, parsley and Scotch bonnet.

Recipe courtesy of Shanice Gore

World.title: Jackie Jackson, legendary Jamaican bass guitarist, dies at 79
World.content:
Jackie Jackson

Clifton “Jackie” Jackson, the legendary bass guitarist who played on countless hit songs by artistes such as Toots And The Maytals, Jimmy Cliff and Paul Simon, died in Montego Bay on Wednesday.

Jackson, 79, was admitted to the Cornwall Regional Hospital in St James recently. He was a fixture on the Montego Bay hotel scene for many years, mentoring artistes and musicians including his wife, Karen Smith, who died in 2021.

From Central Kingston, Jackson got his start in the mid-1960s at the Treasure Isle recording studio of producer Duke Reid. He was a member of The Supersonics, the house band that played on numerous hit singles including Girl I’ve Got A Date by Alton Ellis, Little Nut Tree by The Melodians and Queen Majesty by The Techniques.

Jackson also played on classic songs for producer Leslie Kong, such as Israelites by Desmond Dekker and The Aces, By The Rivers of Babylon by The Melodians as well as The Harder They Come and Wonderful World, Beautiful People by Jimmy Cliff.

In 1972, Jackson and fellow Jamaican musicians including guitarist Hux Brown and keyboardist Neville Hinds played on Simon’s Mother And Child Reunion, which is from the American singer’s debut album released that year.

Some of Jackson’s best work was done with Toots And The Maytals with whom he toured for 50 years. His patented sound can be heard on that group’s biggest hits which include Pressure Drop, Funky Kingston and Sweet And Dandy.

At the Back-2-Bass-es show last February at the Edna Manley College of the Visual and Performing Arts in St Andrew, Jackson told the Observer Online that it is important to teach Jamaican youth about reggae’s history.

“Mentoring the younger generation is paramount to our music industry. The beautiful thing about the music I’ve played over the years, is that it will always be there to provide inspiration for more generations to come; and that is something I can be really proud of,” he said.

That event featured fellow bassists Boris Gardiner, Lloyd Parks, Daniel “Danny Axeman” Thompson, Donald “Danny Bassie” Dennis and Errol “Flabba Holt” Carter.

In 2012, Jackie Jackson was awarded the Order of Distinction for his contribution to the development of Jamaican music.

World.title: 4 takeaways from POLITICO’s interviews with French presidential candidates Le Pen, Mélenchon, Attal
World.content:
No alignment on Ukraine

Attal came out as a strong advocate for increased support for Ukraine. The 37-year-old said backing Ukraine was an “investment for us” rather than a humanitarian expense. He supported seizing Russian assets to help pay for Kyiv’s defense and did not “exclude” sending European planes to police Ukrainian skies.

Le Pen, on the other hand, made it clear that she believes France can no longer afford to assist Ukraine financially given the country’s budgetary constraints.

“We can train their soldiers and their military leadership and provide them with military aid. We can no longer provide financial assistance to Ukraine, and we regret that,” she said.

Jean-Luc Mélenchon speaks at the POLITICO Playbook Paris Live event in Paris on Sept. 24, 2026. | François Le Guen and Mathias Filippini for POLITICO

Le Pen was adamant that she believed French President Emmanuel Macron had not done enough to bring Moscow and Kyiv to the negotiating table. She said she supported U.S. President Donald Trump’s decision to invite Russian President Vladimir Putin to the G20 summit in Miami in December.

“Any initiatives aimed at putting an end to this slaughter are welcome,” she said.

Both Le Pen and Mélenchon argued that supplying any type of military equipment to Ukraine would likely put France in harm’s way.

World.title: TotalEnergies refused rescue aid during deadly Mozambique attack, inquest hears
World.content:
Coroner Jason Pegg ruled on Thursday that Mawer was unlawfully killed by an unknown person, but accepted an argument by lawyers from TotalEnergies’ Mozambican subsidiary that the company had no legal duty of care to him because he was a subcontractor.

The testimony could carry consequences in France, where TotalEnergies faces two criminal complaints over its Mozambique operations, including an involuntary manslaughter case tied to the deaths of contractors during the Palma attack. A French investigating magistrate was appointed last year to examine that complaint.

“These hearings were crucial, crucial, crucial,” said Henri Thulliez, a French human rights lawyer who filed both criminal complaints in Paris and who was in Winchester to watch proceedings. “Finally, we have people talking under oath about what happened in Palma. It’s very important, and very rare when it comes to accountability for multinationals.”

Thulliez’s second complaint accuses TotalEnergies of complicity in war crimes and torture. It alleges the energy giant became an accomplice in a massacre — first reported by POLITICO — in which Mozambican soldiers brutalized, starved, suffocated, executed or disappeared around 200 men at the company's gatehouse from June to September 2021.

TotalEnergies has denied responsibility for the deaths during the ISIS attack, which killed 1,354 civilians, including 55 people working on the TotalEnergies project, according to a house-to-house survey carried out by POLITICO. In response to questions from POLITICO, it acknowledged in 2024 that “a small number” of project workers had been stationed outside its secure compound during the attack and exposed to the bloodbath.

In 2025, the company — through its subsidiary Mozambique LNG — told POLITICO it had no knowledge of the gatehouse killings, adding that its “extensive research” had “not identified any information nor evidence that would corroborate the allegations of severe abuses and torture.”

World.title: France would defend eastern flank borders even outside NATO, says Mélenchon
World.content:
Mélenchon is among the front-runners in next spring’s high-stakes presidential election to replace Emmanuel Macron, according to polls.

He and far-right rival Marine Le Pen both want Paris to pull back from the military alliance, raising alarm bells at NATO headquarters about France’s future defense policy. Leaving NATO is a matter of “dignity” given U.S. President Donald Trump’s behavior toward Europeans, Mélenchon told POLITICO.

He doubled down on his opposition to Germany’s massive rearmament, accusing Berlin of not having coordinated with its neighbors and pointing to the “history” of German attacks against France.

“[The Germans want to build Europe’s] largest conventional army, to do what? ... We need to talk about this, and you’re going to tell us why,” he said.

The far-left political veteran also wants to move toward a ban on Ukrainian deep strikes into Russian territory.

“Do you realize that [they’re] firing with French and British weapons? We’re becoming belligerents,” he said.

World.title: Le Pen welcomes Trump’s G20 invite for Putin
World.content:
Marine Le Pen speaks at the Paris Playbook Live event in Paris on Sept. 24, 2026. | François Le Guen and Mathias Filippini for POLITICO

PARIS — French far-right leader and presidential frontrunner Marine Le Pen is on board with U.S. President Donald Trump’s decision to invite Russian leader Vladimir Putin to the G20 summit in Miami in December.

“Any initiatives aimed at putting an end to this slaughter are welcome,” she said at POLITICO’s Paris Playbook live event Thursday, referring to Russia’s war against Ukraine, after criticizing French President Emmanuel Macron for what she said were insufficient efforts to bring Russia back to the negotiating table.

Le Pen made clear at the same event that if she won the 2027 presidential election, France would halt all financial aid to Ukraine, though she said she was willing to maintain some form of support, including military training.

World.title: Jean-Luc Mélenchon assure qu’un blocage des prix des carburants n’entraînera pas de pénurie
World.content:
Pour ses détracteurs, cette mesure entraînerait une pénurie, notamment parce que la France importe environ la moitié de sa consommation de diesel.

“Une bêtise”, selon Jean-Luc Mélenchon. Selon lui, les entreprises pétrolières n’auront d’autres choix que de baisser le prix de leurs produits raffinés, “parce que la Chine n’en a pas besoin, parce que l’Inde n’en a pas besoin”.

“Pour qui [vendraient-elles], le Zimbabwe ? Soyons sérieux !”

Pour Jean-Luc Mélenchon, charge aux entreprises pétrolières de se “débrouiller” en comprimant leurs marges une fois la mesure appliqué. Il a précisé qu’il faisait référence aux marges de raffineries et d’extraction : “Ce n’est pas le moment d’aller s’en prendre aux petits distributeurs.”

Le candidat en a profité pour critiquer l’attitude du gouvernement français à l’égard de TotalEnergies. “A quoi sert que TotalEnergies soit une compagnie française si on ne peut rien lui demander ?”, a-t-il lancé.

Depuis le début du conflit, le gouvernement est resté mesuré sur l’idée d’une taxation des superprofits pétroliers. A l’inverse, il s’est félicité de compter une major pétrolière parmi les entreprises françaises et a salué le plafonnement des prix mis en place dans les stations de TotalEnergies.

Cela revient, pour l’Insoumis, a faire “la charité” : “Monsieur Total, vous voulez bien me donner un peu de sous ?”, a-t-il singé.

“Jusqu’à présent, on ne réglait pas ça comme ça en France, [mais avec des mécanismes qui] nous posent tous comme des sujets égaux de la République”.

World.title: Le patron d’Intermarché maintient son appel à suspendre les CEE mais reconnaît des difficultés
World.content:
Une fois les certificats d’économies d’énergie suspendus, il serait difficile pour un gouvernement de les relancer, a admis Thierry Cotillard, lors du sommet POLITICO Playbook Paris Live.

PARIS — Face à l’envolée des prix des carburants et la perspective que le “seuil symbolique” des 2,50 euros le litre soit dépassé, il faut envisager une suspension des certificats d’économies d’énergie (CEE), a de nouveau appelé Thierry Cotillard, le président du groupement Les Mousquetaires (Intermarché), jeudi lors du sommet POLITICO Playbook Paris Live.

“Bien évidemment, il ne faudra jamais remettre [ce dispositif] en compte, puisqu’il faut qu’on finance tous les sujets de décarbonation, assure-t-il. Mais à situation exceptionnelle et crise exceptionnelle, il faudra peut-être ‘décliquer’ [pour] rendre 17 centimes précisément au consommateur”.

Les CEE ne sont pas une taxe mais un mécanisme extrabudgétaire qui oblige les énergéticiens à financer des économies d’énergie. Ces quelques 10 milliards d’euros servent à soutenir les véhicules électriques, la rénovation énergétique ou encore la décarbonation de l’industrie, mais sont répercutés sur les factures des consommateurs.

World.title: Le réchauffement climatique n’est “contesté par personne”, assure Marine Le Pen
World.content:
Marine Le Pen speaks at the POLITICO Playbook Paris Live event in Paris on Sept. 14, 2026. | François Le Guen and Mathias Filippini for POLITICO

PARIS — Après plusieurs mois où la France fut frappée de plein fouet par les conséquences du dérèglement climatique, Marine Le Pen est revenue sur ses propos relativisant la crédibilité des scénarios du Giec, la référence scientifique mondiale sur le climat, dans un entretien à POLITICO.

Assurant que le réchauffement climatique “n'est absolument contesté par personne”, Marine Le Pen a tenté de relativiser, lors du sommet POLITICO Playbook Paris Live, estimant que certaines “hypothèses [du Giec] sont optimistes”, d'autres “plus alarmistes”.

“La question qui m’était posée prenait une des hypothèses [...] la plus alarmiste”, a botté en touche en touche la candidate du Rassemblement national à l'élection présidentielle.

World.title: Le Pen says she won’t leave NATO until Russia’s war in Ukraine ends
World.content:
She and far-left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon both want Paris to leave the military alliance, raising alarm bells at NATO headquarters about France's future defense policy.

The National Rally has long advocated withdrawing from NATO's integrated command, but Le Pen's comments indicate a slight shift in her position. Back in May, she said France would pull out during her first term, without referring to the war in Ukraine, while the party's president Jordan Bardella wanted to wait for a peace agreement between Kyiv and Moscow.

Le Pen and Bardella are campaigning as a ticket that would see the 31-year-old become prime minister.

Le Pen also said that France should not enter into a war with Russia, a nuclear-armed power, and rejected the notion that it is currently in a conflict with Moscow despite the Kremlin's hybrid attacks against European nations.

By publishing a statement condemning Russia last week, Le Pen and Bardella sought to fend off attacks from center-right and center-left opponents who have frequently portrayed the party as an ally to Russian President Vladimir Putin.

However, Le Pen repeated her pledge Thursday to stop financial help to Ukraine if she wins next year's presidential election.

World.title: Rutte says Putin is in a 'bad place' as he reassures NATO allies amid threat reports
World.content:
NATO is prepared to respond to sabotage and drone incidents across Europe and has plans in place to address such threats, Secretary General Mark Rutte said on Thursday.

 

"Russia is doing more and more when it comes to the cyber etc. domain, but... NATO is ready for this," Rutte said at an event in New York commemorating the September 11, 2001 attacks on the United States.

"We have all these response options in place... when it comes to hybrids to make sure that we stay strong," he added.

Rutte argued that the growing number of hybrid incidents in NATO countries indicated that Russian President Vladimir Putin was losing the war in Ukraine, now in its fifth year.

"Putin is in a bad place," Rutte said, adding that Russia is not winning the war in Ukraine and that citizens of the 32 NATO countries can remain calm.

He urged NATO members to provide "more support for Ukraine" if they "really want to give a signal to the Russians on every hybrid incident, hybrid attack."

"All the response options are there, and we will use whatever we need," Rutte added.

His remarks came after Danish intelligence on Thursday warned of a growing risk of Russian military action against NATO countries, including further hybrid attacks.

At the same time, Spanish media reported that US intelligence had alerted European countries to a possible Russian drone operation targeting Spain, France or Italy.

U.S. Defense Secretary urges Europe to take the lead on its defense

Meanwhile, US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said on Thursday that European allies must take the lead in defending their continent, calling for NATO to become a "real hard-line military alliance."

Speaking at a meeting of NATO defence ministers, Hegseth proposed a "NATO 3.0" focused on strengthening military capabilities and deterring threats in Europe.

His comments came weeks after Washington informed its allies that it would no longer provide certain warships and aircraft in the event of an attack on a NATO member. European allies and Canada are now assessing how to address the resulting capability gaps.

"NATO 3.0 is post-Cold War recognition that (NATO) needs to go back to a real hard-line military alliance that has real military capabilities capable of deterring right here on the continent and taking the lead for the conventional defense of Europe," Hegseth said.

Under Article 5 of NATO's founding treaty, an attack on one member is considered an attack on all. However, the provision does not automatically require allies to provide military assistance.

The US, which has NATO's largest armed forces, is seeking to reduce its role in Europe's conventional defence. It does not plan to withdraw its nuclear weapons stationed in Europe, which remain a central element of NATO's deterrence strategy.

World.title: Trump and Xi vow cooperation amid 'healthy competition' at the White House
World.content:
US president Donald Trump hailed the “truly great friendship” he has developed with Xi Jinping as the Chinese president began his state visit to the United States on Thursday.

 

In his opening remarks before the formal talks at the White House, Xi told Trump that he is “ready to work with you to steer the giant ship of China-US relationship on a steady course toward the future,” and that the two countries “must hold the line of no conflict and no confrontation.”

The Chinese leader underlined that China and the United States are the two superpowers that “facing the changes in our world, in our times, and of historical significance today”, they “shoulder a historic responsibility of advancing human development and progress”.

“We can certainly find the right path for two great countries to get along on this planet we both call home_,”_ Xi said, adding that “through candid, in-depth, and continued dialogue, our two countries can understand each other better, seek common ground, while shelving differences and build up mutual trust.”

Xi’s highly anticipated visit to Washington started with the two leaders proclaiming their long relationship, but the two global economic rivals were gearing up to discuss the key thorny issues in their formal talks.

“From the time of my first election in 2016, President Xi and I have forged a friendship, a truly great friendship, actually, built on mutual respect and the vital interests of our people,” Trump said, while also touching on cooperation during World War 2.

But moving on, Trump said the US and China were working towards “more balanced” trade relations and that their talks would focus on foreign affairs, trade, financial cooperation, security and artificial intelligence which they identified as a major topic.

In turn, Xi said he hopes “Chinese companies are treated fairly here in the United States” while China would welcome US companies there and that “competition should be a healthy one and should be kept within bounds.”

China has resisted the Trump administration’s urging and economic threats to use its considerable leverage to convince Iran to agree to US terms to end the Iran war, even if China which is far more dependent on Gulf oil than the US.

China condemned the US and Israeli war on Iran and Xi previously expressed concerns that the conflict signalled a return to what he then called “the law of the jungle”.

Xi is expected to press Trump again, in the same way as he did when the two leaders met in Beijing in May, to permanently end arms sales to Taiwan as China has made clear that it views Taiwan as the most sensitive issue in the US-China relationship.

Back in May, Trump described arms sales to Taiwan as a “very good negotiating chip” with China.

On trade, China is pushing for the US to loosen export restrictions on cutting-edge advanced chips.

The two sides agreed on Wednesday to extend by two months a one-year trade truce that was set to expire on November 10 as they work to find a more durable agreement.

“It should be a race of catching up with one another, not a wrestle in which one either wins or loses,” Xi said.

Xi says China and US should make sure AI is ‘always under human control’

Xi also referred to AI in his opening comments, saying that the two countries had a responsibility to ensure that humans always operate AI.

“We have both the capability and responsibility to develop and manage AI for good and ensure that a development of AI is always under human control and serves the well being of the people,” the Chinese leader said.

Trump said in a social media post earlier Thursday that artificial intelligence will be high on the agenda amid growing global anxiety that the technology threatens humanity.

“I want to leave it exactly where it is,” Trump wrote. “That is China’s position also.”

The two countries’ finance ministers met earlier this week, with the US proposing a new “notification mechanism” for AI incidents between the two nations.

As the two leaders wrapped up their opening remarks, Xi also announced that China will invite 100,000 American youth to come to his country for studies and exchanges in the next five years and that China will send two pandas to the zoo in Atlanta.

He called the beloved animals an “envoy of friendship.”

World.title: Uzbekistan highlights Central Asia cooperation at UN General Assembly
World.content:
Uzbekistan called for a more effective United Nations, presenting closer cooperation in Central Asia as an example of how dialogue can ease regional tensions.

 

Saida Mirziyoyeva, who has headed Uzbekistan’s Presidential Administration since June 2025, delivered the country’s address to the 81st session of the General Assembly in New York.

She framed Tashkent’s foreign-policy approach around “openness, good-neighbourliness and dialogue”, adding that Uzbekistan stood for “peace, cooperation and respect for human dignity”.

“No country can solve global problems alone,” she told delegates.

“We need a UN that is capable not only of making decisions, but of implementing them.”

Uzbekistan backed an expansion of the UN Security Council and reiterated its candidacy for a non-permanent seat for 2035–2036.

The country is also due to chair the Non-Aligned Movement from 2027 to 2029, which Tashkent sees as another platform for international dialogue.

Central Asia and Afghanistan

The speech pointed to changes in relations among the five Central Asian states, where disputes over borders and water resources have complicated ties for decades.

“The situation and atmosphere in the region have completely changed,” Mirziyoyeva said, referring to closer cooperation between neighbouring governments.

On Afghanistan, she argued that viewing the country solely as a security threat would not solve its problems and that the Afghan population should not be left to deal with them alone.

At the first EU-Central Asia summit in Samarkand in April 2025, European and Central Asian leaders expressed shared concern about security threats and possible spillover from Afghanistan into both Central Asia and Europe.

Head of Uzbekistan's Presidential Administration, Saida Mirziyoyeva, delivers her speech during UN General Assembly in New York Centre for the Production of Content of Mass Media under the Administration of the President of the Republic of Uzbekistan

Domestic reforms, AI and human rights

The address also reviewed changes inside Uzbekistan over the past decade.

According to the figures presented, the economy grew from $50bn (€44bn) to $147bn (€129bn), while foreign investment exceeded $150bn (€131bn).

Mirziyoyeva put the poverty rate at 4% and said almost 10mn people had moved out of poverty.

She cited wider access to preschool and higher education, as well as improvements in health indicators, as part of the government’s reform record.

On artificial intelligence, she argued that technological development should remain linked to “human rights, security, equal opportunities and responsibility”.

Technology, she added, should improve people’s lives rather than create new forms of dependence.

The Aral Sea and the energy transition

Environmental issues centred on the Aral Sea, whose dramatic shrinkage remains one of Central Asia’s most serious ecological problems.

Mirziyoyeva described the disaster as the result of decisions taken over decades, pointing to water-saving technologies and efforts to restore degraded land.

She also set out Uzbekistan’s energy transition target, with the country aiming to raise the share of renewables to 54% by 2030.

The speech also referred to the UN-backed Decade of Action for Afforestation and Forest Restoration for 2027–2036, calling for international environmental initiatives to be translated into practical projects.

Meetings in New York

In New York, Mirziyoyeva met UN Secretary-General António Guterres to discuss cooperation between Uzbekistan and the United Nations.

Head of Uzbekistan's Presidential Administration, Saida Mirziyoyeva, met with UN General Secretary, António Guterres Centre for the Production of Content of Mass Media under the Administration of the President of the Republic of Uzbekistan

Talks with Google vice-president Karan Bhatia included the possible launch of YouTube monetisation in Uzbekistan.

The Uzbek side linked the discussion to recent changes in legislation on personal data processing and digital payments, which it says are creating wider access to international payment systems.

Mirziyoyeva also met Ben Black, chief executive of the US International Development Finance Corporation.

Their talks covered joint projects in transport and healthcare, with Uzbekistan expressing interest in expanding cooperation with the DFC.
