World.title: The US media boycott hit Trump right where it hurts. Now it’s Hanson’s turn
World.content:
PoliticsFederalPress freedom Opinion The US media boycott hit Trump right where it hurts. Now it’s Hanson’s turn Waleed Aly Columnist, author and academic September 25, 2026 — 3:30am

September 25, 2026 — 3:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Solidarity? In America? Among the media? It seems astonishing that anything quite so unified could grow from America’s famously polarised soil, but here we are, watching as such sworn enemies as Fox News and MS NOW stand in solidarity with each other, and against President Donald Trump’s latest attack on their craft. These are the paradigm cases of American media partisanship: Fox News often Trump’s cheer squad, MS NOW (formerly MSNBC) a kind of progressive riposte. Each symbolises everything the other hates. And yet this week, that was forgotten when Trump declared he was banning MS NOW, alongside CNN and Politico, from the White House, and deactivated their correspondents’ press passes. Illegally so, it turned out, and a court has just ordered they be reinstated. But in the meantime, Fox – alongside ABC, CBS and NBC – had boycotted Trump’s press conferences. Photo: Illustration: Dionne Gain Suddenly, Trump found himself at risk of greatly reduced television coverage in a week of addressing the UN and hosting Xi Jinping. Already, we’ve seen his team forced to capture their own footage of Trump arriving heroically to open the new White House helipad, the kind of thing that news cameras would have filmed. The feed was nigh unwatchable. There he was, saying words no one could hear, exuding exactly no authority. A Trump-shaped tree, falling in the forest. That sort of thing is unimaginable for someone like Trump, who loves and dominates television more than any president ever has. He is famously fixed to Fox News. He appoints its anchors to high office. In his first term, Trump staffers tried giving him briefings in the form of television packages because it was the best way to ensure he would pay attention. He amassed some US$4.6 billion ($6.5 billion) worth of free television coverage in the 2016 election campaign alone, about twice that of Hillary Clinton. He has effectively lived with a television camera on him since. A boycott of this kind hits Trump somewhere near where it hurts.



I’ll admit to being surprised by these developments. After all, Trump has berated the media for his whole premiership without provoking any solidaristic response. You’re familiar with the catchphrases: “the fake news media”, “the enemy of the people”, “corrupt” and “dishonest”. He has attacked individual journalists as “human scum” and “low-life reporters” and told one to be “quiet, piggy”. He has even banned individual reporters from the Pentagon and White House, most notably CNN’s Jim Acosta in 2018. And nothing. The difference this time was that he just went ahead and banned whole outlets. That has two consequences. First, it ends up costing the other outlets much more money because they often share footage, which allows them to operate with fewer resources. Cut two TV networks from the pool and you leave a big shortfall for the others to make up. But second, Trump did so explicitly because their “cumulative stories” led him to regard them as unfavourable. And whatever you think of those outlets, or even of the media in general, that’s an enormous move. Related Article Trump's White House Trump launches ‘Trump TV’ channel after networks boycott him To effectively demand favourable coverage in exchange for access is to undo the very concept of accountability. Trump’s answer to this charge hits all the typically populist notes, but it also had a slip within it: “I don’t have to let them into my … into the people’s house.” Trump seems to regard access as his to give personally. Then he corrects, and asserts it on behalf of the people. By now, some of this should sound familiar to the Australian ear. The pitch isn’t so heightened because Pauline Hanson is not prime minister. But she has taken the step of banning entire outlets from attending some of her press conferences. In this case, it’s the ABC (for whom I am a radio host) and The Guardian, and on the Victorian hustings, occasionally, The Age. The reasoning is also colourfully similar. “I answer to the people, not the media” declared Hanson in her National Press Club address in June.



Party director James Ashby said giving the ABC access would be like “going back to some domestic violence relationship” (Hanson’s views on such violence as a “two-way street” presumably don’t extend this far). The ban is patchy and Barnaby Joyce certainly seems exempt from it. But One Nation has pulled candidates from ABC slots where they were regulars until they joined the party. In short, Hanson has crossed a line the US media has decided not to accept. Might Australian journalists do the same? Could we see, for example, the Murdoch press – broadcast and print – stand on principle and say that if the ABC cannot attend a press conference, then they won’t either? I admit, it’s hard to imagine given the way the Murdoch media talks about the ABC, but is it any harder to imagine than it would have been for Fox News? TV channels take a stand against the ban by Donald Trump. Bloomberg So far in Australia, we’ve seen quiet disapproval from the outlets that aren’t banned, but nothing planting a flag on the ground of principle. We’ve seen the odd commentator say One Nation’s move is a bad political strategy because it becomes a controversy that distracts from the party’s message. For what it’s worth, I think this profoundly misreads the extent to which the strategy only heightens One Nation’s message. But so far, the tone is that it’s something a bit silly. Not a violation of anything serious. The idea of media solidarity, based not on a liking for each other but a belief in the concept of journalism, doesn’t seem to have occurred to anyone. Perhaps that would change if Hanson became prime minister. But by then, the principle at stake may have long since eroded. Trump and Hanson’s wars against the media work precisely because they tap into a rich vein of anti-media sentiment.



Related Article Opinion

Australian economy Barnaby Joyce is indeed not Jesus Christ. He doesn’t need to be Waleed Aly Columnist, author and academic In any conventional age, a politician complaining about the media would look petulant and self-obsessed. Today, their devotees lap up this sort of thing, like it strikes a blow for the common man against the elites. If media organisations want to let that slide, they can. But they should be careful it doesn’t slide away completely. Waleed Aly is a broadcaster, author, academic and regular columnist. The Opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: Local tattoo shop bracing for long night as Dockers fans chase inaugural premiership ink
World.content:
NationalWAAFL grand final Local tattoo shop bracing for long night as Dockers fans chase inaugural premiership ink Hannah Murphy September 25, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

From Wharfie Time to Country Roads, this is your one-stop shop for all things Fremantle and Brisbane in the lead-up to the grand final. See all stories .

A Fremantle tattoo shop is gearing up to work until punters stop coming through the door come Saturday afternoon, with a selection of Flagmantle designs on offer should the Dockers take home their inaugural premiership. Five Star Tattoo shop in Fremantle are ready for an influx of customers over grand final weekend. Hannah Murphy Five Star Tattoo is in the heart of the Fremantle cappuccino strip, and say they are equal parts concerned about the fanfare that could ensue following a Freo win against the Brisbane Lions on Saturday, and excited to host anyone who wishes to get some ink to mark the occasion. “We’re anticipating chaos, maybe either way - so who knows?” Five Star tattooist Mark said. “Fremantle’s going to be a different place, that’s for sure.”



Just some of the designs on offer. Hannah Murphy The shop is extending its hours and has already done a mock-up of several designs, ready for anyone who wants to make what Mark calls the “good decision” to get a tattoo. “We’ve got a sheet of designs done, ready to go - but of course we’ll be doing regular tattoo stuff, so taking walk-ins, appointments, whatever comes,” Mark said. Tattooists at the shop are ready for “chaos” whatever way the game goes. Hannah Murphy In the event of a loss, Mark said he’s still prepared for those to file through the door wanting to nail their colours to the mast after a bumper 2026 season - but remember, it’s cash only.



It’s a feeling echoed by other tattoo shops up and down the strip, with many looking to extend regular trading hours across the board to keep the crowds happy. A pop-up merchandise shop outside the Fremantle markets. Hannah Murphy Fremantle businesses are also gearing up for the “chaos” expected to reign on the port city come Saturday, with some choosing to extend hours to accommodate an influx of crowds and others rostering extra staff. Some shops have painted their front windows with Dockers memorabilia, with staff wearing Fremantle jumpers throughout the main strip of the town. Local businesses are turning their shops purple ahead of grand final eve. Hannah Murphy



One small business pop-up selling Fremantle merchandise outside the local markets sold out of most of its popular gear, and a memorial is going up on Main Street in the port city, curated and painted by street artists from Blank Walls. Blank Walls, a street-art studio set up in Perth and London, has painted across from the Piazza a mural featuring Caleb Serong, Alex Pearce, Murphy Reid and Andrew Brayshaw, which will be going up throughout Thursday and Friday. Authorities said they were planning on an extra 40,000 people to be roaming the streets in the event of a Dockers grand final, and earlier this month the City of Fremantle approved a budget amendment that would allow them to pull the trigger on $230,000 needed to accommodate the influx of visitors.

World.title: Pints and meat: The Wharfie Time effect on Freo’s pubs and WA butchers
World.content:
NationalFremantle Dockers Pints and meat: The Wharfie Time effect on Freo’s pubs and WA butchers Hamish Hastie September 25, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

What does 40,000 rowdy Dockers supporters flowing into the usually laid-back port city of Fremantle mean for one of its biggest pubs? Gage Roads at the A-Shed overlooking the working port has done the math and the estimates are eye watering. Gage Roads expects to pour 2000 of its Purple Reign pints on Saturday. Gage Roads owner Good Drinks Australia’s head of hospitality Miles Hull said they will sell about 1200 serves (or half a tonne) of chips, 1500 pizzas and 7000 pints – 2000 of which they expect will be their Purple Reign beer brewed especially for these finals. Hull said not only would a blowout over the Lions be the best for the town, but it would also be the best for sales.



“If it’s a nail-biter, no one wants to leave their seat or take their eyes off the game and people are caught up in the moment of the game and so it goes quiet at the bar,” he said. “On [the Friday of the elimination final against Geelong] you could track the state of the game by the bar sales. “The beer sales were really strong, but they slowed down in that last quarter and then picked up at the end of the game. “You could see that people were not as engaged halfway through the match because Freo were trailing and people found themselves a bit more time to get to the bar, but in the fourth quarter it was a different story. At least until after the game.” Police, the City of Fremantle and the state government are expecting a huge number of people to come to Fremantle to watch the game and party afterwards, with road closures in place in the CBD and four massive screens set up.



Tony Scarfo with his purple sausages. Scarfos Meating Place/Supplied A sold-out event is also being held at the Dockers’ spiritual home of South Fremantle Oval with thousands expected to attend. Karl Bullers, the owner of Fremantle institutions the Old Court House and the National Hotel, said he was expecting triple the normal Saturday sales. “People are just starting to realise just how big this is going to be, so we are over-ordering on everything because the last thing we want to be doing is run out of anything,” he said. Bullers has a ticketed event at the National, which sold out immediately. He said his pubs had been receiving calls asking whether they could camp out at 5.30am to secure a spot in front of their screens.



For those unable to get to Melbourne or want to avoid the chaos in Fremantle the humble backyard barbecue is shaping up as a popular choice. Butchers across the state have already reported an uptick in sales with most doing some form of purple sausage to commemorate the Dockers’ historic second grand final appearance. Tony Scarfo of Scarfos Meating Place in Myaree, east of Fremantle, has again whipped out the purple food colouring and expects to sell up to half a tonne of purple sausage by Saturday afternoon. “Over a week, you could push probably 400 to 500 kilos of actual purple ones,” he said. Scarfos became famous for the purple sausages back in 2013 ahead of the Dockers’ first grand final. They were devised through trial and error, but are simply barbecue beef sausages dipped in purple food colouring and water.



Plantagenet Meats purple chicken sausages. Plantagenet Meats/Supplied Scarfo said he expects his trade to be up 30 per cent on a normal week. Willetton butcher Nick Thomson expects his sales to pick up by about 20 per cent. Thomson is an Essendon fan, but most of his team are Dockers mad and have come up with a purple and white chicken and cheese sausage. Regionally, butcher shops are also experiencing a finals rush.



Willetton Butcher is serving purple and white chicken and cheese sausages. Willetton Butcher/Supplied Plantagenet Meats owner Josh Liebeck also sold purple sausages back in 2013, but it didn’t quite work. “We didn’t do the right sausage and we didn’t get the colours right so they went this horrible green colour,” he said. Liebeck added that they have now mastered the purple chicken sausage and expects sales could double over Thursday, Friday and Saturday. “It’s been a character building 32 years. Hopefully, we can come away with a win,” the long-suffering Dockers fan said.

World.title: Trump and Xi exchange pleasantries, pandas as White House lifts reporter ban
World.content:
Breaking WorldNorth AmericaForeign relations Trump and Xi exchange pleasantries, pandas as White House lifts reporter ban Michael Koziol Updated September 25, 2026 — 2:27am ,first published 12:28am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: News outlets CNN, MS NOW and Politico were allowed back into the White House after a judge ruled President Donald Trump’s ban on their entry was likely unconstitutional and must be temporarily lifted. But the outlets did not regain entry until about noon on Thursday (2am Friday AEST), after Trump and Xi Jinping began their high-stakes bilateral meeting on the Chinese leader’s first White House visit since 2015. There were no cameras from the main US television networks present as Trump welcomed Xi to the premises, with the news outlets continuing a boycott in solidarity with CNN. Xi’s arrival was broadcast on the White House’s official social media channel. A select group of print reporters and photographers, known as the daily “pool”, was present – along with Chinese state media.



Fox News was using an aerial shot of the White House and file footage when discussing the summit, while also covering other news stories. Phone footage from reporters in the pool showed there was a loud and sustained disagreement between the American photographers, Chinese photographers and the Secret Service about where the Chinese group could set up their cameras while awaiting Xi’s arrival. President Donald Trump and First Lady Melania Trump welcomed Chinese President Xi Jinping and his wife Peng Liyuan to the White House. AP Photo/Alex Brandon Judge Timothy Kelly ruled late on Wednesday (US time) that Trump’s ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico was likely unconstitutional, and blocked the White House from enforcing it for 14 days. But journalists from those the three outlets were still unable to access the White House on Thursday morning.



They lodged a request for an emergency hearing with the court. That request, seen by this masthead, said Secret Service agents had also “confiscated the hard passes of journalists whose hard passes had not previously been confiscated”. Trump had enacted the ban on Saturday due to his objections to the three outlets’ reporting, though he said there was no particular trigger for it other than his accusations of “fake news”. CNN reporter Betsy Klein regained access to the White House at about midday on Thursday. AP Photo/Alex Brandon But at about noon, reporters from the affected outlets regained access to the White House grounds. Their passes were reactivated while a bilateral meeting between Trump and Xi was already under way. Following the arrival ceremony, Trump and Xi delivered statements in the Grand Foyer of the White House, which were also broadcast on the White House’s official social media feed, but not on US television networks.



Trump noted there had been many physical changes at the White House since Xi’s last visit in 2015, and praised his “truly great friendship” with the Chinese leader. In relatively brief remarks, Trump spoke in broad terms about efforts to create “a more balanced trade relationship” between the world’s two largest economies, and doubled down on his attempt to rebrand artificial intelligence “super intelligence”. US President Donald Trump and China’s President Xi Jinping meet in the Oval Office. AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin “If we focus on our common interests, I am confident there is much we can achieve,” he said. Xi spoke for longer, and made numerous observations and recommendations about particular policy areas – including American market access for Chinese firms.



“China keeps its door wide open, welcomes American companies wanting to invest and do business there. We hope Chinese companies are treated fairly here in the United States,” he said. On AI, Xi said both countries had the capability and responsibility to ensure development was “always under human control” and served the wellbeing of people. Related Article Updated

Trump diplomacy ‘Partners, not rivals’: Xi Jinping lands in Washington with Trump waiting on the tarmac Both countries would gain from co-operation and lose from confrontation, he said. He once again invoked the Thucydides Trap, which describes the high risk of war when a rising power starts displacing an existing power. “The Thucydides Trap can be overcome,” Xi said. “China-US co-operation may not solve every problem in the world, but without our co-operation, it would be hard to solve many of the world’s problems.”



Xi raised the possibility of further co-operation on fentanyl, increasing direct flights between the two nations and his new invitation for 100,000 American students to undertake exchange in China over the next five years. Two Chinese pandas – male Ping Ping and female Fu Shuang – would also arrive at Zoo Atlanta shortly, Xi said, as part of China’s diplomacy efforts. Chinese President Xi Jinping said he hoped Chinese businesses would be treated fairly in the United States. Bloomberg “Achieving the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again can go hand in hand,” he said, a reference to Trump’s main political slogan. After the speeches, the leaders and their wives watched a US military review and flyover. Trump and Xi proceeded to a bilateral meeting, while the First Lady and Madam Peng travelled to the Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art.



On Thursday night, they will attend a state dinner organised by the First Lady. The menu, designed to showcase “American ingredients with subtle Chinese influence”, includes a yellow squash velouté with wild mushrooms, sesame crusted sea bass with baby bok choy and a vanilla crémeux with sour cherry confit centre. Entertainment will come from tenor Christopher Macchio, who performed at Trump’s 2025 inauguration. US President Donald Trump and China’s President Xi Jinping walk along the Colonnade of the White House. AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Asylum seekers trigger UK protests, arrests as 781 arrive in one day
World.content:
Breaking WorldEuropeAsylum seekers Asylum seekers trigger UK protests, arrests as 781 arrive in one day David Crowe September 25, 2026 — 2:09am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: Britain is engulfed in a new row over asylum seekers after 781 arrived in a single day on small boats in the English Channel, with video footage showing one man leaving a young child in the water in his scramble to board a boat. The surge triggered calls for a right-wing rally against migration despite UK government claims that it was curbing the influx, which has become one of the most potent and divisive issues in British national life. Protest organiser Danny Tommo was arrested after he sought to stop one of the inflatable boats by slashing it with a knife. YouTube One high-profile protest organiser, Danny Tommo, sought to stop one of the inflatable boats by slashing it with a knife while it had at least one person on board, escalating the confrontations off the English coast. British police arrested Tommo, whose real name is Daniel Thomas, on suspicion of destroying a boat and endangering personal safety, and kept him in custody.



When news emerged that he was detained in the English town of Basingstoke, right-wing activists including Tommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, called on social media on Thursday morning – about 11pm AEST – for supporters to gather at the town’s police station to demand his release. Robinson, who has gained support from billionaire Elon Musk when organising large rallies against migration, has described the small boat arrivals as an “invasion” and encouraged protests at hotels used to house the migrants. He has been convicted of assault in the past, and was jailed for seven months in 2024 for breaching a High Court injunction that banned him from repeating false claims about a Syrian refugee. Related Article Immigration Police injured as protesters descend on homes for asylum seekers in England On Thursday, amid the attention on the boat arrivals, Robinson also aired his support for Russia’s criticism of the West in the war in Ukraine. “The people are seeing through the whole ‘it’s Russias fault’ [sic] Western propaganda war machine,” he posted. He visited Moscow in June, when he met Musk’s father, Errol, in the Russian capital. The protests against asylum seekers increased over recent days when two small boats landed on English shores, avoiding the surveillance of UK Border Force in the busy channel.



Most of the small inflatable boats do not make it all the way across the channel because they are intercepted in open water by Border Force officers, who transfer them to UK vessels and take them to a detention centre at Dover. The arrival of the two dinghies on beaches near Portsmouth triggered demonstrations on Tuesday and led to the arrest of six people, three of whom were later charged. Hampshire police said they charged one woman, Shannon Dodds, 32, with two counts of assault for allegedly beating an emergency services worker. They charged another woman, Sally Pearson, 31, with a racially aggravated public order offence as well as assaulting an emergency worker. A man, Toby Matthews, 33, was also charged with assaulting an emergency worker. Police arrested Tommo on Wednesday night after he slashed the inflatable boat when at least one rescue worker remained on board, after the asylum seekers had been removed. “A man has been arrested after a boat that had an emergency responder on board was damaged in the English Channel,” the police said.



Tommo shared a video of his actions on social media. The chaotic scenes on French beaches this week included a rush of asylum seekers onto 10 boats on Wednesday alone, with authorities confirming that 781 people had made it to the UK. On Tuesday, 154 arrived on three boats. On Monday, 150 arrived on three boats. Related Article Immigration nation ‘You can’t put everything on immigration’: The suburbs at breaking point An English photographer captured footage on Wednesday of one asylum seeker wading through waves on a French beach to reach an inflatable boat while he carried a young child in a black outfit and fitted with a life vest. The video showed the child appeared to go limp after crashing through waves, and the asylum seeker chose to leave the child floating in the water alongside the boat and then tried to climb aboard the vessel.



French rescuers approached quickly to lift the child out of the water and place him or her on a surf-ski. One of the rescuers appeared to try to keep the man with the child, but he chose to stay with the other asylum seekers. World.title: Flawed reasons for a just outcome: Why Neale playing in the grand final is the right thing
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Opinion Flawed reasons for a just outcome: Why Neale playing in the grand final is the right thing Jake Niall Chief football writer, The Age September 24, 2026 — 9:55pm

September 24, 2026 — 9:55pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

From Wharfie Time to Country Roads, this is your one-stop shop for all things Fremantle and Brisbane in the lead-up to the grand final. See all stories . Loading

Lachie Neale did not deserve to miss the grand final for his less-than-forceful gut punch on Jack Ginnivan. The final outcome, which must rank among the most stunning and contentious in the annals of AFL judicial hearings, was just. Fremantle fans will not agree, and conspiracy theorists will enjoy speculating about the tendency for high-profile players to be cleared for grand finals, as though the overturning of the original verdict was preordained. Lachie Neale spoke to the media on Thursday night after having his one-match ban overturned on appeal. Nine News This is a case of questionable reasoning by the appeals tribunal that, nonetheless, has arrived at a fair outcome. Neale’s minor swinging punch on Ginnivan – call it a jog-by – was not an action that warranted the player missing the grand final. A flawed argument – based on improvisational application of elastic AFL rules – can, and did, arrive at the fair outcome.



The appeals board, comprised of three ex-player/lawyers and headed by Richard Loveridge, invoked the rule that allows for exceptional circumstances, in this case Neale’s record of zero suspensions over 320 games; the panel argued that the AFL tribunal, which upheld the match review officer’s original decision to suspend Neale for one match, had not given Neale’s record sufficient weight. Loading Downgrading the ban to a $10,000 fine was an unusual call, too. The player’s advocate, Adrian Anderson, had floated the notion that the suspension be served next year (when Neale will be a Collingwood player, we think). Those with memories of past grand final judicial cases will note that good players who are on the borderline of suspension are usually acquitted, one way or another. Andrew Dunkley had his three-match ban for belting James Hird (who sported a cut eye in his joint Brownlow Medal victory with Michael Voss) postponed three decades ago and won the chance to man Wayne Carey in the grand final. This was a flat out travesty – Dunkley should not have played via a court injunction.



Loading Another critical Swan, Barry Hall, had his match review verdict for a punch to Matt Maguire’s midriff – much more of a gut-wrenching blow than Neale’s – overturned in 2005 via the convenient argument that the punch had been “in play”, rather than off the ball. Hall was seen as lucky, and “big Bazza” did not have an unblemished record to fall back on. Related Article AFL grand final AFL grand final teams, expert tips: Is this Freo’s first premiership side, or will Lions get their three-peat? Carlton’s Aaron Hamill had his two-match suspension for kneeing Bomber Dean Wallis in that extraordinary 1999 preliminary final overturned via the appeals board. The biomechanics expert witness had worked his magic. Richmond skipper Trent Cotchin’s high bump on Dylan Shiel was given the all-clear by the match review panel (of three members then) in a judgment that players would have little hope of gaining in today’s more concussion-conscious times. Shiel was off for the remainder of the game. As with Hall, there was considerable sentiment around the team the skipper represented, and who were about to break lengthy premiership droughts.



The players who were not cleared in grand final week, such as Jason McCartney (1999) and Anthony Rocca (2003), were too far over the line to get leniency. Related Article Brisbane Lions Appeals board stunner: Neale free to play in the grand final, cops fine instead The original verdict of the MRO and upholding of the ban by the AFL tribunal were instances in which those bodies followed the rules that the league has outlined. The AFL, at the direction of football boss and immediate ex-Lions CEO Greg Swann, had instituted crackdown on punches to the body, such as Neale’s. The practical test – would you want someone to miss a grand final for that? – was conducted, and answered in the affirmative by the MRO (which consults the AFL bosses) and then the tribunal. The issue, thus, was not that the MRO or tribunal erred. They applied the rules at their disposal.



The underlying wrinkle was that the match review system leaves little room for shades of grey in the grading of offences. Neale’s advocate, Adrian Anderson, contended that there must be exceptions to the grading grid, the ex-AFL football boss so ironically having been the architect of the grading system back in the 2000s. Neale’s was deemed “medium force” and intentional, when the force was not at the level that deserved suspension, in round 15, let alone a grand final. Loading The appeals panel took a different stance. In effect, they viewed it with fresh eyes, as if it was a de novo case. The difference they found to the tribunal seems to derive from a view that Neale did not deserve to miss the grand final. A reason and rule were invoked to that end.



I had thought on Monday that Neale would be cleared by dint of his record, believing that the tribunal would not so strictly apply Swann’s handiwork and would find an exception for lucky Lachie. He was cleared, eventually. The footy gods smiled on the Lions, at least until Saturday. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: The US media boycott hit Trump right where it hurts. Now it’s Hanson’s turn
World.content:
PoliticsFederalPress freedom Opinion The US media boycott hit Trump right where it hurts. Now it’s Hanson’s turn Waleed Aly Columnist, author and academic September 25, 2026 — 3:30am

September 25, 2026 — 3:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Solidarity? In America? Among the media? It seems astonishing that anything quite so unified could grow from America’s famously polarised soil, but here we are, watching as such sworn enemies as Fox News and MS NOW stand in solidarity with each other, and against President Donald Trump’s latest attack on their craft. These are the paradigm cases of American media partisanship: Fox News often Trump’s cheer squad, MS NOW (formerly MSNBC) a kind of progressive riposte. Each symbolises everything the other hates. And yet this week, that was forgotten when Trump declared he was banning MS NOW, alongside CNN and Politico, from the White House, and deactivated their correspondents’ press passes. Illegally so, it turned out, and a court has just ordered they be reinstated. But in the meantime, Fox – alongside ABC, CBS and NBC – had boycotted Trump’s press conferences. Photo: Illustration: Dionne Gain Suddenly, Trump found himself at risk of greatly reduced television coverage in a week of addressing the UN and hosting Xi Jinping. Already, we’ve seen his team forced to capture their own footage of Trump arriving heroically to open the new White House helipad, the kind of thing that news cameras would have filmed. The feed was nigh unwatchable. There he was, saying words no one could hear, exuding exactly no authority. A Trump-shaped tree, falling in the forest. That sort of thing is unimaginable for someone like Trump, who loves and dominates television more than any president ever has. He is famously fixed to Fox News. He appoints its anchors to high office. In his first term, Trump staffers tried giving him briefings in the form of television packages because it was the best way to ensure he would pay attention. He amassed some US$4.6 billion ($6.5 billion) worth of free television coverage in the 2016 election campaign alone, about twice that of Hillary Clinton. He has effectively lived with a television camera on him since. A boycott of this kind hits Trump somewhere near where it hurts.



I’ll admit to being surprised by these developments. After all, Trump has berated the media for his whole premiership without provoking any solidaristic response. You’re familiar with the catchphrases: “the fake news media”, “the enemy of the people”, “corrupt” and “dishonest”. He has attacked individual journalists as “human scum” and “low-life reporters” and told one to be “quiet, piggy”. He has even banned individual reporters from the Pentagon and White House, most notably CNN’s Jim Acosta in 2018. And nothing. The difference this time was that he just went ahead and banned whole outlets. That has two consequences. First, it ends up costing the other outlets much more money because they often share footage, which allows them to operate with fewer resources. Cut two TV networks from the pool and you leave a big shortfall for the others to make up. But second, Trump did so explicitly because their “cumulative stories” led him to regard them as unfavourable. And whatever you think of those outlets, or even of the media in general, that’s an enormous move. Related Article Trump's White House Trump launches ‘Trump TV’ channel after networks boycott him To effectively demand favourable coverage in exchange for access is to undo the very concept of accountability. Trump’s answer to this charge hits all the typically populist notes, but it also had a slip within it: “I don’t have to let them into my … into the people’s house.” Trump seems to regard access as his to give personally. Then he corrects, and asserts it on behalf of the people. By now, some of this should sound familiar to the Australian ear. The pitch isn’t so heightened because Pauline Hanson is not prime minister. But she has taken the step of banning entire outlets from attending some of her press conferences. In this case, it’s the ABC (for whom I am a radio host) and The Guardian, and on the Victorian hustings, occasionally, The Age. The reasoning is also colourfully similar. “I answer to the people, not the media” declared Hanson in her National Press Club address in June.



Party director James Ashby said giving the ABC access would be like “going back to some domestic violence relationship” (Hanson’s views on such violence as a “two-way street” presumably don’t extend this far). The ban is patchy and Barnaby Joyce certainly seems exempt from it. But One Nation has pulled candidates from ABC slots where they were regulars until they joined the party. In short, Hanson has crossed a line the US media has decided not to accept. Might Australian journalists do the same? Could we see, for example, the Murdoch press – broadcast and print – stand on principle and say that if the ABC cannot attend a press conference, then they won’t either? I admit, it’s hard to imagine given the way the Murdoch media talks about the ABC, but is it any harder to imagine than it would have been for Fox News? TV channels take a stand against the ban by Donald Trump. Bloomberg So far in Australia, we’ve seen quiet disapproval from the outlets that aren’t banned, but nothing planting a flag on the ground of principle. We’ve seen the odd commentator say One Nation’s move is a bad political strategy because it becomes a controversy that distracts from the party’s message. For what it’s worth, I think this profoundly misreads the extent to which the strategy only heightens One Nation’s message. But so far, the tone is that it’s something a bit silly. Not a violation of anything serious. The idea of media solidarity, based not on a liking for each other but a belief in the concept of journalism, doesn’t seem to have occurred to anyone. Perhaps that would change if Hanson became prime minister. But by then, the principle at stake may have long since eroded. Trump and Hanson’s wars against the media work precisely because they tap into a rich vein of anti-media sentiment.



Related Article Opinion

Australian economy Barnaby Joyce is indeed not Jesus Christ. He doesn’t need to be Waleed Aly Columnist, author and academic In any conventional age, a politician complaining about the media would look petulant and self-obsessed. Today, their devotees lap up this sort of thing, like it strikes a blow for the common man against the elites. If media organisations want to let that slide, they can. But they should be careful it doesn’t slide away completely. Waleed Aly is a broadcaster, author, academic and regular columnist. The Opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: Local tattoo shop bracing for long night as Dockers fans chase inaugural premiership ink
World.content:
NationalWAAFL grand final Local tattoo shop bracing for long night as Dockers fans chase inaugural premiership ink Hannah Murphy September 25, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

From Wharfie Time to Country Roads, this is your one-stop shop for all things Fremantle and Brisbane in the lead-up to the grand final. See all stories .

A Fremantle tattoo shop is gearing up to work until punters stop coming through the door come Saturday afternoon, with a selection of Flagmantle designs on offer should the Dockers take home their inaugural premiership. Five Star Tattoo shop in Fremantle are ready for an influx of customers over grand final weekend. Hannah Murphy Five Star Tattoo is in the heart of the Fremantle cappuccino strip, and say they are equal parts concerned about the fanfare that could ensue following a Freo win against the Brisbane Lions on Saturday, and excited to host anyone who wishes to get some ink to mark the occasion. “We’re anticipating chaos, maybe either way - so who knows?” Five Star tattooist Mark said. “Fremantle’s going to be a different place, that’s for sure.”



Just some of the designs on offer. Hannah Murphy The shop is extending its hours and has already done a mock-up of several designs, ready for anyone who wants to make what Mark calls the “good decision” to get a tattoo. “We’ve got a sheet of designs done, ready to go - but of course we’ll be doing regular tattoo stuff, so taking walk-ins, appointments, whatever comes,” Mark said. Tattooists at the shop are ready for “chaos” whatever way the game goes. Hannah Murphy In the event of a loss, Mark said he’s still prepared for those to file through the door wanting to nail their colours to the mast after a bumper 2026 season - but remember, it’s cash only.



It’s a feeling echoed by other tattoo shops up and down the strip, with many looking to extend regular trading hours across the board to keep the crowds happy. A pop-up merchandise shop outside the Fremantle markets. Hannah Murphy Fremantle businesses are also gearing up for the “chaos” expected to reign on the port city come Saturday, with some choosing to extend hours to accommodate an influx of crowds and others rostering extra staff. Some shops have painted their front windows with Dockers memorabilia, with staff wearing Fremantle jumpers throughout the main strip of the town. Local businesses are turning their shops purple ahead of grand final eve. Hannah Murphy



One small business pop-up selling Fremantle merchandise outside the local markets sold out of most of its popular gear, and a memorial is going up on Main Street in the port city, curated and painted by street artists from Blank Walls. Blank Walls, a street-art studio set up in Perth and London, has painted across from the Piazza a mural featuring Caleb Serong, Alex Pearce, Murphy Reid and Andrew Brayshaw, which will be going up throughout Thursday and Friday. Authorities said they were planning on an extra 40,000 people to be roaming the streets in the event of a Dockers grand final, and earlier this month the City of Fremantle approved a budget amendment that would allow them to pull the trigger on $230,000 needed to accommodate the influx of visitors.

World.title: Pints and meat: The Wharfie Time effect on Freo’s pubs and WA butchers
World.content:
NationalFremantle Dockers Pints and meat: The Wharfie Time effect on Freo’s pubs and WA butchers Hamish Hastie September 25, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

What does 40,000 rowdy Dockers supporters flowing into the usually laid-back port city of Fremantle mean for one of its biggest pubs? Gage Roads at the A-Shed overlooking the working port has done the math and the estimates are eye watering. Gage Roads expects to pour 2000 of its Purple Reign pints on Saturday. Gage Roads owner Good Drinks Australia’s head of hospitality Miles Hull said they will sell about 1200 serves (or half a tonne) of chips, 1500 pizzas and 7000 pints – 2000 of which they expect will be their Purple Reign beer brewed especially for these finals. Hull said not only would a blowout over the Lions be the best for the town, but it would also be the best for sales.



“If it’s a nail-biter, no one wants to leave their seat or take their eyes off the game and people are caught up in the moment of the game and so it goes quiet at the bar,” he said. “On [the Friday of the elimination final against Geelong] you could track the state of the game by the bar sales. “The beer sales were really strong, but they slowed down in that last quarter and then picked up at the end of the game. “You could see that people were not as engaged halfway through the match because Freo were trailing and people found themselves a bit more time to get to the bar, but in the fourth quarter it was a different story. At least until after the game.” Police, the City of Fremantle and the state government are expecting a huge number of people to come to Fremantle to watch the game and party afterwards, with road closures in place in the CBD and four massive screens set up.



Tony Scarfo with his purple sausages. Scarfos Meating Place/Supplied A sold-out event is also being held at the Dockers’ spiritual home of South Fremantle Oval with thousands expected to attend. Karl Bullers, the owner of Fremantle institutions the Old Court House and the National Hotel, said he was expecting triple the normal Saturday sales. “People are just starting to realise just how big this is going to be, so we are over-ordering on everything because the last thing we want to be doing is run out of anything,” he said. Bullers has a ticketed event at the National, which sold out immediately. He said his pubs had been receiving calls asking whether they could camp out at 5.30am to secure a spot in front of their screens.



For those unable to get to Melbourne or want to avoid the chaos in Fremantle the humble backyard barbecue is shaping up as a popular choice. Butchers across the state have already reported an uptick in sales with most doing some form of purple sausage to commemorate the Dockers’ historic second grand final appearance. Tony Scarfo of Scarfos Meating Place in Myaree, east of Fremantle, has again whipped out the purple food colouring and expects to sell up to half a tonne of purple sausage by Saturday afternoon. “Over a week, you could push probably 400 to 500 kilos of actual purple ones,” he said. Scarfos became famous for the purple sausages back in 2013 ahead of the Dockers’ first grand final. They were devised through trial and error, but are simply barbecue beef sausages dipped in purple food colouring and water.



Plantagenet Meats purple chicken sausages. Plantagenet Meats/Supplied Scarfo said he expects his trade to be up 30 per cent on a normal week. Willetton butcher Nick Thomson expects his sales to pick up by about 20 per cent. Thomson is an Essendon fan, but most of his team are Dockers mad and have come up with a purple and white chicken and cheese sausage. Regionally, butcher shops are also experiencing a finals rush.



Willetton Butcher is serving purple and white chicken and cheese sausages. Willetton Butcher/Supplied Plantagenet Meats owner Josh Liebeck also sold purple sausages back in 2013, but it didn’t quite work. “We didn’t do the right sausage and we didn’t get the colours right so they went this horrible green colour,” he said. Liebeck added that they have now mastered the purple chicken sausage and expects sales could double over Thursday, Friday and Saturday. “It’s been a character building 32 years. Hopefully, we can come away with a win,” the long-suffering Dockers fan said.

World.title: Trump and Xi exchange pleasantries, pandas as White House lifts reporter ban
World.content:
Breaking WorldNorth AmericaForeign relations Trump and Xi exchange pleasantries, pandas as White House lifts reporter ban Michael Koziol Updated September 25, 2026 — 2:27am ,first published 12:28am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: News outlets CNN, MS NOW and Politico were allowed back into the White House after a judge ruled President Donald Trump’s ban on their entry was likely unconstitutional and must be temporarily lifted. But the outlets did not regain entry until about noon on Thursday (2am Friday AEST), after Trump and Xi Jinping began their high-stakes bilateral meeting on the Chinese leader’s first White House visit since 2015. There were no cameras from the main US television networks present as Trump welcomed Xi to the premises, with the news outlets continuing a boycott in solidarity with CNN. Xi’s arrival was broadcast on the White House’s official social media channel. A select group of print reporters and photographers, known as the daily “pool”, was present – along with Chinese state media.



Fox News was using an aerial shot of the White House and file footage when discussing the summit, while also covering other news stories. Phone footage from reporters in the pool showed there was a loud and sustained disagreement between the American photographers, Chinese photographers and the Secret Service about where the Chinese group could set up their cameras while awaiting Xi’s arrival. President Donald Trump and First Lady Melania Trump welcomed Chinese President Xi Jinping and his wife Peng Liyuan to the White House. AP Photo/Alex Brandon Judge Timothy Kelly ruled late on Wednesday (US time) that Trump’s ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico was likely unconstitutional, and blocked the White House from enforcing it for 14 days. But journalists from those the three outlets were still unable to access the White House on Thursday morning.



They lodged a request for an emergency hearing with the court. That request, seen by this masthead, said Secret Service agents had also “confiscated the hard passes of journalists whose hard passes had not previously been confiscated”. Trump had enacted the ban on Saturday due to his objections to the three outlets’ reporting, though he said there was no particular trigger for it other than his accusations of “fake news”. CNN reporter Betsy Klein regained access to the White House at about midday on Thursday. AP Photo/Alex Brandon But at about noon, reporters from the affected outlets regained access to the White House grounds. Their passes were reactivated while a bilateral meeting between Trump and Xi was already under way. Following the arrival ceremony, Trump and Xi delivered statements in the Grand Foyer of the White House, which were also broadcast on the White House’s official social media feed, but not on US television networks.



Trump noted there had been many physical changes at the White House since Xi’s last visit in 2015, and praised his “truly great friendship” with the Chinese leader. In relatively brief remarks, Trump spoke in broad terms about efforts to create “a more balanced trade relationship” between the world’s two largest economies, and doubled down on his attempt to rebrand artificial intelligence “super intelligence”. US President Donald Trump and China’s President Xi Jinping meet in the Oval Office. AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin “If we focus on our common interests, I am confident there is much we can achieve,” he said. Xi spoke for longer, and made numerous observations and recommendations about particular policy areas – including American market access for Chinese firms.



“China keeps its door wide open, welcomes American companies wanting to invest and do business there. We hope Chinese companies are treated fairly here in the United States,” he said. On AI, Xi said both countries had the capability and responsibility to ensure development was “always under human control” and served the wellbeing of people. Related Article Updated

Trump diplomacy ‘Partners, not rivals’: Xi Jinping lands in Washington with Trump waiting on the tarmac Both countries would gain from co-operation and lose from confrontation, he said. He once again invoked the Thucydides Trap, which describes the high risk of war when a rising power starts displacing an existing power. “The Thucydides Trap can be overcome,” Xi said. “China-US co-operation may not solve every problem in the world, but without our co-operation, it would be hard to solve many of the world’s problems.”



Xi raised the possibility of further co-operation on fentanyl, increasing direct flights between the two nations and his new invitation for 100,000 American students to undertake exchange in China over the next five years. Two Chinese pandas – male Ping Ping and female Fu Shuang – would also arrive at Zoo Atlanta shortly, Xi said, as part of China’s diplomacy efforts. Chinese President Xi Jinping said he hoped Chinese businesses would be treated fairly in the United States. Bloomberg “Achieving the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again can go hand in hand,” he said, a reference to Trump’s main political slogan. After the speeches, the leaders and their wives watched a US military review and flyover. Trump and Xi proceeded to a bilateral meeting, while the First Lady and Madam Peng travelled to the Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art.



On Thursday night, they will attend a state dinner organised by the First Lady. The menu, designed to showcase “American ingredients with subtle Chinese influence”, includes a yellow squash velouté with wild mushrooms, sesame crusted sea bass with baby bok choy and a vanilla crémeux with sour cherry confit centre. Entertainment will come from tenor Christopher Macchio, who performed at Trump’s 2025 inauguration. US President Donald Trump and China’s President Xi Jinping walk along the Colonnade of the White House. AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Asylum seekers trigger UK protests, arrests as 781 arrive in one day
World.content:
Breaking WorldEuropeAsylum seekers Asylum seekers trigger UK protests, arrests as 781 arrive in one day David Crowe September 25, 2026 — 2:09am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: Britain is engulfed in a new row over asylum seekers after 781 arrived in a single day on small boats in the English Channel, with video footage showing one man leaving a young child in the water in his scramble to board a boat. The surge triggered calls for a right-wing rally against migration despite UK government claims that it was curbing the influx, which has become one of the most potent and divisive issues in British national life. Protest organiser Danny Tommo was arrested after he sought to stop one of the inflatable boats by slashing it with a knife. YouTube One high-profile protest organiser, Danny Tommo, sought to stop one of the inflatable boats by slashing it with a knife while it had at least one person on board, escalating the confrontations off the English coast. British police arrested Tommo, whose real name is Daniel Thomas, on suspicion of destroying a boat and endangering personal safety, and kept him in custody.



When news emerged that he was detained in the English town of Basingstoke, right-wing activists including Tommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, called on social media on Thursday morning – about 11pm AEST – for supporters to gather at the town’s police station to demand his release. Robinson, who has gained support from billionaire Elon Musk when organising large rallies against migration, has described the small boat arrivals as an “invasion” and encouraged protests at hotels used to house the migrants. He has been convicted of assault in the past, and was jailed for seven months in 2024 for breaching a High Court injunction that banned him from repeating false claims about a Syrian refugee. Related Article Immigration Police injured as protesters descend on homes for asylum seekers in England On Thursday, amid the attention on the boat arrivals, Robinson also aired his support for Russia’s criticism of the West in the war in Ukraine. “The people are seeing through the whole ‘it’s Russias fault’ [sic] Western propaganda war machine,” he posted. He visited Moscow in June, when he met Musk’s father, Errol, in the Russian capital. The protests against asylum seekers increased over recent days when two small boats landed on English shores, avoiding the surveillance of UK Border Force in the busy channel.



Most of the small inflatable boats do not make it all the way across the channel because they are intercepted in open water by Border Force officers, who transfer them to UK vessels and take them to a detention centre at Dover. The arrival of the two dinghies on beaches near Portsmouth triggered demonstrations on Tuesday and led to the arrest of six people, three of whom were later charged. Hampshire police said they charged one woman, Shannon Dodds, 32, with two counts of assault for allegedly beating an emergency services worker. They charged another woman, Sally Pearson, 31, with a racially aggravated public order offence as well as assaulting an emergency worker. A man, Toby Matthews, 33, was also charged with assaulting an emergency worker. Police arrested Tommo on Wednesday night after he slashed the inflatable boat when at least one rescue worker remained on board, after the asylum seekers had been removed. “A man has been arrested after a boat that had an emergency responder on board was damaged in the English Channel,” the police said.



Tommo shared a video of his actions on social media. The chaotic scenes on French beaches this week included a rush of asylum seekers onto 10 boats on Wednesday alone, with authorities confirming that 781 people had made it to the UK. On Tuesday, 154 arrived on three boats. On Monday, 150 arrived on three boats. Related Article Immigration nation ‘You can’t put everything on immigration’: The suburbs at breaking point An English photographer captured footage on Wednesday of one asylum seeker wading through waves on a French beach to reach an inflatable boat while he carried a young child in a black outfit and fitted with a life vest. The video showed the child appeared to go limp after crashing through waves, and the asylum seeker chose to leave the child floating in the water alongside the boat and then tried to climb aboard the vessel.



French rescuers approached quickly to lift the child out of the water and place him or her on a surf-ski. One of the rescuers appeared to try to keep the man with the child, but he chose to stay with the other asylum seekers. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Flawed reasons for a just outcome: Why Neale playing in the grand final is the right thing
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Opinion Flawed reasons for a just outcome: Why Neale playing in the grand final is the right thing Jake Niall Chief football writer, The Age September 24, 2026 — 9:55pm

September 24, 2026 — 9:55pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

From Wharfie Time to Country Roads, this is your one-stop shop for all things Fremantle and Brisbane in the lead-up to the grand final. See all stories . Loading

Lachie Neale did not deserve to miss the grand final for his less-than-forceful gut punch on Jack Ginnivan. The final outcome, which must rank among the most stunning and contentious in the annals of AFL judicial hearings, was just. Fremantle fans will not agree, and conspiracy theorists will enjoy speculating about the tendency for high-profile players to be cleared for grand finals, as though the overturning of the original verdict was preordained. Lachie Neale spoke to the media on Thursday night after having his one-match ban overturned on appeal. Nine News This is a case of questionable reasoning by the appeals tribunal that, nonetheless, has arrived at a fair outcome. Neale’s minor swinging punch on Ginnivan – call it a jog-by – was not an action that warranted the player missing the grand final. A flawed argument – based on improvisational application of elastic AFL rules – can, and did, arrive at the fair outcome.



The appeals board, comprised of three ex-player/lawyers and headed by Richard Loveridge, invoked the rule that allows for exceptional circumstances, in this case Neale’s record of zero suspensions over 320 games; the panel argued that the AFL tribunal, which upheld the match review officer’s original decision to suspend Neale for one match, had not given Neale’s record sufficient weight. Loading Downgrading the ban to a $10,000 fine was an unusual call, too. The player’s advocate, Adrian Anderson, had floated the notion that the suspension be served next year (when Neale will be a Collingwood player, we think). Those with memories of past grand final judicial cases will note that good players who are on the borderline of suspension are usually acquitted, one way or another. Andrew Dunkley had his three-match ban for belting James Hird (who sported a cut eye in his joint Brownlow Medal victory with Michael Voss) postponed three decades ago and won the chance to man Wayne Carey in the grand final. This was a flat out travesty – Dunkley should not have played via a court injunction.



Loading Another critical Swan, Barry Hall, had his match review verdict for a punch to Matt Maguire’s midriff – much more of a gut-wrenching blow than Neale’s – overturned in 2005 via the convenient argument that the punch had been “in play”, rather than off the ball. Hall was seen as lucky, and “big Bazza” did not have an unblemished record to fall back on. Related Article AFL grand final AFL grand final teams, expert tips: Is this Freo’s first premiership side, or will Lions get their three-peat? Carlton’s Aaron Hamill had his two-match suspension for kneeing Bomber Dean Wallis in that extraordinary 1999 preliminary final overturned via the appeals board. The biomechanics expert witness had worked his magic. Richmond skipper Trent Cotchin’s high bump on Dylan Shiel was given the all-clear by the match review panel (of three members then) in a judgment that players would have little hope of gaining in today’s more concussion-conscious times. Shiel was off for the remainder of the game. As with Hall, there was considerable sentiment around the team the skipper represented, and who were about to break lengthy premiership droughts.



The players who were not cleared in grand final week, such as Jason McCartney (1999) and Anthony Rocca (2003), were too far over the line to get leniency. Related Article Brisbane Lions Appeals board stunner: Neale free to play in the grand final, cops fine instead The original verdict of the MRO and upholding of the ban by the AFL tribunal were instances in which those bodies followed the rules that the league has outlined. The AFL, at the direction of football boss and immediate ex-Lions CEO Greg Swann, had instituted crackdown on punches to the body, such as Neale’s. The practical test – would you want someone to miss a grand final for that? – was conducted, and answered in the affirmative by the MRO (which consults the AFL bosses) and then the tribunal. The issue, thus, was not that the MRO or tribunal erred. They applied the rules at their disposal.



The underlying wrinkle was that the match review system leaves little room for shades of grey in the grading of offences. Neale’s advocate, Adrian Anderson, contended that there must be exceptions to the grading grid, the ex-AFL football boss so ironically having been the architect of the grading system back in the 2000s. Neale’s was deemed “medium force” and intentional, when the force was not at the level that deserved suspension, in round 15, let alone a grand final. Loading The appeals panel took a different stance. In effect, they viewed it with fresh eyes, as if it was a de novo case. The difference they found to the tribunal seems to derive from a view that Neale did not deserve to miss the grand final. A reason and rule were invoked to that end.



I had thought on Monday that Neale would be cleared by dint of his record, believing that the tribunal would not so strictly apply Swann’s handiwork and would find an exception for lucky Lachie. He was cleared, eventually. The footy gods smiled on the Lions, at least until Saturday. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Family of man who fatally stabbed grandmother tried to get him mental health help
World.content:
Warning: This story contains content some may find disturbing.

The family of a man who stabbed his grandmother to death had been frustrated trying to get him mental health treatment, a coroner has found.

Two or three months had passed since Tremaine Hati was seen prior to the fatal attack on 72-year-old Maria Morgan on 15 March, 2023.

Now, Coroner Ian Telford has determined that public interest would be served by this being investigatied by the Health and Disability Commissioner.

The Health And Disability Commissioner is a Crown entity responsible for resolving complaints about infringements of health and disability rights.

Hati, who had serious and long-standing mental health problems, had been staying with his grandmother in Ngāruawāhia.

It was about 6.35pm on the night in question when Morgan's son and his daughter arrived for dinner, part of what was a weekly routine.

They left around 8.30pm, leaving Morgan and Hati alone.

Not long later, Hati's sister messaged Morgan regarding a call she'd had with the mental health crisis team concerning her brother.

"This was the latest in a number of communications to mental health services," Telford said, which reflected the family's growing concern about Hati's mental state.

About 9.15pm, Hati arrived at his sister's home, which was about 800 metres from Morgan's.

She noticed blood on his hands and abdomen and asked him what happened, but got no reply.

After asking a second time with no reply, she sent him inside to wash and called her mother, who suggested she contact police and the mental health crisis team.

After the call, she told Hati to get in the car and they drove to Morgan's, where she saw a bloodstained butcher's knife lying near the front entrance.

The front door was open and she saw Morgan lying on the floor with her head resting on a cupboard. She called out to her grandmother but got no response and called emergency services.

Police arrived shortly after and one arrested Hati, while another entered the home. The officer noticed Morgan slumped forward with her t-shirt saturated in blood.

Telford said it was immediately apparent she was dead.

Pathologist Dr S Stables said Morgan had been stabbed multiple times, with wounds to the chin, left side of the neck, left shoulder, left arm, left chest, left hand and upper central abdomen.

The deepest of these had penetrated her chest and had gone through her heart. This was identified as the fatal wound.

Hati was taken into custody and charged with murder.

The court found, on the balance of probabilities, he was unfit to stand trial because of his mental condition.

But the judge also found that he'd carried out the acts and ordered he be detained as a special patient.

Telford said Hati's first engagement with mental health services was his admission to a mental health unit in Whangarei in 2018 under the Compulsory Assessment and Treatment Act.

He reportedly responded well to treatment and was diagnosed with an unspecified psychotic disorder.

"After that he experienced a pattern of irregular but reasonably frequent admissions and readmissions, often involving compulsory assessment and treatment," Telford said.

It was in January 2023 when Hati moved to Ngāruawāhia to live with his grandmother.

"It seems clear from the evidence that, at this time, Mr Hati's compliance with his medication was sub-optimal and his behaviour was causing widespread concern to those around him.

"The family reported that their efforts to have Mr Hati seen by mental health services in the Waikato as frustrated and ultimately, he was not seen at the time of the offending, by which time two to three months had lapsed and during which he appears to have become increasingly unwell."

Telford said Health New Zealand did a "learning review" which appeared comprehensive and was done in good faith.

But, he said while the report clearly identified a number of issues and contributory factors, "it's less clear how those findings related to the actions taken following the event and to the recommendations arising from the review".

"I therefore appointed counsel to assist the inquiry by, in the first instance, reviewing the file and canvassing the views of whānau.

"Having considered those views, and the circumstances of the case, I concluded that the public interest would be best served by referring the matter to the Health and Disability Commissioner, particularly given the number of services involved and the interconnected nature of their involvement and decision-making."
